hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that Glutathione Disulfide Reductase (GSR) plays a crucial role in mitigating oxidative stress in Aminoacylase-1 deficiency by maintaining the reduced glutathione pool. In this disease, impaired amino acid metabolism leads to accumulation of toxic intermediates, causing oxidative damage. GSR, by reducing glutathione disulfide, helps to neutralize reactive oxygen species. We predict that GSR activity will be increased in cells from Aminoacylase-1 deficient patients as a compensatory mechanism. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through elevated GSR enzyme activity in patient-derived cells, while refutation would be seen if GSR activity is decreased or unchanged. This connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of glutathione metabolism and its role in protecting against oxidative stress.

We hypothesize that AKR1A1, an aldo-keto reductase, plays a crucial role in the development of Ethylmalonic encephalopathy by regulating the metabolism of short-chain fatty acids, particularly ethylmalonic acid. AKR1A1's reductive activity may mitigate toxic aldehyde accumulation, a known contributor to the disease. We predict that overexpression of AKR1A1 in patient-derived cells will decrease ethylmalonic acid levels and alleviate disease-associated phenotypes, whereas AKR1A1 inhibition will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant reduction in ethylmalonic acid levels and improved cellular viability in AKR1A1-overexpressing cells. Refutation would be evidenced by no change or worsening of disease phenotypes upon AKR1A1 modulation.

We hypothesize that NDUFA10, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in regulating the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in neutrophils, which is essential for the proper functioning of myeloperoxidase. In Myeloperoxidase deficiency, the impaired ROS production due to altered NDUFA10 function leads to reduced myeloperoxidase activity. We predict that overexpressing NDUFA10 in neutrophils from Myeloperoxidase deficiency patients will increase ROS production and partially restore myeloperoxidase activity. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased myeloperoxidase-mediated killing of pathogens in vitro, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in myeloperoxidase activity despite NDUFA10 overexpression.

We hypothesize that PPIP5K2, an enzyme involved in inositol phosphate metabolism, contributes to the pathogenesis of AICA-ribosuria due to ATIC deficiency. Specifically, PPIP5K2's product, 5-IP7, may inhibit the residual activity of ATIC, exacerbating the disease. We predict that overexpression of PPIP5K2 in cells with ATIC deficiency will increase AICA-riboside accumulation, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, PPIP5K2 knockdown will reduce AICA-riboside levels, refuting our hypothesis. This connection is grounded in the known biochemical link between inositol phosphate metabolism and purine biosynthesis, which ATIC regulates. Experimental validation of this hypothesis will provide insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying AICA-ribosuria and potential therapeutic targets.

We hypothesize that ribose-5-phosphate isomerase A (RPIA) plays a crucial role in the development of Leigh syndrome by impairing the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), leading to decreased NADPH production and increased oxidative stress. In Leigh syndrome, mitochondrial dysfunction disrupts energy metabolism, and we propose that RPIA's reduced activity exacerbates this imbalance. Specifically, we predict that RPIA knockdown in cellular models of Leigh syndrome will result in decreased NADPH levels and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, RPIA overexpression will rescue these phenotypes, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of the PPP and its role in maintaining redox balance, and is specifically relevant to Leigh syndrome due to its characteristic mitochondrial dysfunction.

We hypothesize that LIPT1, a key enzyme in lipoic acid synthesis, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Mucopolysaccharidosis 7 (MPS 7) by regulating the activity of mitochondrial enzymes involved in glycosaminoglycan (GAG) degradation. Specifically, we propose that LIPT1-derived lipoic acid is essential for the proper functioning of the beta-glucuronidase enzyme, which is deficient in MPS 7. We predict that overexpression of LIPT1 will increase beta-glucuronidase activity and reduce GAG accumulation in MPS 7 cells, whereas LIPT1 knockdown will exacerbate GAG accumulation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased GAG degradation in MPS 7 cells overexpressing LIPT1, while refutation would be shown by no change in GAG accumulation in response to LIPT1 modulation.

We hypothesize that GNPNAT1, a glucosamine-phosphate N-acetyltransferase, plays a crucial role in the biosynthesis of Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) by regulating the availability of precursors for its synthesis. Specifically, GNPNAT1's activity in the hexosamine biosynthesis pathway influences the production of UDP-N-acetylglucosamine, which in turn affects the expression of COQ6, a gene involved in CoQ10 biosynthesis. We predict that reduced GNPNAT1 activity will lead to decreased COQ6 expression, resulting in impaired CoQ10 production and contributing to primary Coenzyme Q10 deficiency, 6. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased COQ6 mRNA levels and reduced CoQ10 production in cells with GNPNAT1 knockdown, while refutation would be evident if GNPNAT1 inhibition does not affect COQ6 expression or CoQ10 levels.

We hypothesize that PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) regulates the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, which in turn modulates the expression of squalene synthase, an enzyme crucial for cholesterol biosynthesis. In Squalene synthase deficiency, impaired cholesterol production leads to accumulation of upstream intermediates. PTEN's lipid phosphatase activity may mitigate this accumulation by suppressing PI3K/Akt-mediated feedback inhibition of squalene synthase. We predict that PTEN overexpression will increase squalene synthase activity and alleviate disease symptoms, whereas PTEN inhibition will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased squalene synthase activity and improved cholesterol profiles in cells overexpressing PTEN, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or worsened disease phenotypes.

We hypothesize that NDUFS1, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Phosphohydroxylysinuria by regulating the mitochondrial membrane potential and thereby influencing the activity of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), an enzyme involved in gluconeogenesis. Impaired NDUFS1 function leads to decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, resulting in increased PEPCK activity and subsequent accumulation of phosphohydroxylysine. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of NDUFS1 in hepatic cells will increase phosphohydroxylysine levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFS1 will decrease phosphohydroxylysine levels, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial complex I and gluconeogenesis.

We hypothesize that NDUFA5, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Transaldolase deficiency. Specifically, we propose that impaired NDUFA5 function leads to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, which in turn damages the pentose phosphate pathway, where Transaldolase is a key enzyme. This damage disrupts the pathway's ability to regulate NADPH levels, exacerbating the disease. We predict that Transaldolase deficiency patients with NDUFA5 mutations will exhibit elevated ROS levels and decreased NADPH production. Confirmation would come from observing a significant correlation between NDUFA5 mutation severity and ROS/NADPH imbalance in patient samples. Refutation would occur if no such correlation is found, suggesting an alternative mechanism underlying Transaldolase deficiency.

We hypothesize that GLS2 (glutaminase 2) plays a crucial role in the development of Meconium ileus, a condition characterized by intestinal obstruction in newborns. Specifically, we propose that GLS2 regulates glutamine metabolism in intestinal epithelial cells, influencing the viscosity of meconium. Elevated GLS2 activity may lead to excessive glutamate production, altering the balance of intestinal mucins and resulting in abnormally thick meconium. We predict that GLS2 inhibition will reduce meconium viscosity in vitro, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if GLS2 inhibition has no effect on meconium viscosity, our hypothesis will be refuted. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of glutaminase enzymes and their role in regulating amino acid metabolism.

We hypothesize that VNN2 (vanin-2) contributes to the pathogenesis of Glutathione synthetase deficiency by regulating the cellular levels of cysteine, a crucial precursor for glutathione synthesis. VNN2 catalyzes the conversion of cysteine to cysteine sulfinate, reducing cysteine availability for glutathione production. In Glutathione synthetase deficiency, this VNN2-mediated cysteine depletion exacerbates the already impaired glutathione synthesis. We predict that inhibiting VNN2 will increase cysteine levels and partially restore glutathione production in cells from Glutathione synthetase deficiency patients. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased glutathione levels in patient cells treated with a VNN2 inhibitor, while refutation would be shown by no change in glutathione levels upon VNN2 inhibition.

terminal_shown: Cerebellar ataxia, deafness, and narcolepsy, autosomal dominant
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that NDUFB1, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Cerebellar ataxia, deafness, and narcolepsy, autosomal dominant. Specifically, we propose that mutations in NDUFB1 lead to impaired mitochondrial complex I function, resulting in decreased ATP production and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in affected tissues. This, in turn, disrupts the function of cerebellar Purkinje cells, auditory hair cells, and hypothalamic neurons, contributing to the disease phenotype. We predict that patients with this disease will exhibit decreased complex I activity and increased ROS levels in affected tissues, which can be confirmed by biochemical assays and refuted by normal complex I activity and ROS levels.

We hypothesize that glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD, also known as GLA) plays a crucial role in the development of Dyskinesia, limb and orofacial, infantile-onset. Specifically, we propose that reduced GLA activity leads to impaired GABA synthesis, disrupting the balance between excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission in the brain. This imbalance causes abnormal motor control, resulting in dyskinetic movements. We predict that infants with this disease will have lower GLA enzyme activity and decreased GABA levels in the brain. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that GLA enzyme replacement or GABA supplementation alleviates dyskinetic symptoms, while refutation would come from experiments demonstrating no correlation between GLA activity and disease severity.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities, and seizures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ALAS1, the enzyme responsible for the first step in heme biosynthesis, plays a crucial role in the development of Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities, and seizures. Specifically, we propose that decreased ALAS1 activity leads to impaired heme production, disrupting the function of heme-dependent enzymes involved in neuronal development and synaptic transmission. This disruption results in the characteristic symptoms of the disorder. We predict that patients with this disorder will have reduced ALAS1 expression and heme levels in the brain, which can be confirmed by measuring ALAS1 mRNA and heme concentrations in patient brain tissue. Refutation of this hypothesis would be provided by normal ALAS1 expression and heme levels in affected individuals.

We hypothesize that PRKACA, the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A, plays a crucial role in the development of Temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome through aberrant regulation of Indian hedgehog (Ihh) signaling in chondrocytes. Specifically, we propose that PRKACA hyperactivity leads to excessive phosphorylation and activation of protein kinase A targets, disrupting the normal balance of Ihh signaling and resulting in impaired chondrocyte differentiation and bone growth. We predict that inhibition of PRKACA will restore normal Ihh signaling and rescue the brachydactyly phenotype in vitro. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced phosphorylation of protein kinase A targets and improved chondrocyte differentiation in response to PRKACA inhibition, while failure to rescue the phenotype would refute it.

We hypothesize that SPHK2, by phosphorylating sphingosine to produce sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), contributes to the development of Cardiomyopathy, dilated, 1GG. Specifically, elevated SPHK2 activity in cardiac myocytes leads to increased S1P production, which in turn activates S1P receptors, promoting pathological cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis. We predict that inhibition of SPHK2 will reduce S1P levels, decrease cardiac myocyte size, and improve cardiac function in models of Cardiomyopathy, dilated, 1GG. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved cardiac function and reduced fibrosis in SPHK2-inhibited models, while refutation would be shown by no significant changes in cardiac function or pathology despite SPHK2 inhibition.

We hypothesize that ETHE1, a mitochondrial sulfur dioxygenase, plays a crucial role in the development of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, kyphoscoliotic type, 1, by regulating the sulfuration status of collagen proteins. Specifically, we propose that ETHE1 deficiency leads to impaired sulfuration of collagen, resulting in its misfolding and reduced stability. This, in turn, disrupts the structural integrity of connective tissue, contributing to the characteristic kyphoscoliosis and joint hypermobility of the disease. We predict that experimental reduction of ETHE1 activity in fibroblasts will result in decreased collagen sulfuration and increased collagen degradation, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, ETHE1 overexpression will rescue collagen stability, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed.

We hypothesize that SOS1, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, contributes to the development of Encephalopathy, porphyria-related, by modulating the activity of the heme biosynthetic pathway. Specifically, SOS1 regulates the Ras signaling pathway, which in turn affects the expression of aminolevulinic acid synthase 1 (ALAS1), a key enzyme in heme synthesis. Elevated ALAS1 activity leads to increased production of toxic heme intermediates, causing neurotoxicity and encephalopathy in porphyria patients. We predict that SOS1 inhibition will decrease ALAS1 expression and alleviate encephalopathy symptoms in porphyria models. Confirmation would come from reduced ALAS1 levels and improved neurological function in SOS1-inhibited porphyria models, while refutation would be demonstrated by unchanged or worsened symptoms.

terminal_shown: Vertebral, cardiac, renal, and limb defects syndrome 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ceramide kinase (CERK) plays a crucial role in the development of Vertebral, cardiac, renal, and limb defects syndrome 2 (VCRRLS2) by regulating sphingolipid metabolism in embryonic tissues. Specifically, CERK's phosphorylation of ceramides to ceramide-1-phosphate modulates the activity of key signaling pathways involved in tissue morphogenesis. We predict that CERK deficiency or inhibition will lead to altered ceramide-1-phosphate levels, disrupting normal tissue development and resulting in VCRRLS2-like phenotypes. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from observing rescue of VCRRLS2-like defects in CERK-deficient embryos via exogenous ceramide-1-phosphate supplementation, while refutation would result from failure to observe such rescue or from identifying alternative, CERK-independent mechanisms underlying VCRRLS2 pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that YARS2, a mitochondrial tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase, plays a crucial role in the regulation of mitochondrial translation and function, which is connected to Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1) deficiency. Specifically, impaired YARS2 activity leads to defective mitochondrial translation, resulting in decreased CPS1 protein levels and activity. We predict that YARS2 overexpression will increase CPS1 protein levels and alleviate the metabolic defects associated with CPS1 deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased CPS1 activity and improved urea cycle function in cells overexpressing YARS2. Refutation would be shown by no change in CPS1 activity or urea cycle function despite YARS2 overexpression.

We hypothesize that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) plays a crucial role in the development of Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy limb-girdle C7 by regulating the O-linked glycosylation of α-dystroglycan. Specifically, ASNS-derived asparagine is essential for the synthesis of glycosyltransferase substrates, which in turn modify α-dystroglycan. We predict that ASNS overexpression will increase α-dystroglycan glycosylation, leading to improved muscle function in Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy limb-girdle C7 models. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased muscle strength and reduced pathology in ASNS-overexpressing mice. Refutation would be shown by unchanged or worsened muscle function in these models, indicating that ASNS does not play a significant role in α-dystroglycan glycosylation or disease pathology.

We hypothesize that ARAF (A-Raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase) plays a role in the regulation of Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) activity through the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway. Specifically, ARAF-mediated activation of ERK may phosphorylate and inhibit PAH, leading to decreased phenylalanine hydroxylation and contributing to Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of ARAF will increase PAH activity and reduce phenylalanine levels in cells from patients with Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased PAH activity and decreased phenylalanine levels in ARAF-knockdown cells, while refutation would be shown by no change in PAH activity or phenylalanine levels. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of the MAPK/ERK pathway and its role in regulating enzyme activity.

We hypothesize that ENTPD2, an ectonucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase, contributes to the pathogenesis of Pyruvate dehydrogenase E1-alpha deficiency by regulating ATP levels, which in turn affect the energy-intensive process of pyruvate dehydrogenation. Specifically, reduced ENTPD2 activity leads to increased ATP levels, inhibiting the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of ENTPD2 in patient-derived cells will result in decreased pyruvate dehydrogenase activity, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of ENTPD2 will increase pyruvate dehydrogenase activity, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of energy metabolism and nucleotide regulation.

We hypothesize that Sucrose Isomaltase (SI) contributes to the development of Portal hypertension, non-cirrhotic, 1, through its role in glucose metabolism and subsequent effects on vascular endothelial function. Specifically, SI's enzymatic activity leads to increased glucose uptake in intestinal endothelial cells, promoting the production of endothelin-1, a potent vasoconstrictor. This, in turn, increases vascular resistance in the portal vein, contributing to portal hypertension. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of SI in intestinal endothelial cells will reduce endothelin-1 production and alleviate portal pressure in a non-cirrhotic portal hypertension model. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant decrease in portal pressure, while refutation would be indicated by no change in portal pressure following SI knockdown.

We hypothesize that the enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase (AGA) plays a crucial role in the development of Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP) by modulating the degradation of glycosaminoglycans in the endoplasmic reticulum. Specifically, impaired AGA activity leads to accumulation of sulfated glycosaminoglycans, which in turn disrupts the proper folding and function of uroporphyrinogen III synthase, a key enzyme in the heme biosynthesis pathway. We predict that AGA deficiency will result in increased levels of uroporphyrin I, a hallmark of CEP. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating a significant increase in uroporphyrin I levels in cells with AGA knockdown, while refutation would be achieved by showing no effect on uroporphyrin I levels despite AGA deficiency.

We hypothesize that D-glucuronyl enzyme (DGLUCY) is mechanistically connected to Pentosuria through its role in glucuronic acid metabolism. In Pentosuria, the deficiency of L-xylulose reductase leads to accumulation of L-xylulose. DGLUCY, involved in glucuronic acid production, may interact with this pathway. We predict that increased DGLUCY activity will exacerbate L-xylulose accumulation, worsening Pentosuria symptoms. Confirmation would come from experiments showing that DGLUCY inhibition reduces L-xylulose levels in Pentosuria patients. Refutation would occur if DGLUCY inhibition has no effect on L-xylulose accumulation, indicating a distinct pathway. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of glucuronic acid and pentose metabolism, and specifically addresses the metabolic imbalance in Pentosuria.

We hypothesize that HAO2 (hydroxyacid oxidase 2) contributes to the development of Inosine triphosphate pyrophosphohydrolase deficiency by modulating the purine nucleotide metabolism pathway. Specifically, HAO2's peroxisomal localization and role in glyoxylate detoxification may influence the availability of precursors for inosine triphosphate (ITP) synthesis. We predict that HAO2 overexpression will decrease ITP levels, exacerbating the deficiency, whereas HAO2 knockdown will increase ITP levels, alleviating the deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased ITP pyrophosphohydrolase activity in cells overexpressing HAO2, while refutation would be seen if HAO2 modulation has no effect on ITP levels or ITP pyrophosphohydrolase activity.

We hypothesize that Adenosine Kinase (ADK) plays a crucial role in the development of Visceral neuropathy, familial, 1, autosomal recessive, by regulating adenosine levels in the enteric nervous system. Elevated ADK activity leads to decreased adenosine, disrupting its neuroprotective effects and causing neuronal damage. We predict that ADK inhibition will reduce disease severity, confirmed by improved neuronal function in patient-derived enteric nervous system cells. Conversely, ADK overexpression will exacerbate neuropathy, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanism is grounded in adenosine's known role in neuroprotection and ADK's regulation of adenosine levels, providing a testable link between ADK and Visceral neuropathy, familial, 1, autosomal recessive.

We hypothesize that the enzyme HYI (hydroxylamine imine oxidoreductase) plays a crucial role in the development of 3-ketothiolase deficiency by modulating the levels of 3-ketoacyl-CoA, a substrate for 3-ketothiolase. Specifically, HYI's activity on hydroxylamine-containing compounds may indirectly influence the production of 3-ketoacyl-CoA, thereby affecting the flux through the 3-ketothiolase-catalyzed reaction. We predict that overexpression of HYI will lead to decreased 3-ketothiolase activity, resulting in elevated 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA levels, a hallmark of 3-ketothiolase deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by measuring increased 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA levels in cells overexpressing HYI, while refutation would be demonstrated by unchanged or decreased levels.

We hypothesize that ATP6V1FP2, a V-ATPase assembly factor, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS) by regulating cholesterol trafficking in the endolysosomal system. In SLOS, mutations in the DHCR7 gene impair cholesterol synthesis, leading to accumulation of 7-dehydrocholesterol. We propose that ATP6V1FP2-mediated acidification of endolysosomes is essential for proper cholesterol transport and metabolism. If ATP6V1FP2 function is compromised, cholesterol accumulation will exacerbate, worsening SLOS symptoms. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating increased 7-dehydrocholesterol levels in cells with ATP6V1FP2 knockdown, while refutation would involve showing no effect on cholesterol metabolism in ATP6V1FP2-deficient cells.

terminal_shown: Polycystic liver disease 3 with or without kidney cysts
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that BRCA1, a tumor suppressor enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Polycystic liver disease 3 with or without kidney cysts through its regulation of hepatocyte cell cycle and DNA damage response. Specifically, BRCA1's deficiency or dysfunction leads to aberrant cell proliferation and cyst formation in the liver and kidneys. We predict that BRCA1's interaction with the PKHD1 gene, which is mutated in Polycystic liver disease 3, disrupts the normal functioning of primary cilia, leading to cystogenesis. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the presence of BRCA1-PKHD1 protein complexes in hepatocytes and the rescue of cystic phenotypes by BRCA1 overexpression in PKHD1-mutant cells. Refutation would be shown by the lack of BRCA1-PKHD1 interaction and no effect of BRCA1 overexpression on cyst formation.

We hypothesize that B3GALT6, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Glutathione synthetase deficiency by modifying the glycosylation pattern of glutathione synthetase, thereby affecting its stability and activity. Specifically, we propose that B3GALT6-mediated glycosylation enhances the interaction between glutathione synthetase and its chaperone proteins, facilitating proper folding and function. We predict that overexpression of B3GALT6 will increase glutathione synthetase activity in cells, while its knockdown will decrease activity, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if B3GALT6 overexpression has no effect on glutathione synthetase activity, our hypothesis will be refuted. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known importance of glycosylation in protein function and stability, and its dysregulation in various diseases, including metabolic disorders like Glutathione synthetase deficiency.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and cortical atrophy
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ASAH1, an acid ceramidase, plays a crucial role in Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and cortical atrophy by regulating ceramide levels in neuronal cells. Elevated ceramides can induce apoptosis and disrupt neuronal development. We propose that ASAH1 deficiency leads to ceramide accumulation, triggering a pro-apoptotic cascade that impairs neurogenesis and contributes to microcephaly and cortical atrophy. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating increased ceramide levels and enhanced apoptosis in ASAH1-deficient neuronal cells. Refutation would require showing no significant changes in ceramide levels or neuronal viability upon ASAH1 inhibition. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of ceramide metabolism and its impact on cellular survival and development.

We hypothesize that phosphopantothenoylcysteine decarboxylase (PPCDC) plays a crucial role in the development of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 89 (DEE89) through its involvement in coenzyme A (CoA) biosynthesis. Impaired PPCDC activity may lead to decreased CoA levels, disrupting mitochondrial energy metabolism and increasing oxidative stress. This, in turn, may contribute to the neurodevelopmental abnormalities and seizures characteristic of DEE89. We predict that PPCDC deficiency will result in decreased CoA levels and increased oxidative stress in patient-derived cells. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experimental evidence showing decreased CoA levels and increased oxidative stress markers in DEE89 patient cells, while refutation would be provided by normal CoA levels and oxidative stress profiles despite PPCDC deficiency.

We hypothesize that hexose phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) plays a crucial role in the development of Spastic paraplegia 64, autosomal recessive, by regulating the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) in neurons. H6PD's impairment leads to decreased NADPH production, affecting lipid synthesis and antioxidant defenses. This disruption specifically impairs the function of the SPG64 protein, causing axonal degeneration. We predict that H6PD deficiency will increase oxidative stress and decrease neuronal lipid synthesis in SPG64 patient-derived cells. Confirmation would come from observing increased lipid peroxidation and decreased fatty acid synthesis in these cells upon H6PD knockdown. Refutation would occur if H6PD overexpression fails to rescue the axonal degeneration phenotype in SPG64 models.

We hypothesize that CSGALNACT2, a glycosyltransferase, plays a crucial role in the development of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2N, by aberrantly glycosylating axonal proteins, disrupting axonal transport and stability. Specifically, we propose that CSGALNACT2-mediated glycosylation of neurofilament proteins alters their interaction with motor proteins, leading to impaired axonal transport and subsequent axonal degeneration. We predict that inhibition of CSGALNACT2 will reduce axonal degeneration in vitro, confirmed by decreased neurofilament accumulation and improved axonal transport. Conversely, overexpression of CSGALNACT2 will exacerbate axonal degeneration, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of glycosyltransferases and their role in modifying protein function and interactions.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 4
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that TMEM86A, a transmembrane enzyme, plays a crucial role in regulating mitochondrial complex I assembly by interacting with NDUFS4, a nuclear-encoded subunit of complex I. Specifically, TMEM86A facilitates the proper folding and targeting of NDUFS4 to the mitochondrial inner membrane. In Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 4, mutations in NDUFS4 disrupt this interaction, leading to impaired complex I assembly and function. We predict that overexpressing TMEM86A in cells with NDUFS4 mutations will rescue complex I activity, whereas knocking down TMEM86A will exacerbate the deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would require co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrating a physical interaction between TMEM86A and NDUFS4, and functional assays showing restored complex I activity upon TMEM86A overexpression.

We hypothesize that the Fragile Histidine Triad (FHIT) enzyme plays a crucial role in the development of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 71 (DEE71) through its regulation of the purine metabolism pathway. Specifically, FHIT's tumor suppressor function is impaired, leading to altered adenine and guanine nucleotide pools, which in turn disrupt neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity. We predict that FHIT deficiency will result in increased AMP/ATP ratios, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of FHIT or supplementation with adenine nucleotides will rescue the DEE71 phenotype, refuting our hypothesis if no improvement is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in FHIT's known role in purine metabolism and its impact on cellular energy homeostasis.

terminal_shown: Triokinase and FMN cyclase deficiency syndrome
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that the ND5 enzyme, a subunit of NADH dehydrogenase in mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the regulation of cellular energy metabolism, which is disrupted in Triokinase and FMN cyclase deficiency syndrome. Specifically, we propose that ND5-mediated electron transport chain activity influences the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which in turn affects the activity of triokinase and FMN cyclase enzymes. We predict that overexpression of ND5 will increase ROS production, leading to decreased activity of triokinase and FMN cyclase, thereby exacerbating the syndrome's symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased triokinase and FMN cyclase activity in cells overexpressing ND5, while refutation would be seen if ND5 overexpression has no effect on these enzyme activities.

We hypothesize that glucokinase (GK) plays a crucial role in the development of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis 11 (ALS11) by regulating glucose metabolism in motor neurons. Specifically, GK's activity in modulating glycolytic flux affects the production of neurotoxic intermediates, such as advanced glycosylation end-products (AGEs). Elevated AGEs levels can lead to oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, contributing to motor neuron degeneration in ALS11. We predict that overexpressing GK in motor neurons will reduce AGEs accumulation and slow disease progression, whereas GK inhibition will exacerbate it. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved motor function and reduced AGEs levels in GK-overexpressing ALS11 models, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or worsened disease outcomes.

We hypothesize that CDS1 (CDP-diacylglycerol--inositol 3-phosphatidyltransferase), an enzyme involved in phosphatidylinositol biosynthesis, plays a crucial role in the development of Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Specifically, we propose that CDS1 regulates the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, which is often hyperactivated in HCC. Elevated CDS1 activity leads to increased phosphatidylinositol production, enhancing PI3K/AKT signaling and promoting cell proliferation and survival. We predict that CDS1 overexpression in HCC cells will increase AKT phosphorylation, while CDS1 inhibition will reduce AKT activation and suppress tumor growth. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experimental evidence showing a direct correlation between CDS1 expression and AKT activation in HCC tissues, while refutation would be demonstrated by the lack of such correlation.

We hypothesize that PLCG1 (phospholipase C gamma 1) plays a crucial role in the development of Combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria (CMAMMA) by regulating the expression of ACSF3, a key enzyme involved in the metabolism of malonyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-CoA. Specifically, PLCG1-mediated signaling pathways modulate ACSF3 activity, leading to impaired metabolism of these intermediates and subsequent accumulation of malonic and methylmalonic acids. We predict that PLCG1 inhibition will decrease ACSF3 expression and exacerbate CMAMMA symptoms, whereas PLCG1 activation will increase ACSF3 expression and alleviate symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experimental evidence showing a direct correlation between PLCG1 activity and ACSF3 expression in CMAMMA patient cells. Refutation would be provided by evidence showing no effect of PLCG1 modulation on ACSF3 expression or CMAMMA symptoms.

We hypothesize that NDUFS4, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Juvenile arthritis by regulating mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in immune cells. Specifically, we propose that reduced NDUFS4 expression leads to increased ROS production, activating the NF-κB pathway and promoting pro-inflammatory cytokine release. This, in turn, contributes to joint inflammation and damage characteristic of Juvenile arthritis. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of NDUFS4 in immune cells will increase ROS production and enhance NF-κB activation, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFS4 will reduce ROS production and alleviate inflammation, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of mitochondrial dysfunction in immune cell regulation and the involvement of ROS in inflammatory signaling pathways.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 7
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that HIBADH (3-hydroxyisobutyrate dehydrogenase) plays a crucial role in the development of Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 7, by regulating the metabolism of valine, a branched-chain amino acid. Specifically, impaired HIBADH activity leads to the accumulation of 3-hydroxyisobutyrate, which inhibits the activity of mitochondrial complex I. We predict that overexpressing HIBADH in cells from patients with Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 7, will restore complex I activity and reduce 3-hydroxyisobutyrate levels. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased complex I activity and decreased 3-hydroxyisobutyrate levels in treated cells, while refutation would be shown by no change in complex I activity or 3-hydroxyisobutyrate levels.

We hypothesize that ACER3, an alkaline ceramidase, plays a crucial role in the development of Erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva 4 (EKVP4) by regulating ceramide metabolism in the skin. Specifically, we propose that reduced ACER3 activity leads to accumulation of ceramides, disrupting the skin's barrier function and causing the characteristic erythematous and hyperkeratotic lesions of EKVP4. We predict that EKVP4 patients will exhibit decreased ACER3 expression and activity in affected skin tissues, which can be confirmed by immunohistochemistry and enzymatic assays. Conversely, refutation of this hypothesis would be supported by normal ACER3 expression and activity in EKVP4 skin tissues, suggesting an alternative disease mechanism.

We hypothesize that JAG1 (Jagged1) enzyme plays a crucial role in the development of Mucopolysaccharidosis 3A (MPS IIIA) by regulating the expression of heparan sulfate-degrading enzymes. Specifically, JAG1 modulates the Notch signaling pathway, which in turn affects the transcription of SGSH, the gene encoding the enzyme deficient in MPS IIIA. We predict that overexpression of JAG1 will lead to increased SGSH expression and subsequent reduction in heparan sulfate accumulation, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, JAG1 knockdown will exacerbate heparan sulfate storage, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of Notch signaling in regulating gene expression and the biochemical link between heparan sulfate degradation and MPS IIIA pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that TOP2A, a DNA topoisomerase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Neuronopathy, distal hereditary motor, X-linked. Specifically, we propose that TOP2A's dysregulation leads to aberrant DNA topology, disrupting the expression of genes essential for motor neuron function. This disruption triggers a cascade of events, ultimately resulting in the degeneration of motor neurons characteristic of the disease. We predict that inhibiting TOP2A activity will exacerbate motor neuron degeneration, while TOP2A overexpression will mitigate it. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased motor neuron survival in TOP2A-overexpressing models, while refutation would be shown by no significant difference in motor neuron survival between TOP2A-inhibited and control models. This hypothesis is grounded in TOP2A's known role in maintaining genomic stability and regulating gene expression.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 4
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that MTM1 (myotubularin 1) plays a crucial role in regulating mitochondrial complex I assembly by dephosphorylating and activating a key assembly factor. Specifically, MTM1 dephosphorylates and activates ACAD9, a protein involved in complex I biogenesis. This activation enhances complex I assembly, thereby maintaining mitochondrial function. We predict that MTM1 deficiency will lead to decreased ACAD9 activity, resulting in impaired complex I assembly and contributing to Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 4. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced complex I activity and decreased ACAD9 phosphorylation in cells with MTM1 knockdown. Refutation would be shown by unchanged complex I activity and ACAD9 phosphorylation in MTM1-deficient cells.

We hypothesize that Pyruvate Carboxylase (PC) plays a crucial role in the development of Spastic paraplegia 26, autosomal recessive, by regulating the metabolism of oxaloacetate, a key intermediate in the citric acid cycle. Specifically, PC's impairment leads to decreased oxaloacetate production, disrupting the malonyl-CoA synthesis pathway, which is essential for fatty acid synthesis and myelin maintenance. We predict that PC deficiency will result in reduced myelin lipid synthesis, leading to axonal damage and spastic paraplegia. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased malonyl-CoA levels and impaired myelin lipid profiles in patient-derived cells. Refutation would be evident if PC overexpression fails to rescue myelin defects in patient-derived cells or if alternative metabolic pathways compensate for PC deficiency.

We hypothesize that thymidylate synthase (TYMS) contributes to the pathogenesis of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, dominant intermediate C, by impairing mitochondrial nucleotide pools. Specifically, TYMS dysfunction leads to altered dTTP levels, disrupting mitochondrial DNA replication and repair. This results in mitochondrial dysfunction, a known contributor to Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. We predict that TYMS overexpression in neuronal cells will exacerbate mitochondrial abnormalities, confirmed by decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased oxidative stress. Conversely, TYMS inhibition will rescue these defects. Refutation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by unchanged mitochondrial function in TYMS-modulated neuronal cells. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of TYMS and its role in nucleotide metabolism, and provides a testable link between TYMS and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, dominant intermediate C.

We hypothesize that phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PEMT) plays a crucial role in the development of Spastic paraplegia 39, autosomal recessive, by regulating the synthesis of phosphatidylcholine in the nervous system. PEMT's activity affects the methylation of phosphatidylethanolamine, influencing membrane lipid composition and axonal integrity. We predict that reduced PEMT activity will lead to decreased phosphatidylcholine levels, disrupting axonal function and contributing to the disease's spastic paraplegia phenotype. Confirmation would come from observing decreased phosphatidylcholine levels in patient-derived neurons with mutated PEMT, while refutation would result from finding no correlation between PEMT activity and phosphatidylcholine levels in these cells. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of PEMT and its role in lipid metabolism.

We hypothesize that CYP2A13, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Lenz-Majewski hyperostotic dwarfism by aberrantly metabolizing a specific osteogenic signaling molecule, leading to enhanced bone growth and hyperostosis. Specifically, we propose that CYP2A13 dysregulation results in altered metabolism of Indian hedgehog (Ihh) signaling pathway intermediates, disrupting normal bone homeostasis. We predict that experimental inhibition of CYP2A13 in Lenz-Majewski hyperostotic dwarfism patient-derived cells will decrease Ihh pathway activity and subsequent bone growth, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of CYP2A13 will enhance Ihh signaling and bone growth, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of CYP2A13 in metabolizing signaling molecules and the established link between Ihh signaling and bone development.

We hypothesize that FGF2 (fibroblast growth factor 2) contributes to the development of Leukoencephalopathy, porphyria-related, by disrupting heme biosynthesis. FGF2 stimulates the expression of aminolevulinic acid synthase 1 (ALAS1), the rate-limiting enzyme in heme production. Elevated ALAS1 activity leads to increased levels of toxic heme intermediates, which accumulate in the brain and cause damage to white matter, characteristic of Leukoencephalopathy. We predict that inhibiting FGF2 signaling will reduce ALAS1 expression and alleviate disease symptoms. Confirmation would come from experiments showing decreased ALAS1 activity and improved neurological function in porphyria models treated with FGF2 inhibitors. Refutation would result from failure to observe these effects, indicating an alternative mechanism underlying the disease.

We hypothesize that gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCT) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency by regulating the carboxylation of glutamate residues in proteins involved in the mitochondrial transport of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA. Impaired GGCT activity leads to defective protein function, resulting in reduced mitochondrial uptake of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA and subsequent accumulation of toxic intermediates. We predict that GGCT overexpression will increase mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA uptake and alleviate disease symptoms, whereas GGCT inhibition will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA uptake in cells overexpressing GGCT, while refutation would be shown by no change in uptake in GGCT-overexpressing cells.

We hypothesize that CYP2R1, a vitamin D 25-hydroxylase, plays a crucial role in the development of Dyskinesia, limb and orofacial, infantile-onset. Specifically, we propose that impaired CYP2R1 activity leads to altered vitamin D metabolism, disrupting the regulation of calcium homeostasis in the brain. This, in turn, affects the development and function of basal ganglia circuits, contributing to the characteristic involuntary movements of Dyskinesia. We predict that patients with infantile-onset Dyskinesia will exhibit reduced CYP2R1 expression and decreased 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. Confirmation would come from observing a significant correlation between CYP2R1 expression and disease severity, while refutation would result from finding no difference in CYP2R1 activity or vitamin D levels between affected and unaffected individuals.

We hypothesize that IDO2 (indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 2) contributes to the pathogenesis of Platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase deficiency by modulating the kynurenine pathway, leading to increased production of neurotoxic metabolites. Specifically, IDO2's catabolism of tryptophan to kynurenine disrupts the balance of platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase substrates, exacerbating the disease. We predict that IDO2 inhibition will decrease kynurenine levels and alleviate disease symptoms, whereas IDO2 overexpression will worsen symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced disease severity in IDO2 knockout models, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in disease symptoms upon IDO2 modulation.

We hypothesize that AGPAT1, an enzyme involved in triglyceride and phospholipid biosynthesis, contributes to the pathogenesis of Aspartylglucosaminuria by modulating the lipid composition of lysosomal membranes. Specifically, we propose that AGPAT1's activity affects the membrane fluidity and stability, thereby influencing the proper functioning of the aspartylglucosaminidase enzyme, which is deficient in Aspartylglucosaminuria. We predict that overexpression of AGPAT1 will exacerbate the disease phenotype, leading to increased accumulation of aspartylglucosamine in cells. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased aspartylglucosamine levels in cells overexpressing AGPAT1, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in aspartylglucosamine levels upon AGPAT1 overexpression.

We hypothesize that ACSS3, an enzyme involved in acetate metabolism, contributes to the development of Tumoral calcinosis, hyperphosphatemic, familial, 3 by regulating the production of acetyl-CoA, a key precursor for lipid synthesis and energy metabolism. In this disease, mutations in genes involved in phosphate homeostasis lead to hyperphosphatemia, which may alter ACSS3 activity. We predict that increased ACSS3 activity will enhance acetyl-CoA production, leading to increased lipid synthesis and subsequent formation of calcified lesions. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased ACSS3 expression and activity in patient-derived cells, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased ACSS3 activity in these cells.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 3
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that PLPP4, a phospholipid phosphatase, plays a crucial role in regulating mitochondrial membrane phospholipid composition, which is essential for the proper assembly and function of Mitochondrial complex IV. Specifically, we propose that PLPP4 modulates the levels of phosphatidic acid, a key phospholipid, to facilitate the interaction between COX4I1 and other subunits of Mitochondrial complex IV. We predict that overexpression of PLPP4 will increase complex IV activity in cells with nuclear type 3 Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, while PLPP4 knockdown will exacerbate the deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased COX4I1 complex formation and enhanced complex IV activity in PLPP4-overexpressing cells, whereas refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased complex IV activity.

terminal_shown: Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that glucokinase (GCK) plays a crucial role in the development of Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay. GCK regulates glucose metabolism, and its dysfunction may lead to impaired energy production in mitochondria. We propose that reduced GCK activity disrupts the glucose-pyruvate axis, resulting in decreased pyruvate uptake by mitochondria, thereby impairing the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. This would confirm our hypothesis if experimental results show that GCK knockdown in muscle cells leads to decreased mitochondrial ATP production and increased oxidative stress. Conversely, our hypothesis would be refuted if GCK overexpression in these cells fails to rescue mitochondrial function and energy metabolism.

We hypothesize that cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH) plays a crucial role in the development of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 84 (DEE84) through its regulation of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) production. CTH catalyzes the conversion of cystathionine to cysteine, producing H2S as a byproduct. We propose that altered CTH activity leads to disrupted H2S signaling, affecting neuronal excitability and contributing to DEE84. Specifically, we predict that CTH overexpression will increase H2S production, exacerbating DEE84 symptoms, while CTH inhibition will reduce H2S levels, alleviating symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased H2S levels in DEE84 patient samples, while refutation would be shown by unchanged H2S levels despite CTH modulation.

We hypothesize that Fibroblast growth factor 1 carboxy-terminal stretch kinase (FCSK) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) by regulating the activity of arylsulfatase A (ARSA), the enzyme deficient in MLD. Specifically, FCSK phosphorylates and activates ARSA, enhancing its ability to break down sulfatides. We predict that FCSK overexpression will increase ARSA activity and reduce sulfatide accumulation in MLD patient-derived cells. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased ARSA activity and decreased sulfatide levels in cells overexpressing FCSK. Refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased ARSA activity in response to FCSK overexpression, indicating an alternative mechanism underlying MLD pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that the mechanistic target of rapamycin (MTOR) enzyme plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Congenital disorder of glycosylation 2T (CDG2T) by regulating the biosynthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins. Specifically, MTOR's modulation of the unfolded protein response (UPR) pathway affects the expression of genes involved in GPI-anchor biosynthesis, leading to impaired protein glycosylation. We predict that MTOR inhibition will increase GPI-anchor biosynthesis and alleviate CDG2T symptoms, whereas MTOR activation will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased GPI-anchored protein expression in CDG2T patient cells treated with MTOR inhibitors, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased expression.

We hypothesize that Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) contributes to the development of Polymicrogyria, bilateral temporooccipital, through its role in regulating neuroinflammation and neuronal migration. Specifically, TNF-induced activation of the NF-κB pathway disrupts the normal migration of neurons during cortical development, leading to the formation of abnormal gyri. We predict that inhibition of TNF signaling will reduce the severity of polymicrogyria in a mouse model of the disease, as measured by decreased cortical folding abnormalities. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by a significant reduction in cortical folding defects in TNF-inhibited mice, while refutation would be indicated by no change in disease severity. This hypothesis is grounded in the known role of TNF in neuroinflammation and the importance of NF-κB signaling in neuronal development.

We hypothesize that PSTK (phosphoseryl-tRNA kinase) plays a crucial role in the development of Parkinson disease through its involvement in mitochondrial translation and function. Specifically, we propose that PSTK's activity in phosphorylating seryl-tRNA is essential for the proper translation of mitochondrial genes, and its dysregulation leads to impaired mitochondrial function, a known contributor to Parkinson disease pathogenesis. We predict that PSTK overexpression will rescue mitochondrial dysfunction in Parkinson disease models, whereas its knockdown will exacerbate the disease phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved motor function and reduced neurodegeneration in PSTK-overexpressing Parkinson disease models, while refutation would be shown by no significant effect on disease progression.

We hypothesize that kynurenine monooxygenase (KMO) contributes to the pathogenesis of Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase medium-chain deficiency by modulating the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in mitochondria. In this disease, impaired fatty acid oxidation leads to accumulation of medium-chain acyl-CoAs, which can disrupt mitochondrial function. KMO, involved in tryptophan catabolism, generates 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, a precursor to ROS-producing quinolinic acid. We predict that KMO inhibition will reduce ROS production and alleviate disease symptoms, whereas KMO overexpression will exacerbate them. Confirmation would come from decreased ROS levels and improved mitochondrial function in patient-derived cells treated with KMO inhibitors, while refutation would be demonstrated by unchanged or worsened symptoms in response to KMO modulation.

We hypothesize that ALOX15B, an enzyme involved in lipid peroxidation, contributes to the pathogenesis of Ethylmalonic encephalopathy by modulating the levels of toxic short-chain fatty acids. Specifically, ALOX15B's activity on polyunsaturated fatty acids may lead to the formation of reactive aldehydes, which can accumulate and exacerbate the disease's characteristic mitochondrial dysfunction. We predict that inhibition of ALOX15B will reduce the levels of these toxic metabolites and alleviate disease symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased ethylmalonic acid levels in patient-derived cells treated with ALOX15B inhibitors. Refutation would be shown by unchanged or increased ethylmalonic acid levels, indicating an alternative disease mechanism.

We hypothesize that ALDH2 (aldehyde dehydrogenase 2) plays a crucial role in mitigating the toxic effects of sulfite accumulation in Sulfite oxidase deficiency, isolated. In this disease, the deficiency of sulfite oxidase leads to sulfite buildup. ALDH2, known for its role in detoxifying aldehydes, may also facilitate the oxidation of sulfite to sulfate, thereby reducing its toxicity. We predict that overexpression of ALDH2 in cells from patients with Sulfite oxidase deficiency, isolated will decrease sulfite levels and alleviate disease symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant reduction in sulfite levels and improvement in clinical outcomes in response to ALDH2 overexpression. Refutation would occur if ALDH2 overexpression fails to decrease sulfite levels or improve disease symptoms.

We hypothesize that methionine synthase (MTR) plays a crucial role in the development of Retinitis pigmentosa 17 (RP17) through its impact on homocysteine metabolism and subsequent effects on photoreceptor cell health. Specifically, MTR's role in converting homocysteine to methionine is essential for maintaining low homocysteine levels, which can be toxic to photoreceptor cells. We predict that reduced MTR activity will lead to elevated homocysteine levels, causing oxidative stress and apoptosis in photoreceptor cells, thereby contributing to RP17. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that MTR knockdown in photoreceptor cells increases homocysteine levels and enhances cell death, while refutation would come from experiments demonstrating no significant effect of MTR knockdown on homocysteine levels or photoreceptor cell viability.

We hypothesize that NAMPT (Nicotinamide Phosphoribosyltransferase) plays a crucial role in the development of Ethylmalonic encephalopathy by regulating the biosynthesis of NAD+ in the brain. Impaired NAD+ production due to decreased NAMPT activity may lead to mitochondrial dysfunction, resulting in the accumulation of toxic metabolites, such as ethylmalonic acid. We predict that NAMPT overexpression in patient-derived cells will decrease ethylmalonic acid levels, confirming this hypothesis. Conversely, NAMPT inhibition will increase ethylmalonic acid levels, refuting it. This hypothesis is grounded in the known role of NAMPT in NAD+ biosynthesis and the established link between mitochondrial dysfunction and Ethylmalonic encephalopathy. Experimental validation of this hypothesis could provide new insights into the disease mechanism and potential therapeutic strategies.

We hypothesize that UGT2B11, a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, plays a crucial role in the metabolism of 7-dehydrocholesterol, a precursor to cholesterol, in Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome. Specifically, we propose that UGT2B11 glucuronidates 7-dehydrocholesterol, enhancing its excretion and reducing its accumulation. We predict that overexpression of UGT2B11 in cells from Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome patients will decrease 7-dehydrocholesterol levels and alleviate disease symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant reduction in 7-dehydrocholesterol levels in patient cells overexpressing UGT2B11. Refutation would occur if UGT2B11 overexpression has no effect on 7-dehydrocholesterol levels or disease symptoms. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of UGT2B11 and the pathophysiology of Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, where 7-dehydrocholesterol accumulation is a hallmark of the disease.

terminal_shown: Severe combined immunodeficiency autosomal recessive T-cell-negative/B-cell-negative/NK-cell-negative due to adenosine deaminase deficiency
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CYP1B1, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, contributes to the pathogenesis of Severe combined immunodeficiency autosomal recessive T-cell-negative/B-cell-negative/NK-cell-negative due to adenosine deaminase deficiency. Specifically, CYP1B1 metabolizes toxic adenosine and deoxyadenosine levels, which accumulate in adenosine deaminase deficiency. Elevated levels of these metabolites can lead to lymphocyte toxicity. We predict that CYP1B1 overexpression will reduce toxic metabolite levels and alleviate lymphocyte toxicity in adenosine deaminase-deficient cells. Confirmation would come from experiments showing increased lymphocyte survival and reduced metabolite levels in CYP1B1-overexpressing cells. Refutation would occur if CYP1B1 overexpression fails to reduce metabolite levels or improve lymphocyte survival, indicating a lack of mechanistic connection between CYP1B1 and adenosine deaminase deficiency.

We hypothesize that Purine Nucleoside Phosphorylase (PNP) plays a crucial role in the development of Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 12 (COXPD12) by regulating the nucleotide pool available for mitochondrial DNA replication. Specifically, PNP's imbalance in nucleoside metabolism leads to impaired mtDNA replication, causing COXPD12. We predict that PNP overexpression will exacerbate COXPD12 symptoms, while PNP inhibition will alleviate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through increased mtDNA copy numbers and improved oxidative phosphorylation efficiency in COXPD12 cells treated with PNP inhibitors. Refutation would occur if PNP modulation has no effect on mtDNA replication or COXPD12 symptoms. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of PNP and its role in nucleotide metabolism, and provides a testable mechanism for COXPD12 pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that COQ3, a methyltransferase involved in coenzyme Q biosynthesis, contributes to the development of Hyperuricemia, HPRT-related, by modulating the purine nucleotide cycle. Specifically, COQ3's role in maintaining coenzyme Q levels affects the activity of xanthine oxidoreductase, an enzyme involved in uric acid production. We predict that COQ3 overexpression will increase xanthine oxidoreductase activity, leading to elevated uric acid levels in HPRT-deficient cells. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased uric acid production in HPRT-deficient cells overexpressing COQ3, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in uric acid levels. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemical links between coenzyme Q, xanthine oxidoreductase, and purine metabolism.

We hypothesize that ALG1, a mannosyltransferase involved in N-glycosylation, plays a crucial role in the development of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2N. Specifically, we propose that ALG1's dysfunction leads to impaired glycosylation of peripheral nerve proteins, disrupting axonal transport and stability. This results in axonal degeneration, a hallmark of the disease. We predict that ALG1 knockdown in neuronal cells will lead to reduced glycosylation of neurofilament proteins and increased axonal fragmentation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased neurofilament glycosylation and increased axonal damage in ALG1-knockdown cells. Refutation would be shown by unchanged neurofilament glycosylation and axonal integrity despite ALG1 knockdown.

We hypothesize that COASY (Coenzyme A synthase) plays a crucial role in the development of Adrenal hyperplasia 3 by regulating the biosynthesis of coenzyme A (CoA), a essential cofactor for steroid hormone production. Specifically, we propose that decreased COASY activity leads to impaired CoA production, disrupting the normal functioning of 17,20-desmolase, an enzyme involved in the conversion of pregnenolone to dehydroepiandrosterone. This disruption results in the accumulation of pregnenolone, leading to an overproduction of androgens and ultimately contributing to the development of Adrenal hyperplasia 3. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating decreased COASY activity and CoA levels in adrenal tissues of individuals with Adrenal hyperplasia 3, while refutation would be achieved by showing no significant difference in COASY activity or CoA levels between affected and unaffected individuals.

We hypothesize that the enzyme Dihydrolipoyllysine-residue succinyltransferase (DLST) plays a crucial role in the development of Breast cancer through its involvement in the regulation of cellular energy metabolism. Specifically, DLST's role in the Krebs cycle affects the production of alpha-ketoglutarate, a key regulator of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1α), which promotes angiogenesis and tumor growth in Breast cancer. We predict that DLST overexpression will increase HIF1α levels, leading to enhanced tumor growth, whereas DLST inhibition will decrease HIF1α levels, resulting in reduced tumor growth. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased tumor growth in DLST-overexpressing Breast cancer cells, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in tumor growth in response to DLST modulation.

terminal_shown: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that Quinolinate Phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT) plays a crucial role in the development of Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC) by modulating the pentose phosphate pathway and subsequently affecting cellular energy metabolism. Specifically, altered QPRT activity leads to impaired NAD+ biosynthesis, resulting in increased susceptibility to oxidative stress and genomic instability. We predict that QPRT overexpression in HLRCC cells will decrease oxidative stress and slow tumor growth, whereas QPRT inhibition will exacerbate oxidative damage and promote tumor progression. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased tumor growth in QPRT-overexpressing HLRCC cells, while refutation would be shown by no significant difference in tumor growth between QPRT-overexpressing and control cells.

terminal_shown: Severe combined immunodeficiency autosomal recessive T-cell-negative/B-cell-negative/NK-cell-negative due to adenosine deaminase deficiency
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that LPCAT2, an enzyme involved in lipid metabolism, contributes to the pathogenesis of Severe combined immunodeficiency autosomal recessive T-cell-negative/B-cell-negative/NK-cell-negative due to adenosine deaminase deficiency. Specifically, LPCAT2's role in generating phospholipid species may impact membrane fluidity and signaling in immune cells. In adenosine deaminase deficiency, toxic metabolites accumulate, potentially disrupting LPCAT2 activity and lipid metabolism. We predict that LPCAT2 inhibition will exacerbate immune cell dysfunction in adenosine deaminase-deficient cells, confirmed by increased apoptosis and impaired cell signaling. Conversely, LPCAT2 overexpression will mitigate toxicity, refuting our hypothesis if no improvement is observed. This mechanistic connection highlights a potential link between lipid metabolism and purine metabolism in immune cell function.

We hypothesize that MOGAT1, a monoacylglycerol O-acyltransferase, plays a crucial role in the development of 46,XY sex reversal 8 by disrupting the balance of lipid metabolism in gonadal tissues. Specifically, MOGAT1's dysregulation leads to altered diacylglycerol and triacylglycerol levels, affecting the expression of genes involved in testis development, such as SOX9. We predict that MOGAT1 overexpression in 46,XY gonadal tissues will result in reduced SOX9 expression and subsequent testicular dysgenesis, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, MOGAT1 inhibition will rescue SOX9 expression and testis development, refuting our hypothesis. This prediction can be tested through in vitro experiments using MOGAT1-overexpressing or -inhibiting cell lines derived from 46,XY gonadal tissues.

We hypothesize that PIK3C2A, a class II phosphoinositide 3-kinase, plays a crucial role in the development of CLAPO syndrome by regulating lipid metabolism and membrane trafficking in the liver. Specifically, we propose that PIK3C2A's kinase activity modulates the formation of phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) on liver cell membranes, affecting the recruitment of lipid droplet-associated proteins. This, in turn, disrupts lipid storage and secretion, leading to the characteristic hepatomegaly and dyslipidemia observed in CLAPO syndrome. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that PIK3C2A knockdown or inhibition in liver cells increases lipid droplet accumulation and alters PI3P levels. Refutation would result from experiments demonstrating no effect of PIK3C2A modulation on lipid metabolism in CLAPO syndrome patient-derived liver cells.

We hypothesize that CEPT1, a choline/ethanolamine phosphotransferase, contributes to Orthostatic hypotension 1 by regulating the synthesis of phosphatidylcholine, a key component of vascular endothelial cell membranes. Reduced CEPT1 activity may lead to altered phospholipid composition, disrupting endothelial function and nitric oxide production, ultimately impairing blood vessel relaxation and contributing to orthostatic hypotension. We predict that CEPT1 knockdown in endothelial cells will decrease phosphatidylcholine synthesis and nitric oxide production, confirming this hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of CEPT1 will increase phosphatidylcholine synthesis and nitric oxide production, refuting the hypothesis. This mechanism is grounded in the known role of phosphatidylcholine in maintaining endothelial cell membrane structure and function.

We hypothesize that N-acetylglucosamine kinase (NAGK) contributes to the development of gastric cancer by regulating the O-GlcNAcylation of key proteins involved in cell proliferation and survival. Specifically, NAGK's activity in the hexosamine biosynthesis pathway leads to increased UDP-GlcNAc production, which in turn enhances O-GlcNAcylation of proteins such as beta-catenin, promoting its nuclear translocation and subsequent activation of oncogenic transcription programs. We predict that NAGK overexpression in gastric cancer cells will correlate with increased beta-catenin O-GlcNAcylation and nuclear localization, which can be confirmed by immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence experiments. Conversely, NAGK inhibition will reduce beta-catenin O-GlcNAcylation and attenuate gastric cancer cell growth, refuting our hypothesis if no such effects are observed.

We hypothesize that DPM1, an enzyme involved in dolichol phosphate biosynthesis, plays a role in the pathogenesis of AICA-ribosuria due to ATIC deficiency. Specifically, we propose that DPM1's product, dolichol phosphate, affects the stability and activity of ATIC, an enzyme crucial for purine biosynthesis. We predict that overexpression of DPM1 will increase dolichol phosphate levels, leading to enhanced ATIC activity and reduced AICA-ribosuria symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased urinary AICA-riboside levels in ATIC-deficient cells overexpressing DPM1. Refutation would occur if DPM1 overexpression has no effect on ATIC activity or AICA-ribosuria symptoms, suggesting an alternative mechanism underlying the disease.

We hypothesize that COQ3, a methyltransferase involved in coenzyme Q biosynthesis, plays a crucial role in the development of Maple syrup urine disease 2 (MSUD2) by regulating the methylation status of key enzymes in the branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) catabolism pathway. Specifically, COQ3's methyltransferase activity affects the function of the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex (BCKDC), leading to impaired BCAA degradation and accumulation of toxic metabolites. We predict that COQ3 overexpression will rescue BCKDC activity and alleviate MSUD2 symptoms, whereas COQ3 inhibition will exacerbate the disease phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would require demonstration of COQ3-BCKDC interaction and methylation-dependent regulation of BCKDC activity in MSUD2 models. Refutation would involve failure to observe COQ3-BCKDC interaction or methylation-dependent effects on BCKDC activity.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 1
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CERS1 (ceramide synthase 1) plays a crucial role in the development of Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 1, by modulating the ceramide composition of mitochondrial membranes. Specifically, we propose that CERS1-generated ceramides disrupt the interaction between SDHA (succinate dehydrogenase subunit A) and SDHB (succinate dehydrogenase subunit B), leading to impaired complex II assembly and function. We predict that CERS1 inhibition will increase complex II activity in patient-derived cells, while CERS1 overexpression will decrease it. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing a significant increase in complex II activity upon CERS1 inhibition, whereas refutation would be indicated by no change in complex II activity despite CERS1 modulation.

We hypothesize that GADL1, a glutamate decarboxylase-like enzyme, contributes to the development of Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 5 by modulating the succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) pathway. Specifically, GADL1's enzymatic activity may lead to altered succinate levels, which in turn affect the SDHB subunit's function, a known susceptibility factor for this syndrome. We predict that overexpression of GADL1 in pheochromocytoma cells will increase succinate levels and decrease SDHB activity, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, GADL1 knockdown will decrease succinate levels and restore SDHB function, refuting our hypothesis. This proposed mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of the SDH pathway and its link to Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 5.

We hypothesize that HMOX1, the enzyme responsible for heme degradation, plays a crucial role in the development of Pontocerebellar hypoplasia 12 (PCH12) through its regulation of oxidative stress and mitochondrial function. Specifically, we propose that decreased HMOX1 activity leads to accumulation of toxic heme intermediates, causing mitochondrial dysfunction and subsequent impairment of neuronal development in the pontocerebellar region. We predict that experimental knockdown of HMOX1 in neuronal cells will result in increased oxidative stress and mitochondrial damage, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of HMOX1 will rescue these defects, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of heme metabolism and its impact on cellular redox balance.

We hypothesize that CYP2A6 plays a crucial role in the metabolism of malonic acid and methylmalonic acid by catalyzing the hydroxylation of these compounds, thereby facilitating their excretion. In Combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria, impaired CYP2A6 activity leads to the accumulation of these toxic metabolites. We predict that patients with this disease will have reduced CYP2A6 expression and activity, resulting in elevated levels of malonic and methylmalonic acid in urine and plasma. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating a significant correlation between CYP2A6 activity and metabolite levels in patient samples. Refutation would occur if CYP2A6 inhibition or knockout in cellular models fails to increase malonic and methylmalonic acid levels.

We hypothesize that DARS1, an aspartyl-tRNA synthetase, plays a crucial role in the regulation of N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS) expression by ensuring accurate translation of the NAGS mRNA. Impaired DARS1 function may lead to misfolded or truncated NAGS protein, contributing to N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency. We predict that DARS1 knockdown in hepatocytes will result in decreased NAGS enzyme activity, confirming this hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of DARS1 will rescue NAGS activity in cells with impaired DARS1 function, refuting the hypothesis if no effect is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the essential role of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases in maintaining protein homeostasis and the critical function of NAGS in the urea cycle.

We hypothesize that argininosuccinate synthase 1 (ASS1) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Maple syrup urine disease 1A (MSUD 1A) by regulating the availability of alpha-keto acids. In MSUD 1A, the deficiency of branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex leads to accumulation of branched-chain amino acids. ASS1, involved in the urea cycle, may interact with these alpha-keto acids, diverting them from toxic accumulation. We predict that ASS1 overexpression will reduce alpha-keto acid levels in MSUD 1A cells, confirming this hypothesis. Conversely, ASS1 inhibition will exacerbate alpha-keto acid accumulation, refuting it. This mechanistic connection highlights a potential therapeutic target for MSUD 1A, grounded in the known biochemistry of the urea cycle and branched-chain amino acid metabolism.

terminal_shown: Leukoencephalopathy, progressive, infantile-onset, with or without deafness
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that IL4I1, an L-amino acid oxidase, contributes to the pathogenesis of Leukoencephalopathy, progressive, infantile-onset, with or without deafness, by modulating the levels of neurotoxic amino acids in the brain. Specifically, IL4I1's enzymatic activity may lead to the accumulation of toxic metabolites, such as hydrogen peroxide, which damage oligodendrocytes and disrupt myelination. We predict that IL4I1 inhibition will reduce disease severity, as measured by decreased brain damage and improved myelination in a mouse model of the disease. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved neurological function and reduced oligodendrocyte damage in IL4I1-inhibited mice, while refutation would be shown by no significant difference in disease progression between IL4I1-inhibited and control mice.

We hypothesize that PLCD3, a phospholipase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR) deficiency by regulating the phospholipid composition of peroxisomal membranes.
