Specifically, PLCD3-mediated hydrolysis of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) affects the localization and activity of AMACR within peroxisomes. We predict that PLCD3 overexpression will exacerbate the metabolic defects associated with AMACR deficiency, leading to increased accumulation of branched-chain fatty acids. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased disease severity in AMACR-deficient cells overexpressing PLCD3, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in disease phenotype upon PLCD3 overexpression.

We hypothesize that UQCRQ, a subunit of the mitochondrial cytochrome b-c1 complex, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency. Specifically, impaired UQCRQ function leads to decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, resulting in reduced ATP production and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Elevated ROS levels, in turn, damage the glutamate formiminotransferase enzyme, exacerbating its deficiency. We predict that overexpressing UQCRQ in cells from patients with Glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency will restore mitochondrial function and reduce ROS production, thereby improving enzyme activity. Conversely, knocking down UQCRQ will worsen the deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved glutamate formiminotransferase activity in UQCRQ-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by no change in enzyme activity despite UQCRQ modulation.

We hypothesize that NAT8L, an enzyme involved in acetylation of cysteine residues, plays a role in the regulation of glycolytic enzyme activity, including triosephosphate isomerase (TPI). In Triosephosphate isomerase deficiency, a rare genetic disorder, TPI activity is impaired, leading to accumulation of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. We propose that NAT8L-mediated acetylation of TPI or other glycolytic enzymes modulates their activity, and that altered NAT8L expression or activity contributes to the disease pathology. Specifically, we predict that overexpression of NAT8L will increase TPI activity in cells from TPI-deficient patients, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, NAT8L knockdown will exacerbate the glycolytic defects, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection highlights a potential therapeutic target for TPI deficiency.

We hypothesize that Glycine N-methyltransferase (GNMT) plays a crucial role in regulating methionine metabolism, and its deficiency leads to an accumulation of S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe), which in turn disrupts the methylation of key metabolic enzymes. Specifically, we propose that GNMT deficiency impairs the methylation and activation of pyruvate kinase, a key enzyme in glycolysis, resulting in impaired glucose metabolism. We predict that GNMT-deficient cells will exhibit decreased pyruvate kinase activity and altered glucose metabolism, which can be confirmed by measuring pyruvate kinase activity and glucose uptake in GNMT-deficient cells. Refutation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by normal pyruvate kinase activity and glucose metabolism in GNMT-deficient cells.

We hypothesize that the MSH2 enzyme, involved in DNA mismatch repair, contributes to Gaucher disease 1 pathogenesis by modulating the expression of the GBA1 gene, which encodes the deficient enzyme in this disease. Specifically, MSH2 binds to the GBA1 gene promoter, influencing its transcription. We predict that MSH2 deficiency or dysfunction will lead to increased GBA1 expression, partially compensating for the enzyme deficiency in Gaucher disease 1. Confirmation would come from observing increased GBA1 mRNA and protein levels in cells with MSH2 knockdown. Refutation would result from unchanged or decreased GBA1 expression in response to MSH2 modulation. This hypothesis is grounded in the known roles of MSH2 in gene regulation and the genetic basis of Gaucher disease 1.

terminal_shown: Intellectual developmental disorder with or without peripheral neuropathy
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that PCK1, a key enzyme in gluconeogenesis, contributes to Intellectual developmental disorder with or without peripheral neuropathy by disrupting glucose metabolism in the brain. Specifically, PCK1's dysregulation leads to impaired glucose production, affecting neuronal energy homeostasis and synaptic function. We predict that PCK1 overexpression in neuronal cells will result in decreased glucose release and impaired cognitive function, whereas PCK1 inhibition will rescue these defects. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased glucose levels and impaired synaptic transmission in PCK1-overexpressing neurons, while refutation would be shown by unchanged glucose metabolism and cognitive function in PCK1-inhibited neurons. This mechanism is grounded in the known role of glucose metabolism in neuronal function and the established link between energy deficits and neurodevelopmental disorders.

We hypothesize that CYP2R1, a vitamin D 25-hydroxylase, plays a crucial role in regulating immune responses by modulating vitamin D levels, thereby influencing immune dysregulation, autoimmunity, and autoinflammation. Specifically, we propose that CYP2R1-mediated vitamin D activation suppresses the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and promotes regulatory T cell differentiation. We predict that CYP2R1 deficiency or inhibition will lead to decreased vitamin D levels, resulting in enhanced pro-inflammatory cytokine production and increased autoimmune responses. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased autoimmune symptoms in CYP2R1 knockout mice, while refutation would be shown by unchanged immune responses in these mice. This hypothesis is grounded in the known immunomodulatory effects of vitamin D and the role of CYP2R1 in its activation.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 3
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ERBB2, a receptor tyrosine kinase, contributes to Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 3, by modulating the expression of COX10, a gene essential for the assembly of mitochondrial complex IV. Specifically, ERBB2 activates the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, which in turn inhibits the transcription factor FOXO1, leading to reduced COX10 expression. We predict that overexpression of ERBB2 in cells will decrease COX10 mRNA levels and increase the severity of Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant decrease in COX10 expression in ERBB2-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by no change in COX10 expression or complex IV activity.

We hypothesize that CASP9 (caspase 9) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 20 (COXPD20) by regulating mitochondrial dynamics and apoptosis in response to oxidative stress. Specifically, we propose that CASP9 mediates the cleavage of mitochondrial fission factor MFF, leading to impaired mitochondrial fusion and increased oxidative phosphorylation defects. We predict that inhibition of CASP9 will reduce mitochondrial fragmentation and improve oxidative phosphorylation efficiency in COXPD20 patient cells. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased mitochondrial fragmentation and increased ATP production in COXPD20 cells treated with CASP9 inhibitors, whereas increased CASP9 activity would exacerbate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress.

We hypothesize that MPPE1, a metallophosphoesterase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Leukodystrophy, hypomyelinating, 10 (HLD10) by regulating the degradation of sphingomyelin in oligodendrocytes. Specifically, MPPE1 deficiency leads to accumulation of sphingomyelin, disrupting myelin lipid composition and impairing myelination. We predict that MPPE1 knockdown in oligodendrocytes will result in increased sphingomyelin levels and decreased myelin basic protein expression, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of MPPE1 will rescue myelination defects in HLD10 patient-derived cells, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed. This mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of sphingolipid metabolism and its importance in myelin maintenance.

We hypothesize that NDUFA9, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in regulating the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that impact the activity of 5-oxoprolinase, an enzyme involved in glutathione metabolism. Specifically, we propose that impaired NDUFA9 function leads to increased ROS production, which in turn oxidizes and inactivates 5-oxoprolinase, resulting in 5-oxoprolinase deficiency. We predict that overexpressing NDUFA9 in cells from patients with 5-oxoprolinase deficiency will decrease ROS levels and restore 5-oxoprolinase activity, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, knocking down NDUFA9 in healthy cells will increase ROS levels and decrease 5-oxoprolinase activity, refuting our hypothesis if no such effect is observed.

We hypothesize that NDUFS8, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Leber congenital amaurosis 13 (LCA13) by regulating the mitochondrial membrane potential in photoreceptor cells. Specifically, we propose that impaired NDUFS8 function disrupts complex I assembly, leading to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and subsequent damage to the photoreceptor cell mitochondria. We predict that overexpressing NDUFS8 in LCA13 patient-derived retinal cells will reduce ROS levels and improve mitochondrial function, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, knocking down NDUFS8 in healthy retinal cells will increase ROS levels and replicate the LCA13 phenotype, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial complex I and its role in maintaining mitochondrial membrane potential.

We hypothesize that Uridine Monophosphate Synthetase (UMPS) contributes to the development of Portal hypertension, non-cirrhotic, 1, through its role in pyrimidine metabolism. UMPS catalyzes the conversion of orotic acid to UMP, which is then converted to UDP and subsequently to UDP-glucuronic acid, a key component of glycosaminoglycans. We propose that altered UMPS activity leads to increased glycosaminoglycan production, enhancing hepatic stellate cell activation and extracellular matrix deposition, ultimately contributing to portal vein remodeling and increased resistance. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating increased UMPS expression and activity in non-cirrhotic portal hypertension patients, while refutation would involve showing no correlation between UMPS activity and disease severity.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, ataxia, and seizures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ELOVL5, an enzyme involved in fatty acid elongation, plays a crucial role in the development of Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, ataxia, and seizures. Specifically, we propose that ELOVL5 regulates the synthesis of very-long-chain fatty acids essential for brain lipid metabolism and neuronal function. Impaired ELOVL5 activity leads to altered lipid profiles, disrupting neuronal membrane structure and function, and ultimately contributing to the disease phenotype. We predict that patients with this disorder will exhibit reduced ELOVL5 expression and altered very-long-chain fatty acid profiles in brain tissue. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by identifying ELOVL5 mutations or decreased enzyme activity in patient samples, while refutation would be shown by normal ELOVL5 expression and fatty acid profiles in affected individuals.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that IP6K3, an inositol hexakisphosphate kinase, contributes to Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 2, by regulating mitochondrial inositol polyphosphate levels, which in turn affect the assembly and stability of complex I. Specifically, IP6K3-generated inositol pyrophosphates may interact with and modulate the activity of complex I assembly factors, such as NDUFAF1. We predict that IP6K3 overexpression will exacerbate complex I deficiency in nuclear type 2 patient-derived cells, while IP6K3 knockdown will rescue complex I activity. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing a significant increase in complex I activity upon IP6K3 knockdown, while refutation would be indicated by no change in complex I activity upon IP6K3 modulation.

We hypothesize that ELOVL2, an enzyme involved in fatty acid elongation, contributes to the development of Pentosuria through an imbalance in lipid metabolism. Specifically, ELOVL2's role in elongating very-long-chain fatty acids may interfere with the proper functioning of L-xylulose reductase, an enzyme necessary for L-xylulose metabolism. This interference could lead to the accumulation of L-xylulose, a hallmark of Pentosuria. We predict that overexpression of ELOVL2 in cells will result in increased L-xylulose levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibition of ELOVL2 will decrease L-xylulose accumulation, refuting our hypothesis. This proposed mechanism is grounded in the known biochemical pathways of fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism.

We hypothesize that TRX-CAT1-1, a specific thioredoxin glutathione reductase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Laurence-Moon syndrome by regulating the redox state of retinal cells. Specifically, we propose that TRX-CAT1-1 modulates the activity of retinal protein disulfide isomerase, affecting the proper folding and function of rhodopsin. We predict that overexpression of TRX-CAT1-1 in retinal cells will lead to increased rhodopsin misfolding and aggregation, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibition of TRX-CAT1-1 will reduce retinal cell oxidative stress and slow disease progression, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of thioredoxin systems and their role in maintaining protein homeostasis in the retina.

terminal_shown: Rhizomelic skeletal dysplasia with or without Pelger-Huet anomaly
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that the enzyme 1,4-alpha-glucan branching enzyme 1 (GBE1) plays a crucial role in the development of Rhizomelic skeletal dysplasia with or without Pelger-Huet anomaly. Specifically, we propose that GBE1's dysfunction leads to impaired glycogen synthesis, resulting in altered energy metabolism and subsequent disruption of chondrocyte function and bone development. We predict that patients with Rhizomelic skeletal dysplasia will exhibit reduced GBE1 activity and abnormal glycogen accumulation in affected tissues. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the presence of mutated GBE1 alleles and corresponding biochemical defects in patient samples, while refutation would be shown by the absence of GBE1 mutations or normal GBE1 activity in affected individuals.

We hypothesize that NDUFS8, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Meconium ileus, a condition characterized by intestinal obstruction in newborns. We propose that impaired NDUFS8 function leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, resulting in decreased ATP production and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) in intestinal epithelial cells. This, in turn, disrupts the normal mucus secretion and intestinal motility, contributing to the formation of inspissated meconium. We predict that experimental reduction of NDUFS8 expression in intestinal epithelial cells will increase ROS production and decrease ATP levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFS8 will rescue these defects, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial complex I and its role in maintaining cellular energy homeostasis.

We hypothesize that TALDO1, a key enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway, plays a crucial role in the development of Hypotonia-cystinuria syndrome. Specifically, we propose that impaired TALDO1 activity disrupts the balance of reducing equivalents, leading to oxidative stress and subsequent damage to the cystine transporter, SLC7A9. This damage impairs cystine reabsorption in the kidney, resulting in cystinuria. We predict that patients with Hypotonia-cystinuria syndrome will exhibit reduced TALDO1 activity and increased oxidative stress markers. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experimental results showing a significant correlation between TALDO1 activity and cystine transport in patient-derived kidney cells. Refutation would be provided by results showing no difference in TALDO1 activity or oxidative stress markers between patients and healthy controls.

We hypothesize that NADK2, the enzyme responsible for generating NADPH, plays a crucial role in mitigating oxidative stress in Adenylosuccinase deficiency. In this disease, impaired purine metabolism leads to accumulation of toxic intermediates, causing oxidative damage. NADK2-generated NADPH fuels antioxidant defenses, such as glutathione reduction. We predict that NADK2 overexpression will reduce oxidative stress markers in Adenylosuccinase-deficient cells, whereas NADK2 inhibition will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased levels of oxidized glutathione and increased activity of antioxidant enzymes in NADK2-overexpressing cells. Refutation would be evident if NADK2 modulation has no effect on oxidative stress markers, indicating an alternative mechanism underlying Adenylosuccinase deficiency pathology.

We hypothesize that FAHD1, a flavin-dependent dehydrogenase, plays a crucial role in regulating the metabolic pathway affected in Squalene synthase deficiency. Specifically, FAHD1 modulates the levels of farnesyl-CoA, a precursor for squalene synthesis, by oxidizing farnesal to farnesic acid, thereby reducing the substrate availability for squalene synthase. We predict that overexpression of FAHD1 will exacerbate the symptoms of Squalene synthase deficiency by further reducing squalene production, whereas inhibition of FAHD1 will alleviate the disease phenotype by increasing farnesyl-CoA availability. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased squalene levels in cells overexpressing FAHD1, while refutation would be shown by unchanged squalene levels despite FAHD1 overexpression.

We hypothesize that TRI-TAT2-2, a mitochondrial enzyme, plays a crucial role in the regulation of bile acid synthesis by modulating the transport of intermediates across the mitochondrial membrane. In Congenital bile acid synthesis defect 6, mutations in the AKR1D1 gene disrupt the normal bile acid synthesis pathway. We propose that TRI-TAT2-2 interacts with AKR1D1 to facilitate the transport of 3-oxo-Δ4-steroids, a critical step in bile acid synthesis. If TRI-TAT2-2 activity is impaired, bile acid synthesis will be disrupted, leading to the accumulation of toxic intermediates. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating reduced bile acid production and increased 3-oxo-Δ4-steroid levels in cells with impaired TRI-TAT2-2 activity. Refutation would involve showing no effect on bile acid synthesis or 3-oxo-Δ4-steroid levels in the absence of TRI-TAT2-2 activity.

We hypothesize that BCL2L11, a pro-apoptotic enzyme, contributes to the development of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, spondylodysplastic type, 2, by regulating the balance between cell survival and apoptosis in chondrocytes. Specifically, we propose that BCL2L11 modulates the mitochondrial pathway of apoptosis, leading to excessive chondrocyte death and impaired cartilage formation. We predict that overexpression of BCL2L11 in chondrocytes will result in increased apoptosis and cartilage defects, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibition of BCL2L11 will reduce apoptosis and improve cartilage formation, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanism is grounded in the known role of BCL2L11 in regulating apoptosis and the importance of chondrocyte survival in maintaining healthy cartilage.

We hypothesize that BPGM (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate mutase) plays a crucial role in the development of Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 57 (COXPD57) by regulating the glycolytic pathway's intersection with mitochondrial energy metabolism. Specifically, BPGM's activity modulates the levels of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which in turn affects the binding of glycolytic enzymes to the mitochondrial outer membrane, influencing the supply of reducing equivalents to the electron transport chain. We predict that COXPD57 patients will exhibit decreased BPGM activity, leading to impaired glycolytic-mitochondrial crosstalk. Confirmation would come from measuring decreased BPGM activity in COXPD57 patient samples, while refutation would result from finding normal or increased BPGM activity in these patients.

We hypothesize that PIGK (phosphatidylinositol glycan class K) plays a crucial role in the development of Cystathioninuria by regulating the expression of cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH), a key enzyme in the transsulfuration pathway. Specifically, PIGK's GPI-anchor synthesis activity affects CTH's membrane localization and stability. We predict that PIGK deficiency will lead to decreased CTH activity, resulting in elevated cystathionine levels, a hallmark of Cystathioninuria. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that PIGK knockdown or inhibition increases cystathionine levels in cells, while refutation would come from experiments demonstrating no effect of PIGK modulation on CTH activity or cystathionine levels.

We hypothesize that NUDT2, a nucleoside diphosphate-linked moiety X (NUDX) hydrolase, plays a crucial role in the development of Dubin-Johnson syndrome by regulating the levels of cyclic nucleotides in hepatocytes. Specifically, we propose that NUDT2 modulates the cGMP signaling pathway, which affects the expression and function of ABCC2, a transporter involved in bilirubin glucuronide secretion. We predict that overexpression of NUDT2 will decrease cGMP levels, leading to reduced ABCC2 activity and increased bilirubin glucuronide accumulation, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, NUDT2 knockdown will increase cGMP levels, enhancing ABCC2 activity and reducing bilirubin glucuronide accumulation, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of NUDT2 and the pathophysiology of Dubin-Johnson syndrome.

We hypothesize that NDUFA11, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Ichthyosis, congenital, autosomal recessive 14. We propose that impaired NDUFA11 function disrupts mitochondrial energy metabolism, leading to altered lipid synthesis and skin barrier formation. Specifically, reduced complex I activity will decrease the production of ATP, necessary for the activation of enzymes involved in fatty acid synthesis, resulting in abnormal skin lipid composition. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of NDUFA11 in keratinocytes will lead to decreased fatty acid synthesis and impaired skin barrier function, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFA11 will rescue this phenotype, refuting our hypothesis if no improvement is observed.

We hypothesize that N-acetylglutamate kinase (NAGK) plays a crucial role in the development of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) by regulating the arginine-citrulline pathway, which affects mitochondrial function. In LHON, mitochondrial dysfunction is a key feature. NAGK's product, N-acetylglutamate, can influence arginase activity, impacting nitric oxide production and mitochondrial respiration. We predict that NAGK overexpression will exacerbate LHON-related mitochondrial defects, while its inhibition will mitigate them. Confirmation would come from observing decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased oxidative stress in LHON cells with NAGK overexpression. Refutation would occur if NAGK modulation has no effect on mitochondrial function in LHON cells. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of NAGK and the arginine-citrulline pathway's role in mitochondrial function.

terminal_shown: Neuronopathy, distal hereditary motor, autosomal dominant 9
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ATP6V1A, a subunit of the vacuolar-type H+-ATPase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Neuronopathy, distal hereditary motor, autosomal dominant 9. Specifically, we propose that mutations in ATP6V1A disrupt lysosomal acidification, leading to impaired degradation of axonal proteins and subsequent axonal degeneration. We predict that overexpression of wild-type ATP6V1A in patient-derived motor neurons will rescue axonal degeneration, while knockdown of ATP6V1A will exacerbate it. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved axonal survival and reduced protein aggregates in response to ATP6V1A overexpression, whereas refutation would be shown by no significant difference in axonal degeneration upon ATP6V1A modulation.

We hypothesize that CYP3A4, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, contributes to the pathogenesis of Leber congenital amaurosis 9 (LCA9) by aberrantly metabolizing 11-cis retinal, a crucial chromophore for rhodopsin regeneration. In LCA9, mutations in the NMNAT1 gene disrupt retinal homeostasis. We propose that CYP3A4's altered activity leads to impaired 11-cis retinal production, exacerbating retinal degeneration. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating decreased 11-cis retinal levels in LCA9 patient-derived retinal cells with elevated CYP3A4 activity. Refutation would require showing no correlation between CYP3A4 activity and 11-cis retinal levels in these cells. This hypothesis is grounded in CYP3A4's known role in retinoid metabolism and the critical importance of 11-cis retinal in photoreceptor function.

We hypothesize that EXTL2, an enzyme involved in heparan sulfate biosynthesis, plays a crucial role in the development of Rickets vitamin D-dependent 1A. Specifically, we propose that EXTL2 regulates the sulfation of heparan sulfate proteoglycans in the kidney, which in turn affects the binding and activation of vitamin D. Impaired EXTL2 activity leads to abnormal heparan sulfate sulfation, reducing vitamin D activation and resulting in the characteristic hypophosphatemia and rickets of Rickets vitamin D-dependent 1A. We predict that EXTL2 knockdown in kidney cells will decrease vitamin D-dependent phosphate reabsorption, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of EXTL2 will increase phosphate reabsorption, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed.

We hypothesize that PTK2 (protein tyrosine kinase 2) plays a crucial role in the regulation of pyridoxine-5'-phosphate oxidase (PNPO) activity through tyrosine phosphorylation. Specifically, PTK2-mediated phosphorylation of PNPO enhances its enzymatic activity, leading to increased conversion of pyridoxine to pyridoxal phosphate. In Pyridoxine-5'-phosphate oxidase deficiency, reduced PNPO activity impairs this conversion, resulting in decreased pyridoxal phosphate levels. We predict that overexpression of PTK2 in cells from individuals with PNPO deficiency will increase PNPO activity and pyridoxal phosphate levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibition of PTK2 will decrease PNPO activity, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection highlights a potential therapeutic target for Pyridoxine-5'-phosphate oxidase deficiency.

We hypothesize that UQCR10, a subunit of the mitochondrial cytochrome b-c1 complex, plays a crucial role in the regulation of Succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA transferase (SCOT) activity. Specifically, we propose that UQCR10-mediated changes in mitochondrial membrane potential affect the transport of succinyl-CoA, a substrate for SCOT, into the mitochondria. We predict that overexpression of UQCR10 will increase SCOT activity, while its knockdown will decrease SCOT activity, exacerbating the symptoms of Succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA transferase deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased SCOT activity and improved metabolic profiles in cells overexpressing UQCR10, while refutation would be shown by decreased SCOT activity and worsened metabolic profiles in UQCR10-knockdown cells.

We hypothesize that SDHD, a crucial component of the succinate dehydrogenase complex, plays a key role in the development of Immunodeficiency 24 by regulating the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in immune cells. Specifically, we propose that SDHD's dysfunction leads to an imbalance in ROS levels, disrupting the activity of immune cell signaling pathways, ultimately resulting in impaired immune function. We predict that experimental inhibition of SDHD in immune cells will increase ROS production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, refuting our hypothesis would require demonstrating that SDHD inhibition has no effect on ROS levels or immune cell function in the context of Immunodeficiency 24.

We hypothesize that N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS) plays a crucial role in the development of Lenz-Majewski hyperostotic dwarfism through its regulation of arginine synthesis. Specifically, we propose that impaired NAGS activity leads to decreased arginine production, which in turn disrupts the nitric oxide (NO) signaling pathway essential for bone homeostasis. We predict that patients with Lenz-Majewski hyperostotic dwarfism will exhibit reduced NAGS expression and arginine levels, resulting in decreased NO production and subsequent hyperostotic bone formation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased arginine and NO levels in patient samples, while refutation would be shown by normal or elevated levels of these metabolites.

terminal_shown: Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with brain and eye anomalies A1
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that LPCAT4, an enzyme involved in lipid metabolism, contributes to the pathogenesis of Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with brain and eye anomalies A1 by disrupting the glycosylation of α-dystroglycan. Specifically, LPCAT4's activity alters the lipid composition of the cell membrane, affecting the function of glycosyltransferases responsible for α-dystroglycan modification. This leads to hypoglycosylation of α-dystroglycan, impairing its binding to laminin and disrupting the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex. We predict that inhibiting LPCAT4 will restore α-dystroglycan glycosylation and improve muscle function in affected individuals. Confirmation would come from experiments showing that LPCAT4 inhibition increases α-dystroglycan glycosylation and improves muscle pathology in patient-derived cells or animal models. Refutation would result from experiments demonstrating no effect of LPCAT4 inhibition on α-dystroglycan glycosylation or muscle function.

We hypothesize that Glutamic-Pyruvic Transaminase (GPT) plays a crucial role in the development of ischemic stroke by regulating the metabolism of glutamate, a neurotransmitter that can be neurotoxic in excess. Specifically, we propose that GPT's activity in astrocytes leads to the conversion of glutamate to α-ketoglutarate, reducing glutamate levels in the synaptic cleft. However, under ischemic conditions, decreased GPT activity results in glutamate accumulation, leading to excitotoxicity and neuronal damage. We predict that inhibiting GPT activity in astrocytes will exacerbate ischemic stroke damage, while overexpressing GPT will be protective. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased infarct size in GPT-inhibited mice, while refutation would be shown by no significant difference in infarct size between GPT-inhibited and control mice.

We hypothesize that PMAIP1 (phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate-induced protein 1), also known as NOXA, regulates mitochondrial outer membrane permeability, thereby influencing the transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation. In Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) deficiency, impaired fatty acid transport leads to energy deficits. PMAIP1's modulation of mitochondrial outer membrane permeability may exacerbate or mitigate this defect. We predict that overexpression of PMAIP1 will worsen the energetic deficit in CPT1A-deficient cells, while its knockdown will improve fatty acid oxidation and cellular energy production. Confirmation would come from measuring increased ATP production and decreased fatty acid accumulation in CPT1A-deficient cells with PMAIP1 knockdown. Refutation would be demonstrated by unchanged or worsened energetic deficits in response to PMAIP1 modulation.

terminal_shown: Branchial arch abnormalities, choanal atresia, athelia, hearing loss, and hypothyroidism syndrome
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that NUS1, a mitochondrial dehydrogenase, plays a crucial role in the development of Branchial arch abnormalities, choanal atresia, athelia, hearing loss, and hypothyroidism syndrome. Specifically, NUS1 regulates the metabolism of retinoic acid, a key signaling molecule in embryonic development. Impaired NUS1 activity disrupts retinoic acid homeostasis, leading to aberrant expression of developmental genes involved in branchial arch formation, thyroid development, and auditory system morphogenesis. We predict that NUS1 deficiency will result in decreased retinoic acid levels and altered gene expression profiles in affected tissues. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by rescue of the syndrome's phenotypes with retinoic acid supplementation, while refutation would be shown by normal retinoic acid levels and gene expression profiles in NUS1-deficient models.

We hypothesize that inositol polyphosphate-1-phosphatase (INPP1) plays a crucial role in the development of Parkinsonism-dystonia 3, childhood-onset, by regulating PI(4,5)P2 levels in dopaminergic neurons. Reduced INPP1 activity leads to increased PI(4,5)P2, enhancing Munc13-1 activity and causing excessive dopamine release, ultimately resulting in neurodegeneration. We predict that INPP1 knockdown in mouse dopaminergic neurons will increase Munc13-1 activity and dopamine release, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, INPP1 overexpression will rescue the phenotype, refuting the hypothesis if no effect is observed. This mechanism is grounded in known biochemistry of PI(4,5)P2 signaling and its role in neurotransmitter release.

We hypothesize that the enzyme GNE (UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase/N-acetylmannosamine kinase) plays a crucial role in the development of Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS) by regulating the biosynthesis of glycosaminoglycans, which are essential for proper cholesterol metabolism. In SLOS, impaired cholesterol synthesis leads to accumulation of 7-dehydrocholesterol. We predict that GNE's epimerase activity is necessary for the production of glycosaminoglycans that interact with and stabilize the enzyme 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase, thereby facilitating cholesterol synthesis. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that GNE overexpression rescues cholesterol synthesis defects in SLOS cells, while refutation would result from demonstrating that GNE inhibition has no effect on 7-dehydrocholesterol levels in these cells.

We hypothesize that GLUD1, a key enzyme in glutamate metabolism, plays a crucial role in the development of Coenzyme Q10 deficiency, primary, 6. Specifically, we propose that GLUD1 regulates the biosynthesis of Coenzyme Q10 by modulating the availability of glutamate, a precursor for the synthesis of 4-hydroxybenzoate, a critical intermediate in Coenzyme Q10 production. We predict that overexpression of GLUD1 will increase Coenzyme Q10 levels, while its inhibition will exacerbate the deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased Coenzyme Q10 levels in cells overexpressing GLUD1, while refutation would be shown by no change in Coenzyme Q10 levels despite GLUD1 modulation. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemical pathways of glutamate metabolism and Coenzyme Q10 biosynthesis.

We hypothesize that FAHD1, a flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)-dependent dehydrogenase, plays a crucial role in regulating the tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) cycle, which is essential for phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) activity. Impaired FAHD1 function may lead to decreased BH4 levels, resulting in reduced PAH activity and contributing to Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. We predict that FAHD1 knockdown will decrease BH4 levels and PAH activity in cells, confirming this hypothesis. Conversely, overexpressing FAHD1 will increase BH4 levels and PAH activity, refuting the hypothesis if no effect is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of the BH4 cycle and its importance in PAH function, providing a testable link between FAHD1 and Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency.

We hypothesize that NDUFB7, a subunit of NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (Complex I), plays a crucial role in maintaining the stability and function of dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (DLD) in the mitochondria. Through its interaction with DLD, NDUFB7 facilitates the proper folding and assembly of the DLD enzyme, thereby preventing its degradation. We predict that a decrease in NDUFB7 expression will lead to reduced DLD activity, resulting in Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrating a physical interaction between NDUFB7 and DLD, while refutation would be evident if NDUFB7 knockdown does not affect DLD activity or stability.

We hypothesize that CYP11A1, a cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme, contributes to the pathogenesis of Aminoacylase-1 deficiency by modulating the metabolism of N-acetyl amino acids. Specifically, we propose that CYP11A1-derived steroids influence the expression and activity of Aminoacylase-1, leading to impaired N-acetyl amino acid degradation. We predict that inhibition of CYP11A1 will decrease N-acetyl amino acid accumulation in cells from Aminoacylase-1 deficient patients, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of CYP11A1 will exacerbate N-acetyl amino acid accumulation, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of CYP11A1 in steroidogenesis and the importance of Aminoacylase-1 in N-acetyl amino acid metabolism.

We hypothesize that COX10, a mitochondrial enzyme involved in heme biosynthesis, plays a crucial role in the development of Desbuquois dysplasia 1. Specifically, we propose that COX10's dysfunction affects the production of heme, leading to impaired mitochondrial function and increased oxidative stress in chondrocytes. This, in turn, disrupts cartilage development and leads to the characteristic skeletal abnormalities seen in Desbuquois dysplasia 1. We predict that COX10 overexpression in chondrocytes will rescue the skeletal phenotype in a Desbuquois dysplasia 1 model, while COX10 knockdown will exacerbate it. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by improved skeletal development in COX10-overexpressing models, while refutation would be indicated by no significant change in skeletal phenotype.

We hypothesize that ABCC1, an ATP-binding cassette transporter, plays a crucial role in the development of Methemoglobinemia CYB5R3-related by regulating the efflux of reduced glutathione (GSH) from erythrocytes. In this disease, mutations in CYB5R3 lead to impaired methemoglobin reduction. We propose that ABCC1's decreased activity or expression results in increased intracellular GSH levels, which in turn inhibits the alternative methemoglobin reduction pathways. This leads to an accumulation of methemoglobin, exacerbating the disease. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating a significant increase in methemoglobin levels in erythrocytes with reduced ABCC1 activity. Refutation would involve showing no correlation between ABCC1 expression and methemoglobin levels in CYB5R3-related Methemoglobinemia patients.

terminal_shown: Salt and pepper developmental regression syndrome
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that LCLAT1, a key enzyme in lipid metabolism, plays a crucial role in the development of Salt and pepper developmental regression syndrome. Specifically, we propose that LCLAT1's dysregulation leads to impaired lipid synthesis in neural cells, disrupting normal brain development and resulting in the characteristic regression of skills seen in this syndrome. We predict that LCLAT1 deficiency will lead to decreased levels of specific lipid species in patient-derived neural cells, which can be confirmed by lipidomics analysis. Conversely, overexpression of LCLAT1 in these cells will rescue the lipid profile and improve cellular function, refuting our hypothesis if no improvement is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in LCLAT1's known role in lipid metabolism and the established link between lipid dysregulation and neurodevelopmental disorders.

We hypothesize that GAS6 (growth arrest-specific 6) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2U (CMT2U) by regulating axonal survival and maintenance through the Axl receptor pathway. Specifically, GAS6 binding to Axl receptor promotes activation of downstream signaling cascades that regulate axonal degeneration and survival. We predict that increased GAS6 expression will mitigate axonal degeneration in CMT2U models, whereas GAS6 inhibition will exacerbate disease severity. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved axonal survival and functional recovery in CMT2U models overexpressing GAS6, while refutation would be shown by worsening disease outcomes in models with reduced GAS6 activity.

We hypothesize that AGMAT (arginine:glycine amidinotransferase) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Urocanase deficiency by regulating the levels of arginine, a precursor to the urea cycle. In Urocanase deficiency, the accumulation of urocanic acid leads to an imbalance in nitrogen metabolism. AGMAT, by converting arginine to guanidinoacetate, may exacerbate this imbalance. We predict that inhibition of AGMAT will decrease urocanic acid levels and alleviate disease symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased urocanic acid levels in patient cells treated with AGMAT inhibitors. Refutation would occur if AGMAT inhibition has no effect on urocanic acid levels or worsens disease symptoms, indicating an alternative mechanistic pathway.

We hypothesize that thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Leber congenital amaurosis 14 (LCA14) by regulating the methylation of retinal metabolites. Specifically, TPMT's methyltransferase activity modulates the levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe) in photoreceptor cells, which in turn affects the expression of the LCA14-causing gene, CTNPF6. We predict that reduced TPMT activity will lead to decreased SAMe levels, resulting in increased CTNPF6 expression and exacerbated LCA14 phenotypes. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the observation that TPMT-deficient mice exhibit worsened retinal degeneration and vision loss in an LCA14 model, while refutation would be shown by the lack of effect on LCA14 phenotypes in TPMT-deficient mice.

We hypothesize that Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor Alpha (PPARα), activated by PFAS, disrupts vitamin D metabolism, contributing to Rickets vitamin D-dependent 1A. PPARα activation leads to increased expression of 24-hydroxylase, an enzyme that degrades 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, the active form of vitamin D. This degradation impairs intestinal calcium absorption, resulting in hypocalcemia and rickets. We predict that PFAS exposure will increase 24-hydroxylase expression and decrease 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels in patients with Rickets vitamin D-dependent 1A. Confirmation would come from observing a significant decrease in 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels and a corresponding increase in 24-hydroxylase expression in PFAS-exposed patients. Refutation would occur if PFAS exposure does not alter 24-hydroxylase expression or 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels in these patients.

We hypothesize that APIP (Apoptosis-Inducing Factor-Interacting Protein) plays a crucial role in the development of Hereditary multiple exostoses 1 (HME1) by regulating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. APIP's interaction with apoptosis-inducing factor may modulate β-catenin levels, leading to excessive bone growth characteristic of HME1. We predict that APIP overexpression will enhance Wnt/β-catenin signaling, resulting in increased osteochondroma formation in HME1 models. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by APIP overexpression experiments showing increased β-catenin levels and osteochondroma formation, while refutation would be shown by APIP knockdown experiments with no effect on Wnt/β-catenin signaling or osteochondroma formation.

terminal_shown: Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ACP1 (acid phosphatase 1) plays a crucial role in the development of Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2, by regulating the dephosphorylation of mitochondrial proteins involved in energy metabolism. Specifically, ACP1's enzymatic activity modulates the phosphorylation status of complex I subunits, affecting mitochondrial function and leading to optic nerve degeneration. We predict that ACP1 deficiency or inhibition will result in increased mitochondrial complex I phosphorylation and subsequent optic neuropathy, whereas ACP1 overexpression will mitigate the disease phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the rescue of optic nerve function in ACP1-deficient cells or animals upon ACP1 reintroduction or complex I dephosphorylation. Refutation would be shown by the lack of effect on optic neuropathy upon ACP1 modulation.

We hypothesize that IP6K3, an inositol hexakisphosphate kinase, contributes to the development of Sarcosinemia by regulating the metabolism of sarcosine through the production of IP7 (inositol heptakisphosphate). Specifically, IP6K3-generated IP7 inhibits the activity of sarcosine dehydrogenase, an enzyme responsible for sarcosine degradation. This inhibition leads to the accumulation of sarcosine, a hallmark of Sarcosinemia. We predict that IP6K3 overexpression will increase sarcosine levels in cells, while IP6K3 knockdown will decrease them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experiments showing a direct correlation between IP6K3 activity and sarcosine accumulation, while refutation would come from experiments demonstrating no effect of IP6K3 modulation on sarcosine levels.

We hypothesize that CAMKMT (calmodulin-lysis oxide methyltransferase) plays a crucial role in the development of Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata 2 (RCDP2) by regulating the methylation of phospholipids in peroxisomes. Specifically, CAMKMT's methyltransferase activity is essential for the synthesis of plasmalogens, which are deficient in RCDP2 patients. We predict that CAMKMT's enzymatic activity will be reduced in RCDP2 patient cells, leading to decreased plasmalogen levels. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by measuring decreased CAMKMT activity and plasmalogen levels in RCDP2 patient cells. Refutation would occur if CAMKMT activity and plasmalogen levels are normal in RCDP2 patient cells, suggesting an alternative mechanism underlying the disease.

We hypothesize that ATP5MC1, a mitochondrial ATP synthase subunit, plays a crucial role in maintaining mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) copy number in Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 2 (MDDS2). Specifically, we propose that ATP5MC1 regulates the mitochondrial nucleotide pool by modulating the activity of mitochondrial nucleotide transporters. Disruption of this process leads to impaired mtDNA replication and depletion. We predict that overexpression of ATP5MC1 in MDDS2 patient-derived cells will increase mtDNA copy number, while siRNA-mediated knockdown will exacerbate mtDNA depletion. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant increase in mtDNA copy number upon ATP5MC1 overexpression, while refutation would be shown by no change or a decrease in mtDNA copy number.

We hypothesize that PIP4K2A, an enzyme that phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate to produce phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, plays a crucial role in the development of Hereditary multiple exostoses 1 (HME1) by regulating the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. Abnormal PIP4K2A activity may lead to altered cell growth and differentiation in osteochondroma cells, contributing to the formation of multiple exostoses. We predict that PIP4K2A inhibition will reduce osteochondroma formation in HME1 mouse models, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if PIP4K2A inhibition has no effect on osteochondroma formation, our hypothesis will be refuted. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of PIP4K2A and its role in cell signaling pathways, and specifically addresses the molecular mechanisms underlying HME1.

We hypothesize that AMD1 (adenosylmethionine decarboxylase 1) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency by regulating the methionine cycle and homocysteine levels. Specifically, AMD1's dysregulation leads to altered polyamine synthesis, which in turn affects the expression and activity of cystathionine beta-synthase. We predict that overexpression of AMD1 in cells from patients with Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency will decrease homocysteine levels and increase cystathionine production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibition of AMD1 will exacerbate the disease phenotype, characterized by elevated homocysteine levels and reduced cystathionine production, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of the methionine cycle and polyamine synthesis.

We hypothesize that MOCS2, a crucial enzyme in molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis, plays a key role in the development of Pontocerebellar hypoplasia 16. Specifically, we propose that MOCS2 deficiency impairs sulfite oxidase activity, leading to toxic sulfite accumulation and subsequent oxidative stress in neuronal cells. This stress triggers a cascade of cellular damage, ultimately resulting in the characteristic cerebellar hypoplasia and pontine abnormalities seen in Pontocerebellar hypoplasia 16. We predict that MOCS2 knockdown in neuronal cells will increase sulfite levels and induce oxidative stress, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, supplementation with molybdenum cofactor or antioxidants will rescue this phenotype, refuting our hypothesis if no rescue is observed.

We hypothesize that Tyrosine Hydroxylase (TH) contributes to Congenital disorder of glycosylation 1P (CDG-1P) through impaired dopamine synthesis, leading to altered glycosylation patterns. TH catalyzes the conversion of L-tyrosine to L-DOPA, a precursor for dopamine. Dopamine regulates the activity of phosphofructokinase, a key enzyme in glycolysis, which in turn affects the production of UDP-galactose, a donor for glycosylation reactions. We predict that TH inhibition will decrease dopamine levels, resulting in reduced phosphofructokinase activity and subsequently altered glycosylation patterns, characteristic of CDG-1P. Confirmation would come from observing decreased glycosylated protein levels in cells with TH inhibition, while refutation would result from unchanged glycosylation patterns despite TH inhibition.

We hypothesize that malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (MLYCD) plays a crucial role in the development of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2W, by regulating fatty acid synthesis in peripheral nerves. MLYCD's enzymatic activity affects malonyl-CoA levels, which in turn influence the production of fatty acids essential for myelin maintenance. Impaired MLYCD function leads to altered fatty acid profiles, disrupting myelin structure and function, and ultimately contributing to axonal degeneration. We predict that MLYCD deficiency will result in decreased myelin fatty acid synthesis, confirmed by reduced nerve conduction velocities in MLYCD-knockdown models. Refutation would come from unchanged nerve conduction velocities despite MLYCD deficiency, indicating an alternative disease mechanism.

We hypothesize that Inositol Polyphosphate Multikinase (IPMK) plays a crucial role in the development of Erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva 4 (EKVP4) by regulating the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, which is essential for keratinocyte growth and differentiation. IPMK's phosphoinositide kinase activity modulates the production of inositol polyphosphates, which in turn affect AKT activation. We predict that IPMK overexpression will exacerbate EKVP4 symptoms, while its inhibition will alleviate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased AKT phosphorylation and enhanced keratinocyte proliferation in EKVP4 patient samples with elevated IPMK activity. Refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased AKT phosphorylation in response to IPMK modulation.

We hypothesize that Riboflavin Kinase (RFK) plays a crucial role in the development of Erythrocytosis, familial, 8, by regulating the bioavailability of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) in erythroid progenitor cells. Specifically, RFK's phosphorylation of riboflavin to form flavin mononucleotide (FMN) is essential for the subsequent synthesis of FAD, a cofactor required for the activity of prolyl hydroxylase domain-containing proteins (PHDs). PHDs regulate the stability of hypoxia-inducible factor-2α (HIF-2α), a key transcription factor involved in erythropoiesis. We predict that RFK overexpression will increase FAD levels, leading to enhanced PHD activity, decreased HIF-2α stability, and subsequently, elevated erythrocyte production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, RFK inhibition will refute this hypothesis by reducing erythrocyte production.

We hypothesize that MAP2K1, a kinase involved in the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway, contributes to the pathogenesis of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2W. Specifically, we propose that aberrant MAP2K1 activity disrupts axonal transport by phosphorylating and inhibiting kinesin-1, a motor protein essential for anterograde transport. This leads to accumulation of neurofilaments and other axonal cargo, causing axonal degeneration. We predict that inhibition of MAP2K1 will reduce axonal degeneration in CMT2W patient-derived neurons. Confirmation will be observed as a significant decrease in axonal swellings and improved neurite outgrowth in treated cells. Refutation will be evident if MAP2K1 inhibition fails to rescue axonal transport defects in CMT2W neurons.

We hypothesize that ACAA1 (acetyl-CoA acyltransferase 1) contributes to the development of Chondrosarcoma by regulating fatty acid metabolism and promoting cell proliferation. Specifically, ACAA1's role in mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation leads to increased production of acetyl-CoA, which in turn enhances the activity of histone acetyltransferases, resulting in epigenetic modifications that promote chondrocyte proliferation and tumorigenesis. We predict that ACAA1 overexpression in chondrocytes will increase cell growth and tumor formation, whereas ACAA1 inhibition will suppress Chondrosarcoma development. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased ACAA1 expression in Chondrosarcoma tissues and decreased tumor growth in response to ACAA1 inhibitors. Refutation would be shown by lack of correlation between ACAA1 expression and Chondrosarcoma development.

We hypothesize that HSD17B14, a hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, contributes to Brugada syndrome 2 by modulating the metabolism of androgens, which in turn affect the expression of the SCN5A gene, encoding the cardiac sodium channel. Altered androgen metabolism by HSD17B14 leads to reduced SCN5A expression, resulting in decreased sodium channel function and the characteristic Brugada syndrome 2 electrocardiographic phenotype. We predict that HSD17B14 inhibition will increase SCN5A expression and rescue the Brugada syndrome 2 phenotype in vitro, whereas overexpression of HSD17B14 will exacerbate it. Confirmation of this hypothesis would require demonstration of HSD17B14-mediated androgen metabolism regulating SCN5A expression in cardiac myocytes. Refutation would involve failure to observe a correlation between HSD17B14 activity and SCN5A expression in these cells.

terminal_shown: Congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that HSD17B14, a 17-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, contributes to Congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation 2 by modulating the biosynthesis of GDP-fucose, a crucial donor for fucosylation reactions. Specifically, HSD17B14 may regulate the conversion of steroids that influence the expression of enzymes involved in GDP-fucose production. We predict that overexpression of HSD17B14 will increase GDP-fucose levels and rescue fucosylation defects in cells from patients with Congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation 2. Confirmation would come from mass spectrometry showing increased GDP-fucose levels and lectin blotting demonstrating restored fucosylation patterns. Refutation would be evident if HSD17B14 overexpression fails to correct fucosylation defects or if GDP-fucose levels remain unchanged.

We hypothesize that PIK3C3, a class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, plays a crucial role in regulating the autophagic clearance of Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10)-deficient mitochondria, thereby contributing to the pathogenesis of primary Coenzyme Q10 deficiency, 1. Specifically, PIK3C3's kinase activity is required for the initiation of autophagosome formation, which clears damaged mitochondria. In CoQ10 deficiency, impaired mitochondrial function leads to increased PIK3C3 activity, enhancing autophagic flux. We predict that PIK3C3 inhibition will reduce autophagic clearance of damaged mitochondria, exacerbating CoQ10 deficiency. Confirmation would come from increased mitochondrial damage and decreased cellular CoQ10 levels upon PIK3C3 inhibition in patient-derived cells. Refutation would be demonstrated by unchanged or improved CoQ10 levels and mitochondrial function upon PIK3C3 inhibition.

terminal_shown: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that the GRB2 enzyme plays a crucial role in the development of Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC) by facilitating aberrant signaling through the RAS-MAPK pathway. Specifically, GRB2 binds to the FH mutant protein, leading to enhanced recruitment of SOS1 and subsequent activation of RAS. This results in increased cell proliferation and tumorigenesis. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of GRB2 will reduce tumor growth in HLRCC cell lines. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased RAS-GTP levels and reduced cell proliferation upon GRB2 knockdown, while refutation would be indicated by unchanged or increased RAS-GTP levels and cell proliferation.

terminal_shown: Calvarial doughnut lesions with bone fragility and spondylometaphyseal dysplasia
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that RRM2B, a crucial component of the ribonucleotide reductase complex, plays a key role in the development of Calvarial doughnut lesions with bone fragility and spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. Specifically, we propose that RRM2B's regulation of dNTP pools affects osteoblast proliferation and differentiation, leading to impaired bone formation. We predict that RRM2B overexpression will rescue bone fragility in spondylometaphyseal dysplasia models, whereas its knockdown will exacerbate Calvarial doughnut lesions. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved bone density and reduced lesion formation in RRM2B-overexpressing models, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or worsened bone phenotypes. This hypothesis is grounded in RRM2B's known function in nucleotide metabolism and its impact on cell proliferation and differentiation.

terminal_shown: Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with brain and eye anomalies A10
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (FBP1) plays a crucial role in the development of Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with brain and eye anomalies A10 by regulating glycolytic flux and subsequent O-linked glycosylation of α-dystroglycan. Impaired FBP1 activity leads to increased glycolytic intermediates, which in turn alter the activity of glycosyltransferases responsible for α-dystroglycan modification. This results in hypoglycosylated α-dystroglycan, a hallmark of muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy. We predict that FBP1 overexpression will rescue α-dystroglycan glycosylation defects in patient-derived cells, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, FBP1 knockdown will exacerbate these defects, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of glycolysis and glycosylation pathways.

We hypothesize that KYAT3, a lysine acetyltransferase, plays a crucial role in the development of Anterior segment dysgenesis 6 (ASD6) by regulating the acetylation and subsequent activity of transcription factors involved in ocular morphogenesis. Specifically, KYAT3 acetylates and activates the FOXE3 transcription factor, which is essential for anterior segment development. We predict that overexpression of KYAT3 will enhance FOXE3 activity, leading to increased expression of genes involved in lens and cornea formation, whereas KYAT3 knockdown will result in decreased FOXE3 activity and ASD6-like phenotypes. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the rescue of ASD6 phenotypes in KYAT3-overexpressing models, while refutation would be shown by the lack of effect on ASD6 phenotypes in KYAT3-knockdown models.

We hypothesize that CDKN2A, a tumor suppressor enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Trichothiodystrophy 7, non-photosensitive, by regulating the cell cycle and DNA repair mechanisms. Specifically, CDKN2A's inhibition of CDK4/6 kinases may lead to impaired cell cycle progression, resulting in defective hair follicle and nail development. We predict that overexpression of CDKN2A in patient-derived cells will exacerbate the disease phenotype, characterized by increased hair shaft fragility and brittleness. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased CDKN2A expression in patient samples, while refutation would be shown by no significant difference in CDKN2A expression between patients and healthy controls. This hypothesis is grounded in CDKN2A's known role in cell cycle regulation and its potential impact on tissue development.

We hypothesize that ADPGK (ADP-dependent glucokinase) plays a crucial role in the development of Lethal congenital contracture syndrome 2 (LCCS2) by regulating energy metabolism in neuronal cells. Specifically, we propose that ADPGK's glucokinase activity is essential for maintaining proper ATP levels in motor neurons, and its dysfunction leads to energy deficits, triggering muscle contractures. We predict that ADPGK knockdown in neuronal cells will result in decreased ATP production and increased contracture severity, whereas overexpression will rescue this phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing a significant reduction in ATP levels and increased contracture formation in ADPGK-knockdown neuronal cells, while refutation would be indicated by unchanged ATP levels and contracture severity despite ADPGK manipulation.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that GOT1L1, a glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase, plays a crucial role in regulating the mitochondrial membrane potential by modulating the malate-aspartate shuttle, thereby impacting the function of mitochondrial complex I. In Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 2, we predict that decreased GOT1L1 activity will disrupt the malate-aspartate shuttle, leading to impaired complex I function. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased complex I activity and altered mitochondrial membrane potential in cells with GOT1L1 knockdown. Refutation would be evident if GOT1L1 knockdown does not affect complex I function or mitochondrial membrane potential. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of the malate-aspartate shuttle and its importance in maintaining mitochondrial function.

We hypothesize that PTDSS1, a phosphatidylserine synthase, contributes to the development of Sialuria by disrupting the balance of phospholipid metabolism, leading to altered membrane composition and impaired uridine diphosphate-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) transport. This, in turn, affects the activity of the UDP-GlcNAc 2-epimerase/N-acetylmannosamine kinase (GNE) enzyme, which is deficient in Sialuria. We predict that overexpression of PTDSS1 will exacerbate Sialuria symptoms, while its inhibition will alleviate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through increased sialic acid production in cells with reduced PTDSS1 activity, whereas refutation would be seen if PTDSS1 modulation has no effect on sialic acid levels.

We hypothesize that ASNS (asparagine synthetase) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA transferase (SCOT) deficiency by regulating the availability of asparagine, which in turn affects the synthesis of succinyl-CoA. In SCOT deficiency, the impaired transfer of CoA to succinyl-CoA leads to accumulation of succinyl-CoA precursors. ASNS, by consuming ATP and aspartate, may indirectly influence the energy status and aspartate availability, thereby impacting the synthesis of succinyl-CoA. We predict that ASNS inhibition will decrease succinyl-CoA levels in SCOT-deficient cells, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, ASNS overexpression will exacerbate the metabolic imbalance, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection highlights a potential therapeutic target for SCOT deficiency.

We hypothesize that PRUNE1, a phosphodiesterase, plays a crucial role in regulating pulmonary surfactant metabolism by modulating the activity of lipogenic transcription factors. Specifically, PRUNE1 degrades cyclic nucleotides, thereby influencing the expression of surfactant proteins and lipids. Dysregulation of PRUNE1 activity leads to an imbalance in surfactant homeostasis, contributing to Pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 3. We predict that overexpression of PRUNE1 in lung epithelial cells will result in decreased surfactant protein B expression, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, PRUNE1 inhibition will increase surfactant protein B levels, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of phosphodiesterase regulation of cellular signaling pathways and highlights a potential therapeutic target for Pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 3.

We hypothesize that AMY1A, an alpha-amylase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Pontocerebellar hypoplasia 12 (PCH12) through its involvement in glycogen metabolism. Specifically, we propose that impaired AMY1A activity disrupts normal glycogen breakdown, leading to abnormal energy availability in the developing brain, which in turn contributes to the characteristic cerebellar hypoplasia and pontine atrophy seen in PCH12. We predict that experimental reduction of AMY1A activity in neuronal cells will result in decreased glycogen breakdown and altered cellular energy metabolism, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, rescue of AMY1A activity will restore normal glycogen metabolism and mitigate PCH12-like phenotypes, refuting our hypothesis if unsuccessful.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 8
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that PLPP1 (phospholipid phosphatase 1) plays a crucial role in the development of Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 8, by regulating the phospholipid composition of mitochondrial membranes. Specifically, PLPP1's dephosphorylation activity modulates the levels of phosphatidic acid, a key phospholipid involved in mitochondrial membrane dynamics. We predict that overexpression of PLPP1 will lead to decreased phosphatidic acid levels, disrupting mitochondrial membrane structure and function, thereby exacerbating complex I deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased complex I activity in cells overexpressing PLPP1, while refutation would be shown by unchanged complex I activity in response to PLPP1 overexpression. This mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of phospholipid metabolism and its impact on mitochondrial function.

We hypothesize that Maltase-Glucoamylase (MGAM) plays a crucial role in the development of Familial porphyria cutanea tarda (F-PCT) by modulating the glycosylation status of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD), a key enzyme in the heme biosynthesis pathway. Specifically, MGAM's glucosidase activity affects the degradation of glycogen to glucose, influencing the availability of glucose for glycosylation reactions. We predict that MGAM overexpression will lead to increased UROD glycosylation, resulting in decreased UROD activity and subsequent accumulation of toxic porphyrin intermediates, characteristic of F-PCT. Confirmation would come from experiments showing MGAM overexpression reduces UROD activity in F-PCT patient cells, while refutation would result from experiments demonstrating no effect of MGAM on UROD glycosylation or activity.

terminal_shown: Congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation 1
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that the MSH2 enzyme, involved in DNA mismatch repair, indirectly affects the biosynthesis of GDP-fucose, a crucial donor for fucosylation reactions. Specifically, MSH2 maintains genome stability, ensuring proper expression of genes involved in GDP-fucose production, such as GMD and FPGT. Disruption of MSH2 function may lead to mutations in these genes, resulting in impaired GDP-fucose synthesis and subsequent defective fucosylation, characteristic of Congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation 1. We predict that MSH2-deficient cells will exhibit reduced GDP-fucose levels and impaired fucosylation of glycoproteins, which can be confirmed by metabolomic and glycoproteomic analyses. Refutation would require demonstration of normal GDP-fucose levels and fucosylation patterns in MSH2-deficient cells.

terminal_shown: Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ASRGL1, an enzyme involved in the degradation of L-asparagine, plays a crucial role in maintaining mitochondrial function and energy metabolism. Specifically, we propose that ASRGL1 regulates the levels of L-asparagine in mitochondria, which in turn affects the synthesis of N-acetyl-aspartyl-glutamate, a precursor for the synthesis of acetyl-CoA. Impaired ASRGL1 activity leads to disrupted acetyl-CoA production, causing mitochondrial dysfunction and contributing to the development of Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay. We predict that ASRGL1 deficiency will result in decreased acetyl-CoA levels and impaired mitochondrial respiration in patient-derived cells, which can be confirmed by metabolomic and respirometry assays. Refutation would come from normal acetyl-CoA levels and mitochondrial function in ASRGL1-deficient cells.

We hypothesize that GPLD1, a phospholipase, contributes to Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation 6 (NBIA6) by disrupting phospholipid homeostasis in the brain, leading to impaired mitochondrial function and increased iron accumulation. Specifically, GPLD1's activity on phosphatidylcholine may alter the composition of mitochondrial membranes, enhancing iron uptake and promoting oxidative stress. We predict that GPLD1 overexpression in neuronal cells will increase iron levels and induce mitochondrial dysfunction, whereas GPLD1 inhibition will mitigate these effects. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experimental evidence showing a direct correlation between GPLD1 activity and iron accumulation in NBIA6 patient-derived cells, while refutation would be demonstrated by the absence of such a correlation or by the failure of GPLD1 modulation to impact iron homeostasis.

We hypothesize that PLOD1, a lysyl hydroxylase involved in collagen modification, contributes to Leber congenital amaurosis 14 (LCA14) through aberrant collagen synthesis in the retina. Specifically, PLOD1's dysregulation leads to impaired collagen cross-linking, disrupting the structural integrity of the retinal extracellular matrix. This disruption affects photoreceptor cell function and survival, resulting in vision loss characteristic of LCA14. We predict that PLOD1 knockdown in retinal cells will increase collagen fragmentation and decrease cell adhesion, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpressing PLOD1 will rescue these defects, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of collagen in maintaining retinal structure and function.

We hypothesize that EHMT2, a histone methyltransferase, contributes to the pathogenesis of Galactosemia 4 by epigenetically regulating the expression of genes involved in galactose metabolism. Specifically, EHMT2 methylates histones associated with the GALT gene, leading to its downregulation and impaired galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase activity. We predict that EHMT2 inhibition will increase GALT expression and alleviate galactosemia symptoms in Galactosemia 4 models. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased GALT mRNA and protein levels, and improved galactose tolerance, upon EHMT2 inhibition. Refutation would be evidenced by unchanged or worsened galactosemia phenotypes despite EHMT2 inhibition, indicating an alternative disease mechanism.

We hypothesize that LPCAT3, a key enzyme in phospholipid biosynthesis, contributes to the development of Cholesteryl ester storage disease by modulating the formation of phospholipids that regulate lysosomal cholesterol efflux. Specifically, LPCAT3's activity influences the composition of lysosomal membranes, affecting the function of NPC1 and NPC2 proteins, which are essential for cholesterol export from lysosomes. We predict that LPCAT3 overexpression will exacerbate cholesterol accumulation in lysosomes, while its inhibition will alleviate this phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased lysosomal cholesterol levels in cells overexpressing LPCAT3, whereas refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased cholesterol levels. This mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of lipid metabolism and lysosomal function.

We hypothesize that MAPK8 (c-Jun N-terminal kinase 1) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (DLD) deficiency by regulating the expression of DLD through the mitochondrial stress response pathway. Specifically, we propose that MAPK8 phosphorylates and activates a transcription factor that upregulates DLD expression in response to mitochondrial stress. We predict that inhibition of MAPK8 will decrease DLD expression, exacerbating the disease phenotype, whereas activation of MAPK8 will increase DLD expression, ameliorating the disease. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased DLD activity in cells treated with a MAPK8 inhibitor, while refutation would be shown by no change in DLD activity in response to MAPK8 modulation.

We hypothesize that CISD1, a mitochondrial zinc finger protein, plays a crucial role in regulating mitochondrial dynamics and function in auditory hair cells, contributing to Deafness, autosomal dominant, 77. Specifically, CISD1's dysfunction leads to impaired mitochondrial fission and fusion, causing mitochondrial fragmentation and subsequent cellular energy deficits. This disruption impairs the mechanotransduction machinery in hair cells, ultimately resulting in hearing loss. We predict that CISD1 knockout in auditory hair cells will lead to mitochondrial dysfunction and hearing impairment, whereas CISD1 overexpression will rescue mitochondrial morphology and function, confirming our hypothesis. Refutation would come from observations of normal mitochondrial function and hearing in CISD1-deficient hair cells.

We hypothesize that glycine amidinotransferase (GATM) contributes to the development of Inflammatory bowel disease 13 (IBD13) by modulating the synthesis of creatine, a key regulator of intestinal epithelial cell energy metabolism. Specifically, GATM deficiency leads to impaired creatine production, disrupting the energy homeostasis of intestinal epithelial cells and increasing their susceptibility to inflammation. We predict that GATM knockout mice will exhibit exacerbated colonic inflammation and impaired barrier function, which can be rescued by creatine supplementation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by the observation of reduced creatine levels and increased inflammation in GATM-deficient intestinal epithelial cells, while refutation would be indicated by the lack of effect of GATM deficiency on intestinal inflammation and creatine levels.

We hypothesize that PNPLA6, a patatin-like phospholipase, plays a crucial role in the development of Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX) by impairing the hydrolysis of cholesteryl esters in the brain. Specifically, we propose that PNPLA6 deficiency leads to accumulation of toxic cholesteryl esters, which in turn disrupts bile acid synthesis and leads to the characteristic accumulation of cholestanol in CTX patients. We predict that overexpressing PNPLA6 in CTX patient-derived cells will reduce cholestanol levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, knocking down PNPLA6 in healthy cells will increase cholestanol levels, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of PNPLA6's role in lipid metabolism and the pathological features of CTX.

We hypothesize that PTDSS2, a phosphatidylserine synthase, plays a crucial role in the development of Hypercholanemia, familial 3, by regulating phospholipid composition in bile canalicular membranes. Specifically, we propose that impaired PTDSS2 activity disrupts phosphatidylserine synthesis, leading to altered membrane fluidity and reduced bile salt export pump (BSEP) function. This results in decreased bile salt secretion and subsequent hypercholanemia. We predict that experimental reduction of PTDSS2 activity in hepatocytes will decrease BSEP-mediated bile salt transport, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of PTDSS2 will rescue BSEP function and bile salt secretion, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of phospholipid synthesis and bile salt transport.
