We hypothesize that CYP8B1, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, contributes to MHC class I deficiency 1 by modulating the metabolism of cholesterol, which in turn affects the organization of lipid rafts in the plasma membrane. These lipid rafts are crucial for the proper assembly and transport of MHC class I molecules. Specifically, we predict that altered CYP8B1 activity will lead to changes in cholesterol metabolism, disrupting lipid raft formation and resulting in reduced MHC class I expression on the cell surface. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that CYP8B1 inhibition restores normal lipid raft structure and MHC class I expression in cells from MHC class I deficiency 1 patients. Refutation would occur if CYP8B1 inhibition has no effect on MHC class I expression or lipid raft organization.

We hypothesize that Acetylserotonin Methyltransferase (ASMT) contributes to Rickets vitamin D-dependent 1A by regulating the methylation of vitamin D receptors, thereby affecting the expression of genes involved in bone mineralization. ASMT, typically known for its role in melatonin synthesis, may also methylate vitamin D receptors, reducing their affinity for 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. This decreased affinity impairs the transcriptional activation of genes essential for bone mineralization, leading to the characteristic bone softening in Rickets vitamin D-dependent 1A. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating reduced vitamin D receptor methylation and improved bone mineralization in ASMT-deficient models of the disease. Refutation would come from showing no effect of ASMT inhibition on vitamin D receptor activity or bone mineralization in these models.

We hypothesize that LTA4H (leukotriene A4 hydrolase) plays a crucial role in the development of Osteopetrosis, autosomal recessive 3, by regulating the biosynthesis of leukotriene B4 (LTB4), a potent osteoclast activator. Specifically, LTA4H's enzymatic activity influences osteoclast formation and bone resorption by modulating LTB4 levels. We predict that increased LTA4H activity will lead to enhanced LTB4 production, resulting in increased osteoclast activity and bone resorption, thereby alleviating the bone density phenotype characteristic of Osteopetrosis, autosomal recessive 3. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased bone resorption in osteopetrotic mice treated with LTA4H activators, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased bone resorption in response to LTA4H inhibition.

We hypothesize that PCYT1A, the enzyme responsible for converting CTP to CDP-diacylglycerol, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Adenylosuccinase deficiency. Specifically, we propose that PCYT1A's activity affects the availability of CTP, a precursor for nucleotide synthesis, which in turn impacts the purine nucleotide cycle. Impaired Adenylosuccinase activity leads to accumulation of SAICAR, a toxic intermediate. We predict that overexpression of PCYT1A will exacerbate Adenylosuccinase deficiency by depleting CTP pools, thereby increasing SAICAR accumulation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through increased SAICAR levels in cells overexpressing PCYT1A, while refutation would be demonstrated by unchanged or decreased SAICAR levels.

We hypothesize that galactosylceramidase (GALC) is mechanistically connected to Retinitis pigmentosa 79 through its role in sphingolipid metabolism. Specifically, impaired GALC activity leads to accumulation of toxic galactosylceramides in photoreceptor cells, triggering oxidative stress and apoptosis. We predict that overexpression of GALC in retinal cells of Retinitis pigmentosa 79 models will reduce galactosylceramide levels and mitigate photoreceptor degeneration. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved retinal function and structure in GALC-overexpressing models, while refutation would be shown by no significant difference in retinal degeneration between GALC-overexpressing and control models. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of GALC and its role in sphingolipid metabolism, and specifically addresses the pathogenesis of Retinitis pigmentosa 79.

We hypothesize that UQCRQ, a subunit of the mitochondrial cytochrome b-c1 complex, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long-chain deficiency. Specifically, we propose that UQCRQ's dysfunction impairs the electron transport chain, leading to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, which in turn exacerbates the accumulation of very long-chain acyl-CoAs. This accumulation is due to the impaired activity of very long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (VLCAD), the enzyme deficient in this disease. We predict that overexpressing UQCRQ in VLCAD-deficient cells will reduce ROS production and decrease very long-chain acyl-CoA levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, knocking down UQCRQ will worsen the metabolic defect, refuting our hypothesis.

terminal_shown: Polycystic liver disease 3 with or without kidney cysts
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that xanthine dehydrogenase (XDH) contributes to the development of Polycystic liver disease 3 (PLD3) with or without kidney cysts through its role in purine metabolism and subsequent oxidative stress. Specifically, XDH's production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) leads to increased cystogenesis and fibrosis in the liver. We predict that XDH inhibition will reduce liver cyst formation in PLD3 models, confirmed by decreased cyst size and number. Conversely, XDH overexpression will exacerbate disease severity. This hypothesis is grounded in XDH's known biochemistry and the established link between oxidative stress and cystic disease progression. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating a significant reduction in liver cysts upon XDH inhibition in PLD3 animal models, while refutation would involve showing no effect of XDH modulation on disease progression.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, ataxia, and seizures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that COQ5, an enzyme involved in coenzyme Q biosynthesis, plays a crucial role in the development of Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, ataxia, and seizures. Specifically, we propose that impaired COQ5 activity disrupts mitochondrial energy metabolism in neural progenitor cells, leading to defective neuronal differentiation and brain development. We predict that COQ5 deficiency will result in decreased coenzyme Q levels, increased oxidative stress, and impaired neurogenesis in affected individuals. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the observation of reduced COQ5 expression and coenzyme Q levels in patient-derived neural cells, while refutation would be shown by normal COQ5 activity and coenzyme Q levels in these cells.

We hypothesize that CDKN1A, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor, plays a crucial role in regulating the expression of 3-hydroxyisobutryl-CoA hydrolase (HIBCH) by modulating the activity of transcription factors involved in its expression. Specifically, CDKN1A inhibits cell cycle progression, leading to increased expression of HIBCH. In 3-hydroxyisobutryl-CoA hydrolase deficiency, reduced HIBCH activity disrupts valine catabolism. We predict that overexpression of CDKN1A will increase HIBCH expression and partially rescue the metabolic defect in cells from patients with 3-hydroxyisobutryl-CoA hydrolase deficiency. Confirmation would be demonstrated by increased HIBCH enzyme activity and reduced 3-hydroxyisobutryl-CoA levels in patient cells overexpressing CDKN1A, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased HIBCH activity.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 4
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that B4GALT1, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, contributes to Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 4, by modifying the glycosylation pattern of the SDHB subunit, altering its stability and mitochondrial localization. Specifically, we propose that B4GALT1-mediated glycosylation enhances SDHB degradation, leading to reduced complex II activity. We predict that overexpressing B4GALT1 in cells will decrease SDHB protein levels and complex II activity, while inhibiting B4GALT1 will have the opposite effect. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant decrease in SDHB protein levels and complex II activity in B4GALT1-overexpressing cells, whereas refutation would be shown by no change in SDHB levels or complex II activity upon B4GALT1 modulation.

We hypothesize that GALK1, the galactose kinase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Laurence-Moon syndrome through its impact on galactose metabolism and subsequent effects on insulin signaling. Specifically, we propose that impaired GALK1 activity leads to accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate, which inhibits phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) activity, disrupting insulin signaling and contributing to the syndrome's characteristic insulin resistance. We predict that overexpressing GALK1 in patient-derived cells will restore normal insulin signaling, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if GALK1 overexpression has no effect on insulin signaling, our hypothesis will be refuted. This mechanistic connection is grounded in known biochemistry of galactose metabolism and insulin signaling pathways.

We hypothesize that NUS1, a mitochondrial dehydrogenase, contributes to the development of Inflammatory bowel disease 13 (IBD13) by modulating the mitochondrial respiratory chain and subsequent reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. Specifically, we propose that NUS1 dysfunction leads to impaired mitochondrial Complex I activity, resulting in increased ROS production and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. This, in turn, exacerbates intestinal inflammation characteristic of IBD13. We predict that NUS1 knockdown in intestinal epithelial cells will increase ROS production and NLRP3 activation, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, NUS1 overexpression will reduce ROS production and alleviate inflammation, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of mitochondrial dysfunction in IBD pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that the Src kinase (SRC) contributes to the pathogenesis of Sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase deficiency by phosphorylating and inhibiting the sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase (SQR) enzyme, thereby disrupting mitochondrial sulfide detoxification. This leads to accumulation of toxic sulfide species, causing mitochondrial dysfunction. We predict that SRC inhibition will increase SQR activity and mitigate disease symptoms. Confirmation would come from experiments showing reduced SQR phosphorylation and increased enzyme activity in cells treated with SRC inhibitors. Refutation would occur if SRC inhibition fails to rescue SQR activity or improve mitochondrial function in Sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase deficiency models.

We hypothesize that CH25H, an enzyme involved in cholesterol metabolism, contributes to the pathogenesis of Perrault syndrome 2 by modulating the biosynthesis of 25-hydroxycholesterol, a potent regulator of ovarian function. Specifically, we propose that reduced CH25H activity leads to decreased 25-hydroxycholesterol production, disrupting the normal regulation of ovarian follicle development and contributing to the ovarian dysgenesis characteristic of Perrault syndrome 2. We predict that experimental knockdown of CH25H in ovarian cells will result in decreased 25-hydroxycholesterol levels and impaired follicle development, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of CH25H will rescue follicle development, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of 25-hydroxycholesterol in regulating ovarian function and the established link between cholesterol metabolism and reproductive health.

We hypothesize that AGA (aspartylglucosaminidase) is mechanistically connected to N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency through the regulation of nitrogen metabolism. Specifically, AGA's role in breaking down glycoproteins may influence the availability of glutamate, a precursor for N-acetylglutamate synthesis. We predict that AGA deficiency will lead to decreased glutamate levels, thereby reducing N-acetylglutamate synthase activity and exacerbating the disease. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased N-acetylglutamate levels in AGA-deficient cells. Refutation would occur if AGA deficiency has no effect on glutamate or N-acetylglutamate levels, indicating an alternative mechanism underlying N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of nitrogen metabolism and the role of AGA in glycoprotein degradation.

terminal_shown: Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity, 1, with or without fractures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that DEGS2, a delta-4-desaturase involved in sphingolipid metabolism, plays a crucial role in the development of Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity, 1, with or without fractures. Specifically, we propose that DEGS2 regulates the balance of ceramides and sphingosines in chondrocytes, affecting cartilage matrix composition and joint integrity. We predict that decreased DEGS2 activity will lead to altered sphingolipid profiles, resulting in impaired cartilage formation and increased joint laxity. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the observation of decreased DEGS2 expression and concomitant changes in sphingolipid profiles in patient-derived chondrocytes. Refutation would be evidenced by normal sphingolipid profiles and DEGS2 activity in patient samples.

We hypothesize that SOAT1 (sterol O-acyltransferase 1) plays a crucial role in the development of Hypotrichosis 4 by regulating cholesterol esterification in hair follicle cells. Specifically, SOAT1-mediated cholesterol esterification modulates the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, essential for hair follicle morphogenesis. We predict that overexpression of SOAT1 in hair follicle cells will lead to increased cholesterol esterification, reduced Wnt/β-catenin signaling, and subsequently, impaired hair growth, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, SOAT1 inhibition will rescue hair growth in Hypotrichosis 4 models, refuting our hypothesis. This prediction can be tested through in vitro and in vivo experiments using SOAT1 overexpression or inhibition in hair follicle cells and Hypotrichosis 4 mouse models.

We hypothesize that NDUFS3, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, musculocontractural type 1, by regulating the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in dermal fibroblasts. Elevated ROS levels can lead to the degradation of collagen and other extracellular matrix components, resulting in the characteristic skin hyperextensibility and tissue fragility. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of NDUFS3 in dermal fibroblasts will increase ROS production and decrease collagen synthesis, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFS3 will reduce ROS levels and restore normal collagen production, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial complex I and its role in regulating ROS production.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, dysmorphic facies, and skin abnormalities
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that MAN2A2, an alpha-mannosidase, plays a crucial role in the development of Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, dysmorphic facies, and skin abnormalities. Specifically, we propose that MAN2A2 is involved in the glycoprotein processing pathway, where it trims mannose residues from glycoproteins. Abnormal MAN2A2 activity leads to impaired glycoprotein function, disrupting cell-cell interactions and signaling essential for neurodevelopment and skin homeostasis. We predict that patients with this disorder will have elevated levels of abnormally glycosylated proteins in their skin and brain tissues. Confirmation would come from mass spectrometry analysis of glycoproteins in patient samples, while refutation would be evident if no significant differences in glycoprotein profiles are observed.

We hypothesize that Arylsulfatase A (ARSA) is mechanistically connected to Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase deficiency through the regulation of sulfated glycosaminoglycans in the endoplasmic reticulum. ARSA's enzymatic activity affects the sulfation status of glycosaminoglycans, which in turn influences the proper folding and function of Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase. We predict that ARSA deficiency will lead to increased sulfation of glycosaminoglycans, causing misfolding and decreased activity of Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase activity in cells with ARSA deficiency, while refutation would be seen if ARSA deficiency has no effect on Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase activity or protein structure.

We hypothesize that PGAP2, a phosphatidylglycerophosphatase involved in glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor biosynthesis, plays a crucial role in the development of Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy. Specifically, we propose that impaired PGAP2 activity disrupts GPI-anchored protein function, leading to defective bone and retinal cell signaling. This results in the characteristic skeletal and retinal abnormalities of the disease. We predict that patients with Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy will exhibit reduced PGAP2 enzyme activity and altered GPI-anchored protein profiles. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by identifying PGAP2 mutations in affected individuals and observing rescue of disease phenotypes with PGAP2 enzyme replacement therapy. Refutation would involve failure to detect PGAP2 dysfunction in patients or lack of therapeutic response to PGAP2 supplementation.

We hypothesize that CYP4F8, a fatty acid omega-hydroxylase, contributes to the development of Bachmann-Bupp syndrome by impairing the metabolism of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs). Specifically, reduced CYP4F8 activity leads to the accumulation of toxic VLCFA intermediates, which disrupts the function of peroxisomes, organelles critical for fatty acid degradation. This peroxisomal dysfunction triggers a cascade of cellular events, including oxidative stress and inflammation, ultimately resulting in the characteristic symptoms of Bachmann-Bupp syndrome. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that CYP4F8 overexpression in patient cells reduces VLCFA accumulation and alleviates disease symptoms, while refutation would result from findings that CYP4F8 inhibition has no effect on VLCFA metabolism or disease progression.

terminal_shown: Developmental delay with short stature, dysmorphic facial features, and sparse hair 1
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CARNMT1, a carnitine O-palmitoyltransferase, plays a crucial role in the development of Developmental delay with short stature, dysmorphic facial features, and sparse hair 1. Specifically, we propose that CARNMT1 regulates fatty acid metabolism in developing tissues, and its dysfunction leads to impaired energy production and altered lipid signaling. We predict that CARNMT1 deficiency will result in decreased palmitoylated protein levels and altered gene expression in affected tissues. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced palmitoylation of key developmental proteins in patient-derived cells, while refutation would be shown by normal palmitoylation patterns despite CARNMT1 deficiency. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of carnitine O-palmitoyltransferases and their role in fatty acid metabolism.

We hypothesize that CARS2, a cysteinyl-tRNA synthetase, plays a crucial role in the development of Trichothiodystrophy 9, non-photosensitive, by impairing translation of essential proteins involved in hair follicle and nail development. Specifically, mutations in CARS2 lead to defective aminoacylation of cysteinyl-tRNA, resulting in mistranslation and degradation of key proteins. We predict that cells from Trichothiodystrophy 9 patients will exhibit reduced levels of properly translated proteins, such as keratins and collagens, due to CARS2 dysfunction. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced protein synthesis and increased protein degradation in patient-derived cells, while refutation would be shown by normal protein translation and stability despite CARS2 mutations.

We hypothesize that PPIP5K2, an enzyme involved in inositol phosphate metabolism, contributes to the development of Schizophrenia through its role in regulating neuronal IP3 receptor signaling. Specifically, PPIP5K2-generated inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) modulates IP3 receptor activity, affecting calcium release and neuronal excitability. We predict that increased PPIP5K2 activity will lead to enhanced IP3 receptor-mediated calcium signaling, contributing to the excitatory/inhibitory imbalance characteristic of Schizophrenia. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experiments showing that PPIP5K2 inhibition reduces IP3 receptor activity and alleviates Schizophrenia-like symptoms in animal models. Refutation would be provided by findings that PPIP5K2 inhibition has no effect on IP3 receptor activity or Schizophrenia-like symptoms.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and speech delay, with or without brain abnormalities
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that GALNS (N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase) plays a crucial role in the development of Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and speech delay, with or without brain abnormalities. Specifically, we propose that GALNS deficiency leads to the accumulation of sulfated glycosaminoglycans in the brain, disrupting the regulation of growth factors and signaling pathways essential for neuronal development and migration. This disruption results in abnormal brain formation and function, manifesting as microcephaly and speech delay. We predict that GALNS knockout in neural stem cells will lead to impaired neuronal differentiation and migration, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, rescue of GALNS activity will restore normal neuronal development, refuting our hypothesis if no improvement is observed.

We hypothesize that FAHD1, a flavin-dependent dehydrogenase, plays a crucial role in regulating phosphoserine phosphatase (PSP) activity through a redox-mediated mechanism. Specifically, FAHD1's enzymatic activity modulates the redox state of a critical cysteine residue in PSP, thereby influencing its phosphatase activity. We predict that overexpression of FAHD1 will increase PSP activity, leading to enhanced phosphoserine dephosphorylation, whereas FAHD1 knockdown will decrease PSP activity, exacerbating phosphoserine accumulation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased phosphoserine dephosphorylation in cells overexpressing FAHD1, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased phosphoserine dephosphorylation in response to FAHD1 modulation.

We hypothesize that CHDH (choline dehydrogenase) plays a crucial role in the development of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, kyphoscoliotic type, 1, by regulating the metabolism of choline, a precursor for glycine and hydroxyproline synthesis. Impaired CHDH activity may lead to altered collagen production, characteristic of this disease. Specifically, reduced CHDH activity would decrease the conversion of choline to betaine, disrupting the methylation cycle and subsequently affecting collagen hydroxylation. We predict that patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, kyphoscoliotic type, 1, will exhibit decreased CHDH activity and altered choline metabolism. Confirmation would come from measuring decreased CHDH enzyme activity and altered betaine levels in patient samples, while refutation would be demonstrated by normal CHDH activity and choline metabolism in affected individuals.

We hypothesize that CDO1 (cysteine dioxygenase 1) plays a crucial role in the development of Hyperoxaluria primary 1 (PH1) through its regulation of cysteine metabolism. Specifically, we propose that impaired CDO1 activity leads to increased cysteine availability, which is then converted to oxalate via the cysteine oxidase pathway. This increase in oxalate production contributes to the characteristic hyperoxaluria of PH1. We predict that overexpressing CDO1 in PH1 patient cells will decrease oxalate production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibiting CDO1 activity will increase oxalate production, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of cysteine metabolism and its link to oxalate production, providing a testable hypothesis for the role of CDO1 in PH1.

We hypothesize that PYCR2, an enzyme involved in proline metabolism, contributes to the development of Glutaric aciduria 1 by modulating the levels of alpha-ketoglutarate, a key intermediate in the degradation of glutaryl-CoA. In Glutaric aciduria 1, mutations in the GCDH gene impair glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase activity, leading to accumulation of glutaric acid. We predict that PYCR2's activity will be increased in response to elevated glutaryl-CoA levels, resulting in decreased alpha-ketoglutarate levels and subsequent impairment of the citric acid cycle. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through increased PYCR2 expression and activity in Glutaric aciduria 1 patient cells, while refutation would be demonstrated by unchanged or decreased PYCR2 activity in response to glutaryl-CoA accumulation.

We hypothesize that Mannose Phosphate Isomerase (MPI) plays a crucial role in the development of Usher syndrome 3B by regulating glycoprotein synthesis in the photoreceptor cells of the retina. Specifically, MPI's impairment leads to defective glycosylation of crucial proteins, such as clarin-1, which is essential for photoreceptor function. We predict that MPI deficiency will result in reduced clarin-1 expression and increased photoreceptor cell death, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if MPI overexpression rescues clarin-1 expression and photoreceptor function in Usher syndrome 3B models, our hypothesis will be refuted. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of glycoprotein synthesis and the critical role of clarin-1 in Usher syndrome 3B pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that GLUD1, a glutamate dehydrogenase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of 5-oxoprolinase deficiency by regulating the levels of glutamate, a precursor to 5-oxoproline. In this disease, impaired 5-oxoprolinase activity leads to accumulation of 5-oxoproline. We propose that GLUD1's activity influences the glutamate pool, thereby affecting 5-oxoproline synthesis. Specifically, we predict that overexpression of GLUD1 will decrease 5-oxoproline levels in cells from 5-oxoprolinase deficiency patients, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, GLUD1 inhibition will increase 5-oxoproline levels, refuting our hypothesis. This prediction can be tested through biochemical assays and cellular models of 5-oxoprolinase deficiency, providing insight into the disease's metabolic alterations and potential therapeutic targets.

terminal_shown: Neuropathy, hereditary motor and sensory, 6C, with optic atrophy
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) plays a crucial role in the development of Neuropathy, hereditary motor and sensory, 6C, with optic atrophy. DHFR's role in maintaining tetrahydrofolate levels is essential for purine synthesis and mitochondrial DNA replication. We propose that impaired DHFR activity leads to decreased tetrahydrofolate, disrupting mitochondrial DNA replication and causing mitochondrial dysfunction in peripheral nerves and optic tissues. This results in the characteristic neuropathy and optic atrophy. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating decreased DHFR activity and tetrahydrofolate levels in patient-derived cells, while refutation would require showing no correlation between DHFR activity and disease severity.

terminal_shown: Leukoencephalopathy with dystonia and motor neuropathy
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ACOX1, the enzyme responsible for the initial step in peroxisomal beta-oxidation of fatty acids, plays a crucial role in the development of Leukoencephalopathy with dystonia and motor neuropathy. Specifically, we propose that impaired ACOX1 activity leads to accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, which in turn disrupts myelin lipid composition and function, contributing to the disease's characteristic neurological symptoms. We predict that experimental models with ACOX1 deficiency will exhibit increased levels of very-long-chain fatty acids in brain tissue, which can be confirmed by mass spectrometry analysis. Conversely, rescue of ACOX1 activity will mitigate disease symptoms, refuting our hypothesis if no improvement is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of peroxisomal fatty acid metabolism and its importance in maintaining myelin integrity.

We hypothesize that CYP2B6, through its role in metabolizing arachidonic acid to epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), contributes to the development of Cardiomyopathy, dilated, 2C. Specifically, altered CYP2B6 activity leads to decreased EET production, disrupting normal cardiac myocyte function and promoting dilated cardiomyopathy. We predict that cardiomyocytes from individuals with Cardiomyopathy, dilated, 2C will exhibit reduced CYP2B6 expression and EET levels. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by experimental results showing that CYP2B6 overexpression or EET supplementation rescues cardiomyocyte function in vitro. Refutation would be evidenced by unchanged or worsened cardiomyocyte function following CYP2B6 modulation or EET supplementation. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of CYP2B6 and EETs in cardiovascular health.

We hypothesize that Proactivator Protein (PSAP) plays a crucial role in the development of Brugada syndrome 2 by modulating the sphingolipid metabolism pathway, which affects the function of cardiac sodium channels. Specifically, PSAP's enzymatic activity leads to altered sphingosine levels, influencing the interaction between sphingosine and the SCN5A sodium channel, thereby disrupting normal cardiac ion channel function. We predict that PSAP overexpression will increase sphingosine levels, leading to enhanced SCN5A channel inhibition and exacerbated Brugada syndrome 2 phenotypes. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by experimental results showing a significant correlation between PSAP activity and SCN5A channel dysfunction in Brugada syndrome 2 models. Refutation would be evident if PSAP inhibition fails to rescue SCN5A channel function in these models.

terminal_shown: Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with impaired intellectual development B14
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that HSD11B1, an enzyme converting cortisone to cortisol, contributes to Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with impaired intellectual development B14 by regulating glucocorticoid-induced gene expression in muscle cells. Specifically, HSD11B1's activity modulates the expression of genes involved in dystroglycan processing, leading to impaired dystroglycan function and muscle cell integrity. We predict that inhibiting HSD11B1 in muscle cells from B14 patients will decrease glucocorticoid-induced gene expression and improve dystroglycan processing, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpressing HSD11B1 will exacerbate dystroglycanopathy, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of glucocorticoids in regulating gene expression and the importance of dystroglycan in maintaining muscle cell function.

We hypothesize that the GNAS enzyme, which codes for the stimulatory G-protein alpha subunit, plays a crucial role in the development of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 84 (DEE84) through its regulation of neuronal cAMP signaling. Specifically, we propose that mutated GNAS leads to aberrant cAMP production, disrupting normal neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity. We predict that DEE84 patients with GNAS mutations will exhibit altered cAMP levels in neuronal tissues, which can be confirmed by measuring cAMP concentrations in patient-derived neurons. Refutation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by normal cAMP levels in DEE84 patients with GNAS mutations, suggesting an alternative disease mechanism.

We hypothesize that NUDT13, a nudix hydrolase, plays a crucial role in mitigating the toxic effects of short-chain acyl-CoA esters accumulated in Short/branched-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Specifically, NUDT13 hydrolyzes these toxic metabolites, reducing their levels and subsequent damage to cellular components. We predict that overexpression of NUDT13 in cells from patients with Short/branched-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency will decrease the accumulation of short-chain acyl-CoA esters, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, knocking down NUDT13 will exacerbate the accumulation of these toxic metabolites, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of nudix hydrolases and the pathophysiology of Short/branched-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.

We hypothesize that CYP2J2, an epoxygenase, plays a crucial role in the development of Arterial calcification of infancy, generalized, 1, by regulating the metabolism of fatty acids and producing anti-inflammatory epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs). Decreased CYP2J2 activity leads to reduced EET production, resulting in increased inflammation and vascular calcification. We predict that CYP2J2 overexpression will reduce calcification in arterial tissues, while inhibition will exacerbate it. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased arterial calcification in CYP2J2-overexpressing mouse models of the disease, while refutation would be shown by no significant difference in calcification between CYP2J2-overexpressing and control models. This mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of CYP2J2 and EETs in vascular health.

We hypothesize that ALOX12B, an enzyme involved in lipid peroxidation, contributes to the pathogenesis of Mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency 1 (MTPD1) by disrupting mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation. Specifically, ALOX12B's products may inhibit the activity of the mitochondrial trifunctional protein, exacerbating the deficiency. We predict that inhibiting ALOX12B will reduce oxidative stress and improve fatty acid oxidation in MTPD1 patient cells. Confirmation would come from observing increased trifunctional protein activity and reduced lipid peroxides in patient cells treated with ALOX12B inhibitors. Refutation would occur if ALOX12B inhibition fails to improve mitochondrial function or if ALOX12B's products are found not to interact with the trifunctional protein.

We hypothesize that KARS1, a lysyl-tRNA synthetase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency by modulating the translation of genes involved in the histidine and folate metabolism pathways. Specifically, impaired KARS1 function leads to misfolded or mistranslated proteins, including Glutamate formiminotransferase, resulting in its deficiency. We predict that overexpressing KARS1 in cells from patients with Glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency will increase Glutamate formiminotransferase activity, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, knocking down KARS1 in healthy cells will decrease Glutamate formiminotransferase activity, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed. This connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and their role in maintaining protein homeostasis.

We hypothesize that ENTPD8, an ectonucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase, contributes to the development of Combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria by regulating ATP levels in the mitochondria. Specifically, ENTPD8's nucleotide hydrolysis activity modulates the energy status of the cell, impacting the function of the malonyl-CoA decarboxylase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase enzymes. We predict that overexpression of ENTPD8 will decrease ATP levels, leading to increased accumulation of malonic and methylmalonic acids, whereas inhibition of ENTPD8 will reduce aciduria. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased urinary excretion of malonic and methylmalonic acids in response to ENTPD8 overexpression, while refutation would be shown by no change in aciduria levels upon ENTPD8 modulation.

We hypothesize that Thyroid Peroxidase (TPO) contributes to Erythrocytosis, familial, 8, by modulating the production of hydrogen peroxide, a key regulator of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) signaling. Elevated HIF activity is associated with increased erythropoietin production, leading to excessive erythrocyte production. We predict that TPO overexpression will increase hydrogen peroxide levels, enhancing HIF signaling and erythropoietin production, thereby confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, TPO inhibition will reduce hydrogen peroxide levels, decreasing HIF signaling and erythropoietin production, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of hydrogen peroxide in redox signaling and HIF regulation, and is specifically relevant to Erythrocytosis, familial, 8, where dysregulated erythropoietin production is a key disease mechanism.

We hypothesize that NADH dehydrogenase subunit 1 (ND1) contributes to the development of Juvenile arthritis through its role in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. In juvenile arthritis, ND1-mediated ROS production leads to increased oxidative stress, activating NF-κB and subsequent pro-inflammatory cytokine release. We predict that ND1 inhibition will reduce ROS production, decrease NF-κB activation, and alleviate arthritis symptoms in a juvenile arthritis model. Confirmation would come from reduced joint inflammation and cytokine levels in ND1-inhibited models, while refutation would be evident if ND1 inhibition has no effect on arthritis symptoms or if ROS production is not decreased. This hypothesis is grounded in the known role of mitochondrial ROS in inflammation and the involvement of NF-κB in arthritis pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that CYP4F3, a fatty acid omega-hydroxylase, contributes to the pathogenesis of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2D, by disrupting lipid metabolism in peripheral nerves. Specifically, CYP4F3's abnormal activity leads to altered levels of very-long-chain fatty acids, which accumulate in Schwann cells and axons, causing mitochondrial dysfunction and axonal degeneration. We predict that inhibiting CYP4F3 will reduce disease severity, as measured by improved nerve conduction velocities and reduced axonal damage in mouse models of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2D. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by decreased disease progression in CYP4F3-inhibited mice, while refutation would be indicated by no significant difference in disease severity between treated and untreated mice.

We hypothesize that CYP4F8, a fatty acid omega-hydroxylase, contributes to the development of Deafness, autosomal recessive, 44 (DFNB44) by disrupting the metabolism of fatty acids essential for inner ear function. Specifically, CYP4F8's impaired activity leads to altered levels of long-chain fatty acids, which in turn affect the structure and function of stereocilia in cochlear hair cells. We predict that DFNB44 patients with CYP4F8 mutations will exhibit abnormal fatty acid profiles in their inner ear tissues, which can be confirmed by targeted metabolomics analysis. Conversely, rescue of CYP4F8 activity in patient-derived cells will restore normal fatty acid metabolism and improve hair cell function, refuting the hypothesis if no improvement is observed.

We hypothesize that CYP3A5 plays a crucial role in the development of Hyperoxaluria primary 2 by metabolizing glyoxylate to glycolate, thereby reducing the substrate availability for the disease-causing enzyme, glyoxylate/hydroxypyruvate reductase (GRHPR). Impaired CYP3A5 activity would lead to increased glyoxylate levels, exacerbating oxalate production. We predict that overexpressing CYP3A5 in cells from Hyperoxaluria primary 2 patients will decrease oxalate levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibiting CYP3A5 activity will increase oxalate production, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of glyoxylate metabolism and the disease-causing mutations in GRHPR.

We hypothesize that the enzyme Dihydrolipoyllysine-residue succinyltransferase (DLST) plays a crucial role in the development of Congenital disorder of glycosylation 2T (CDG2T) through its involvement in the regulation of mitochondrial energy metabolism. Specifically, DLST's dysfunction leads to impaired succinylation of mitochondrial proteins, disrupting the tricarboxylic acid cycle and resulting in altered glycosylation patterns. We predict that DLST knockdown in patient-derived cells will lead to decreased mitochondrial respiration and increased glycosylation defects, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of DLST will rescue these defects, refuting the hypothesis if no improvement is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in DLST's known role in mitochondrial metabolism and the established link between energy metabolism and glycosylation pathways.

We hypothesize that HSD17B7, a 17-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, plays a crucial role in the development of AMED syndrome, a digenic disorder. Specifically, we propose that HSD17B7's impaired activity disrupts the conversion of estrone to estradiol, leading to an imbalance in estrogen metabolism. This imbalance triggers an aberrant signaling cascade, affecting the expression of genes involved in bone and tooth development, characteristic of AMED syndrome. We predict that overexpressing HSD17B7 in AMED syndrome patient-derived cells will rescue the disease phenotype, whereas inhibiting HSD17B7 activity will exacerbate it. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing restored bone and tooth development in HSD17B7-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be indicated by unchanged or worsened disease phenotypes.

We hypothesize that CYP11A1, a mitochondrial cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme, contributes to Recurrent myoglobinuria mitochondrial by impairing mitochondrial function through altered cholesterol metabolism. Specifically, CYP11A1's role in converting cholesterol to pregnenolone may be disrupted, leading to accumulation of toxic cholesterol intermediates that damage mitochondrial membranes and disrupt myoglobin import. This would result in myoglobin release into the urine. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that CYP11A1 inhibition or knockdown increases myoglobinuria in mitochondrial disease models. Refutation would occur if CYP11A1 modulation has no effect on myoglobinuria or mitochondrial function in these models.

We hypothesize that AKT3, a serine/threonine kinase, plays a crucial role in the development of Spondyloocular syndrome by regulating the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, which affects osteoclast differentiation and bone resorption. Specifically, AKT3 phosphorylates and activates NF-κB, leading to increased expression of genes involved in osteoclastogenesis. We predict that overexpression of AKT3 in osteoclast precursors will enhance osteoclast formation and bone resorption, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibition of AKT3 will reduce osteoclast activity and alleviate Spondyloocular syndrome symptoms, such as skeletal abnormalities and ocular defects. This hypothesis is grounded in known biochemistry of AKT signaling and its role in bone metabolism, and can be tested through in vitro osteoclast differentiation assays and in vivo models of Spondyloocular syndrome.

We hypothesize that thymidine phosphorylase (TYMP) plays a crucial role in the development of Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, Genevieve type, by regulating the balance of nucleotide pools in chondrocytes. Specifically, TYMP's activity in converting thymidine to thymine affects the availability of nucleotides for DNA synthesis and repair. We predict that overexpression of TYMP in chondrocytes will lead to an imbalance in nucleotide pools, resulting in impaired chondrocyte growth and differentiation, characteristic of Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, Genevieve type. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the observation of increased TYMP activity and altered nucleotide pools in chondrocytes from affected individuals, while refutation would be shown by the lack of correlation between TYMP activity and disease severity.

We hypothesize that GCH1 (GTP cyclohydrolase 1) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase short-chain deficiency by regulating the tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) levels, which are essential for the activity of short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase. Decreased GCH1 activity leads to reduced BH4 levels, impairing short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase function and resulting in the accumulation of short-chain acyl-CoA esters. We predict that supplementation with BH4 or overexpression of GCH1 will improve enzyme activity and reduce disease severity, whereas GCH1 inhibition will exacerbate the condition. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved clinical outcomes in patients with Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase short-chain deficiency treated with BH4 supplementation, while refutation would be shown by lack of response to BH4 treatment.

We hypothesize that DDC (Dopa decarboxylase) contributes to the pathogenesis of Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 deficiency, lethal neonatal, by modulating the synthesis of polyamines, which in turn affect the expression of genes involved in fatty acid metabolism. Specifically, we propose that DDC-derived polyamines regulate the transcription of PPARα, a key transcription factor controlling the expression of CPT2. We predict that inhibition of DDC will decrease polyamine synthesis, leading to reduced PPARα activity and subsequent downregulation of CPT2 expression, exacerbating the disease phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by the observation that DDC inhibition increases disease severity in a mouse model of CPT2 deficiency, while refutation would be demonstrated by the lack of effect on CPT2 expression or disease outcome.

We hypothesize that the BRCA1 enzyme plays a crucial role in maintaining genomic stability, and its dysfunction contributes to the development of Yunis-Varon syndrome. Specifically, BRCA1's involvement in homologous recombination repair is essential for preventing catastrophic genomic instability. In Yunis-Varon syndrome, BRCA1's impaired function leads to an accumulation of DNA damage, triggering a pro-inflammatory response and subsequent tissue degeneration. We predict that patients with Yunis-Varon syndrome will exhibit reduced BRCA1 expression and impaired homologous recombination repair, confirmed by increased frequencies of chromosomal breaks and aberrant DNA repair foci. Refutation would come from observations of normal BRCA1 expression and function in Yunis-Varon syndrome patients, or failure to rescue disease phenotypes with BRCA1 overexpression.

We hypothesize that glycine dehydrogenase (GLDC) plays a crucial role in the development of Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy. Specifically, we propose that impaired GLDC activity disrupts glycine metabolism, leading to an accumulation of glycine in chondrocytes and photoreceptors. This excess glycine alters the redox state, causing oxidative stress and subsequent damage to these cells. We predict that GLDC knockdown in chondrocytes and photoreceptors will result in increased glycine levels, oxidative stress, and cell death, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, GLDC overexpression will rescue these cells, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of glycine metabolism and its role in maintaining cellular redox balance.

We hypothesize that NDST1, an enzyme involved in heparan sulfate biosynthesis, contributes to Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 21 through altered mitochondrial membrane dynamics. Specifically, NDST1's dysregulation leads to impaired heparan sulfate production, disrupting the interaction between heparan sulfate and mitochondrial proteins, ultimately causing mitochondrial membrane instability. This instability triggers a cascade of events resulting in mitochondrial DNA depletion. We predict that NDST1 overexpression will rescue mitochondrial DNA levels in cells from Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 21 patients, while NDST1 knockdown will exacerbate the depletion. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased mitochondrial DNA copy numbers upon NDST1 overexpression, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in mitochondrial DNA levels.

We hypothesize that PGAP4, a phosphatidylglycerophosphatase, plays a crucial role in the development of Microphthalmia, isolated, 8, by regulating the biosynthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins. Specifically, PGAP4's enzymatic activity is necessary for the proper maturation and localization of GPI-anchored proteins involved in eye development. Disruption of PGAP4 function leads to impaired GPI-anchored protein maturation, resulting in abnormal eye morphogenesis and microphthalmia. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of PGAP4 in human retinal pigment epithelial cells will result in reduced cell surface expression of GPI-anchored proteins, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of PGAP4 will rescue this phenotype, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed.

We hypothesize that IDH1, specifically the R132H mutant form, contributes to the development of Spastic paraplegia 81, autosomal recessive, by impairing mitochondrial energy metabolism. IDH1 normally catalyzes the conversion of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate, producing NADPH. In Spastic paraplegia 81, autosomal recessive, mutant IDH1 may lead to decreased NADPH production, disrupting mitochondrial redox balance and energy production. We predict that cells from patients with Spastic paraplegia 81, autosomal recessive, will exhibit decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased oxidative stress, which can be confirmed by measuring mitochondrial membrane potential and oxidative stress markers in patient-derived cells. Refutation would come from normal mitochondrial function and redox balance in patient cells, indicating an alternative disease mechanism.

We hypothesize that Malonyl-CoA:Acyl Carrier Protein Acyltransferase (MCAT) plays a crucial role in breast cancer development by regulating fatty acid synthesis, a key process in cancer cell proliferation. MCAT's activity leads to increased malonyl-CoA levels, which in turn inhibit fatty acid oxidation and promote lipogenesis. This shift enhances cancer cell growth and survival. We predict that MCAT overexpression in breast cancer cells will increase fatty acid synthesis and tumor growth, whereas MCAT inhibition will reduce these processes. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through increased tumor growth in MCAT-overexpressing breast cancer xenografts, while refutation would be seen if MCAT inhibition fails to reduce tumor growth. This hypothesis is grounded in known biochemistry of fatty acid metabolism and its role in cancer cell metabolism.

We hypothesize that dihydroxyacetone phosphate acyltransferase (DHAPAT) is not the enzyme of interest, instead, the source enzyme DCXR (dihydroxyacetone phosphate reductase, also known as carbonyl reductase 1) plays a crucial role in Congenital bile acid synthesis defect 2. DCXR is involved in the reduction of dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glycerol, which can then be used for bile acid synthesis. We propose that impaired DCXR activity leads to reduced glycerol availability, disrupting bile acid synthesis and contributing to the disease. If DCXR activity is increased in cells from patients with Congenital bile acid synthesis defect 2, bile acid production will increase, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if DCXR overexpression does not rescue bile acid synthesis, our hypothesis will be refuted.

We hypothesize that COLGALT2, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Dowling-Degos disease 4 by aberrantly glycosylating and thereby inactivating the KRT5 protein, a key component of keratin intermediate filaments. This disruption leads to skin fragility and reticular pigmentation characteristic of the disease. We predict that COLGALT2 overexpression in keratinocytes will result in decreased KRT5 function and increased disease-like phenotypes, whereas COLGALT2 inhibition will rescue KRT5 function and ameliorate symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing decreased KRT5 activity in COLGALT2-overexpressing keratinocytes, while refutation would be demonstrated by unchanged KRT5 function despite COLGALT2 overexpression.

We hypothesize that BCL2, an anti-apoptotic enzyme, contributes to Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 57 (COXPD57) by regulating mitochondrial outer membrane permeability, thereby modulating the interaction between mitochondria and the cytosol. Specifically, we propose that BCL2's anti-apoptotic function disrupts the normal balance of mitochondrial dynamics, leading to impaired mitochondrial biogenesis and function, characteristic of COXPD57. We predict that overexpression of BCL2 in COXPD57 patient cells will exacerbate oxidative phosphorylation defects, while BCL2 inhibition will restore mitochondrial function. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant decrease in oxidative phosphorylation complex activity in BCL2-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by no change in mitochondrial function upon BCL2 modulation.

We hypothesize that ABCB11, a bile salt export pump, plays a crucial role in the development of Neu-Laxova syndrome 2 by disrupting cholesterol homeostasis. Specifically, we propose that impaired ABCB11 function leads to accumulation of toxic bile acids, which in turn inhibit the expression of genes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis, resulting in severe developmental abnormalities characteristic of Neu-Laxova syndrome 2. We predict that experimental knockdown of ABCB11 in cellular models will lead to decreased cholesterol production and increased bile acid toxicity, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, rescue of ABCB11 function will restore cholesterol homeostasis and alleviate disease symptoms, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed. This mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of bile acid and cholesterol metabolism.

We hypothesize that TRI-TAT2-2, a mitochondrial enzyme, plays a crucial role in regulating the levels of toxic dipeptides in cells, which is disrupted in Prolidase deficiency. Normally, Prolidase breaks down these dipeptides, but in its deficiency, they accumulate. TRI-TAT2-2, through its interaction with the mitochondrial membrane, facilitates the transport of these dipeptides into the mitochondria for degradation. We predict that overexpressing TRI-TAT2-2 in cells from Prolidase deficiency patients will reduce dipeptide accumulation and alleviate disease symptoms. Confirmation would come from measuring decreased dipeptide levels in patient cells overexpressing TRI-TAT2-2. Refutation would occur if dipeptide levels remain unchanged, indicating TRI-TAT2-2 does not contribute to dipeptide degradation in this context.

We hypothesize that ELOVL5, an enzyme involved in fatty acid elongation, plays a crucial role in the development of Pontocerebellar hypoplasia 2D (PCH2D) through its impact on sphingolipid biosynthesis. Specifically, we propose that ELOVL5's dysfunction leads to altered very-long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) production, disrupting sphingolipid metabolism and subsequently affecting neuronal development and survival. We predict that PCH2D patients will exhibit abnormal VLCFA profiles and altered sphingolipid composition in brain tissue. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by detecting significant changes in VLCFA and sphingolipid levels in PCH2D patient samples compared to controls. Refutation would occur if no significant differences in VLCFA and sphingolipid profiles are observed between PCH2D patients and controls.

We hypothesize that ATP6V1FP2, a vacuolar ATPase regulatory subunit, plays a crucial role in maintaining Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) homeostasis by regulating the pH-dependent transport of CoQ10 precursors in the lysosome. We propose that ATP6V1FP2 dysfunction impairs CoQ10 biosynthesis, leading to primary Coenzyme Q10 deficiency, 1. Specifically, we predict that ATP6V1FP2 knockdown will decrease CoQ10 levels in cells, which can be confirmed by measuring CoQ10 concentrations in ATP6V1FP2-deficient cells. Conversely, overexpression of ATP6V1FP2 will increase CoQ10 levels, refuting our hypothesis if no such increase is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of vacuolar ATPases in regulating lysosomal pH and the importance of CoQ10 in mitochondrial energy metabolism.

terminal_shown: Epileptic encephalopathy, infantile or early childhood, 3
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that BCL2-associated agonist of cell death (BAD) plays a crucial role in the development of Epileptic encephalopathy, infantile or early childhood, 3, by regulating mitochondrial dynamics and energy metabolism in neuronal cells. Specifically, we propose that BAD modulates the activity of the mitochondrial fission factor Drp1, leading to impaired mitochondrial function and increased oxidative stress. This, in turn, disrupts neuronal excitability and contributes to the onset of epileptic seizures. We predict that BAD knockdown in neuronal cells will reduce Drp1 activity, decrease oxidative stress, and alleviate seizure-like activity in vitro. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing a significant reduction in seizure frequency in BAD knockdown models, while refutation would be indicated by no change in seizure frequency or mitochondrial function.

We hypothesize that NDUFA10, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Glucocorticoid deficiency 5. Specifically, we propose that impaired NDUFA10 function disrupts mitochondrial energy metabolism in steroidogenic cells, leading to decreased ATP production and subsequent impairment of steroid hormone synthesis. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of NDUFA10 in adrenal cells will result in reduced glucocorticoid production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFA10 will rescue glucocorticoid production, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial complex I and its role in energy metabolism, and is specific to Glucocorticoid deficiency 5, a disease characterized by impaired steroid hormone production.

terminal_shown: Skeletal dysplasia, mild, with joint laxity and advanced bone age
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that 3-Hydroxyanthranilate 3,4-Dioxygenase (HAAO) contributes to the development of Skeletal dysplasia, mild, with joint laxity and advanced bone age by regulating the metabolism of tryptophan-derived catabolites, which in turn affect bone growth and development. Specifically, HAAO's activity influences the production of quinolinic acid, a known inhibitor of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling. We predict that HAAO overexpression will lead to increased quinolinic acid production, resulting in reduced BMP signaling and subsequent advanced bone age and joint laxity. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the observation of decreased BMP signaling and increased quinolinic acid levels in skeletal tissues of individuals with HAAO overexpression, while refutation would be shown by the absence of these effects.

We hypothesize that NDUFA5, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Xanthinuria 2 by modulating the mitochondrial respiratory chain's impact on xanthine dehydrogenase activity. Specifically, impaired NDUFA5 function leads to increased reactive oxygen species production, which in turn inhibits xanthine dehydrogenase, resulting in xanthine accumulation. We predict that overexpressing NDUFA5 in Xanthinuria 2 patient cells will increase xanthine dehydrogenase activity and decrease xanthine levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, knocking down NDUFA5 will exacerbate xanthine accumulation, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial complex I and xanthine metabolism.

We hypothesize that NDUFS1, a subunit of Complex I in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Molybdenum cofactor deficiency C. Specifically, we propose that the impaired molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis in this disease leads to decreased sulfite oxidase activity, resulting in accumulated sulfite that inhibits NDUFS1 function. This inhibition disrupts mitochondrial energy production, exacerbating the disease phenotype. We predict that experimental knockdown of NDUFS1 in cells from Molybdenum cofactor deficiency C patients will worsen their metabolic defects, while NDUFS1 overexpression will partially rescue the phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be supported by decreased Complex I activity in patient cells, while refutation would be indicated by unchanged or improved Complex I activity upon NDUFS1 manipulation.

We hypothesize that FASLG (Fas ligand) contributes to Phosphohydroxylysinuria by modulating the immune response and inflammation in the kidney, leading to impaired hydroxylation of lysine residues in collagen. Specifically, FASLG-induced apoptosis of renal cells disrupts the function of lysyl hydroxylase, an enzyme essential for collagen hydroxylation. This results in the accumulation of under-hydroxylated collagen, characteristic of Phosphohydroxylysinuria. We predict that inhibition of FASLG will reduce disease severity, as measured by decreased levels of under-hydroxylated collagen in patient urine. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experimental results showing reduced FASLG expression or activity correlates with improved collagen hydroxylation, while refutation would be indicated by unchanged or worsened collagen hydroxylation despite FASLG inhibition.

We hypothesize that ELOVL5, an enzyme involved in the elongation of long-chain fatty acids, plays a crucial role in the development of Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 deficiency, infantile. Specifically, we propose that ELOVL5's activity leads to the accumulation of very-long-chain acyl-CoAs, which competitively inhibit Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 (CPT2), thereby exacerbating the disease. We predict that overexpression of ELOVL5 in a cellular model of CPT2 deficiency will worsen the disease phenotype, as measured by increased acylcarnitine levels. Conversely, inhibition of ELOVL5 will alleviate the phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experimental evidence showing a direct correlation between ELOVL5 activity and CPT2 inhibition, while refutation would be demonstrated by the absence of such a correlation.

We hypothesize that Delta-like 3 (DLL3) enzyme plays a crucial role in the development of Familial porphyria cutanea tarda (F-PCT) by regulating the expression of hepcidin, a key hormone involved in iron homeostasis. DLL3, a Notch signaling ligand, modulates the transcription of hepcidin, leading to increased iron absorption and accumulation in the liver. This excess iron catalyzes the formation of reactive oxygen species, which in turn inactivate uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD), a critical enzyme in the heme biosynthesis pathway. We predict that DLL3 overexpression will lead to decreased UROD activity and increased porphyrin accumulation, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, DLL3 inhibition will refute our hypothesis by restoring UROD activity and reducing porphyrin levels.

We hypothesize that ABCC2, an ATP-binding cassette transporter, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata 2 (RCDP2) by regulating the intracellular levels of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs). Specifically, we propose that ABCC2 mediates the efflux of VLCFAs from peroxisomes, where they are synthesized. Impaired ABCC2 function would lead to VLCFA accumulation, disrupting peroxisomal function and contributing to RCDP2. We predict that overexpressing ABCC2 in RCDP2 patient cells will reduce VLCFA levels and alleviate disease symptoms, while inhibiting ABCC2 will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would require demonstration of ABCC2-mediated VLCFA transport in peroxisomes and its impact on RCDP2 pathology.

We hypothesize that NDUFA5, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Glucocorticoid deficiency 5 by impairing the mitochondrial function necessary for steroidogenesis in adrenal cells. Specifically, we propose that reduced NDUFA5 expression or activity disrupts the mitochondrial respiratory chain, leading to decreased ATP production and altered redox states, which in turn impede the proper functioning of steroidogenic enzymes. We predict that experimental knockdown of NDUFA5 in adrenal cells will result in decreased glucocorticoid production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFA5 will rescue glucocorticoid production, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial function and steroidogenesis.

We hypothesize that TRT-AGT1-3, a specific enzyme, contributes to the development of Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) by modulating the heme biosynthesis pathway. Specifically, TRT-AGT1-3 may interact with and inhibit the activity of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD), a key enzyme in the heme biosynthesis pathway. This inhibition would lead to the accumulation of porphobilinogen and other heme precursors, characteristic of AIP. We predict that overexpression of TRT-AGT1-3 in cells will decrease PBGD activity and increase porphobilinogen levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, knocking down TRT-AGT1-3 will restore PBGD activity and reduce porphobilinogen accumulation, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of heme biosynthesis and AIP pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that COX10, a mitochondrial enzyme involved in heme biosynthesis, contributes to the development of Cataract 44 through a mechanism involving oxidative stress and protein aggregation. Specifically, COX10 deficiency leads to impaired heme production, disrupting mitochondrial function and increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. Elevated ROS levels damage lens proteins, promoting aggregation and cataract formation. We predict that COX10 overexpression in lens epithelial cells will reduce ROS production and prevent cataract formation in a Cataract 44 model. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced cataract incidence in COX10-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or increased cataract formation despite COX10 overexpression.

terminal_shown: Congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform erythroderma and limb defects
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that VARS2, a mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, plays a crucial role in the development of Congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform erythroderma and limb defects (CHILD) syndrome. Specifically, we propose that mutations in VARS2 lead to impaired aminoacylation of mitochondrial tRNAs, disrupting mitochondrial protein synthesis and causing an energy deficit in developing tissues. This deficit triggers a stress response, activating pro-inflammatory pathways and disrupting limb and skin development. We predict that CHILD syndrome patients with VARS2 mutations will exhibit decreased mitochondrial respiratory complex activity in affected tissues. Confirmation would come from observing reduced complex activity in patient-derived cells, while refutation would result from normal complex activity in these cells.

We hypothesize that EPRS1, a bifunctional enzyme with glutamyl-prolyl-tRNA synthetase and glutamyl-tRNA synthetase activities, plays a crucial role in the development of Rhizomelic dysplasia, Ain-Naz type. Specifically, we propose that impaired EPRS1 function disrupts aminoacyl-tRNA synthesis, leading to defective protein translation and subsequent skeletal dysplasia. We predict that patients with Rhizomelic dysplasia, Ain-Naz type, will exhibit reduced EPRS1 enzyme activity and altered aminoacyl-tRNA profiles. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by experimental results showing decreased EPRS1 activity in patient-derived cells, while refutation would be indicated by normal EPRS1 activity and aminoacyl-tRNA profiles in affected individuals. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and their essential role in protein synthesis.

We hypothesize that pyridoxine 5'-phosphate oxidase (PNPO) plays a crucial role in Lenz-Majewski hyperostotic dwarfism by regulating the bioavailability of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), a cofactor essential for bone metabolism enzymes. Impaired PNPO activity leads to decreased PLP levels, disrupting the function of enzymes involved in collagen cross-linking and bone mineralization. This results in the characteristic hyperostotic and skeletal abnormalities seen in Lenz-Majewski hyperostotic dwarfism. We predict that PNPO enzyme activity will be significantly reduced in patient-derived cells, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if PNPO activity is normal, our hypothesis will be refuted. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of PNPO and PLP in bone metabolism.

We hypothesize that CHKA (choline kinase alpha) plays a crucial role in the development of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 36 (DEE36) through its regulation of phospholipid biosynthesis in neuronal membranes. Specifically, we propose that CHKA's dysregulation leads to altered phosphatidylcholine production, disrupting neuronal membrane structure and function. This, in turn, impairs synaptic transmission and contributes to the epileptic phenotype. We predict that CHKA inhibition will exacerbate DEE36 symptoms, while CHKA activation will ameliorate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing worsened seizure severity in DEE36 models with CHKA inhibitors, while refutation would come from failed replication or opposite effects in these models. This hypothesis is grounded in CHKA's known role in phospholipid metabolism and its importance in maintaining neuronal membrane integrity.

We hypothesize that DHRSX, a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase, contributes to the development of Thrombocytopenia 13, syndromic, by modulating the metabolism of retinoic acid, a regulator of hematopoiesis. Specifically, DHRSX's enzymatic activity alters the balance of retinoic acid, disrupting the differentiation and maturation of megakaryocytes, leading to thrombocytopenia. We predict that overexpression of DHRSX in megakaryocyte precursors will result in decreased platelet production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibition of DHRSX will rescue platelet production, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanism is grounded in the known role of retinoic acid in hematopoiesis and the enzymatic function of DHRSX, providing a testable connection between this enzyme and Thrombocytopenia 13, syndromic.

We hypothesize that NT5C1B-RDH14, a 5'-nucleotidase, plays a crucial role in maintaining nucleotide homeostasis, which is essential for the proper functioning of the glycosylation pathway in Congenital disorder of glycosylation 1J (CDG1J). Specifically, we propose that NT5C1B-RDH14 regulates the levels of nucleotide sugars, such as GDP-mannose, required for glycoprotein synthesis. We predict that overexpression of NT5C1B-RDH14 will lead to increased degradation of nucleotide sugars, resulting in impaired glycosylation and exacerbation of CDG1J symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased glycoprotein synthesis in cells overexpressing NT5C1B-RDH14, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or improved glycosylation patterns.

We hypothesize that FPGT (folylpolyglutamate synthase), an enzyme involved in folate metabolism, plays a crucial role in the development of Barrett esophagus through its impact on DNA methylation and gene expression. Specifically, altered FPGT activity leads to disrupted folate homeostasis, resulting in aberrant methylation of tumor suppressor genes in esophageal epithelial cells. This epigenetic modification promotes the transition from normal esophageal epithelium to metaplastic Barrett's epithelium. We predict that FPGT overexpression in esophageal cells will increase DNA methylation and silence tumor suppressor genes, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, FPGT inhibition will reduce methylation and prevent metaplastic changes, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of folate metabolism and its role in regulating gene expression.

We hypothesize that CH25H (cholesterol 25-hydroxylase) contributes to the pathogenesis of Adenylosuccinase deficiency by modulating the mevalonate pathway, which intersects with purine metabolism. CH25H-derived oxysterols may inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, reducing mevalonate production and subsequently decreasing the synthesis of adenylosuccinate, a substrate for adenylosuccinase. This decrease would exacerbate the enzymatic deficiency, leading to accumulated toxic metabolites. We predict that CH25H inhibition will increase adenylosuccinate levels in Adenylosuccinase-deficient cells, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, CH25H overexpression will decrease adenylosuccinate levels, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of cholesterol and purine metabolism, and testing this hypothesis will reveal a novel link between CH25H and Adenylosuccinase deficiency.

We hypothesize that the enzyme beta-glucuronidase (GUSB) plays a role in the development of Hyperprolinemia 2 through its involvement in the degradation of glycosaminoglycans, which in turn affects the expression of the gene encoding the enzyme delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase (ALDH4A1). Impaired GUSB activity may lead to the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, resulting in the downregulation of ALDH4A1 and subsequent accumulation of delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate, a precursor to proline. We predict that GUSB deficiency will exacerbate proline accumulation in Hyperprolinemia 2 patients. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through the detection of increased glycosaminoglycan levels and decreased ALDH4A1 expression in GUSB-deficient cells, while refutation would be evident if GUSB deficiency has no effect on ALDH4A1 expression or proline levels.

We hypothesize that ELOVL6, an enzyme involved in fatty acid elongation, contributes to the development of Cole disease by disrupting the balance of very-long-chain fatty acids in the skin. Specifically, we propose that ELOVL6's activity leads to an accumulation of toxic fatty acid intermediates, which in turn activate inflammatory pathways and disrupt skin barrier function. We predict that inhibiting ELOVL6 in Cole disease patient-derived skin cells will reduce inflammatory marker expression and improve skin barrier integrity. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant decrease in IL-1β expression and increased filaggrin production in ELOVL6-inhibited cells. Refutation would be evidenced by no change in these markers, suggesting an alternative mechanism underlying Cole disease pathogenesis.

terminal_shown: Muscular dystrophy, congenital hearing loss, and ovarian insufficiency syndrome
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CDO1 (cysteine dioxygenase 1) plays a crucial role in the development of Muscular dystrophy, congenital hearing loss, and ovarian insufficiency syndrome through its regulation of taurine and hypotaurine metabolism. Specifically, CDO1's enzymatic activity affects the balance of these metabolites, which are essential for maintaining muscle, auditory, and ovarian function. We predict that CDO1 deficiency will lead to impaired taurine and hypotaurine production, resulting in increased oxidative stress and tissue damage. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased taurine and hypotaurine levels in tissues of individuals with these diseases, while refutation would be shown by normal or elevated levels of these metabolites.

terminal_shown: Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that COX10, a crucial enzyme in the biosynthesis of heme a, plays a key role in the development of Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2. Specifically, we propose that impaired COX10 activity disrupts the assembly and function of mitochondrial complex IV, leading to increased reactive oxygen species production and mitochondrial dysfunction in retinal ganglion cells. We predict that patients with Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2, will exhibit reduced COX10 expression and complex IV activity in affected tissues. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased complex IV activity in patient-derived cells, while refutation would be shown by normal complex IV activity and no correlation between COX10 expression and disease severity.

We hypothesize that RDH12, a retinol dehydrogenase, contributes to Congenital disorder of glycosylation 1L (CDG1L) by modulating the NAD+/NADH ratio, which in turn affects the activity of phosphomannomutase 2 (PMM2), a key enzyme in glycosylation. Specifically, altered RDH12 activity disrupts NAD+/NADH homeostasis, leading to decreased PMM2 function and impaired glycosylation. We predict that overexpressing RDH12 in CDG1L patient cells will exacerbate glycosylation defects, while RDH12 knockdown will rescue PMM2 activity and improve glycosylation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased glycosylation efficiency in RDH12-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by no change in glycosylation patterns upon RDH12 modulation.

We hypothesize that B3GALT4, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of the anterior segment of the eye by modifying glycoproteins involved in cell adhesion and migration.
