Conversely, inhibition of ACER3 will rescue the hair phenotype, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of ceramides in skin and hair biology.

We hypothesize that Phosphopantothenoylcysteine Synthetase (PPCS) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Transaldolase deficiency by modulating the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). In Transaldolase deficiency, the impaired PPP leads to an accumulation of sedoheptulose-7-phosphate, which in turn inhibits PPCS activity. This inhibition disrupts coenzyme A (CoA) biosynthesis, exacerbating the metabolic imbalance. We predict that PPCS overexpression will alleviate the metabolic defects in Transaldolase-deficient cells by restoring CoA levels. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through increased CoA levels and improved metabolic profiles in PPCS-overexpressing Transaldolase-deficient cells, while refutation would be evident if PPCS overexpression fails to rescue the metabolic phenotype.

We hypothesize that squalene synthase reductase (SRR) plays a crucial role in the development of Hypophosphatemic rickets, autosomal recessive, 2, by regulating the mevalonate pathway, which affects vitamin D synthesis. SRR's modulation of this pathway impacts the production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, essential for phosphate homeostasis. We predict that SRR deficiency will lead to decreased 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels, resulting in impaired phosphate absorption and hypophosphatemia. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels in SRR-deficient patients, while refutation would be evident if SRR deficiency does not affect vitamin D synthesis or phosphate homeostasis. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of the mevalonate pathway and its connection to vitamin D synthesis.

We hypothesize that methionine synthase (MTR) plays a crucial role in the development of Coenzyme Q10 deficiency, primary, 2, by regulating the methylation status of the ADCK3 gene promoter. MTR's activity affects the availability of methyl groups, which in turn influences the expression of ADCK3, a gene implicated in Coenzyme Q10 biosynthesis. We predict that reduced MTR activity will lead to decreased ADCK3 expression, resulting in impaired Coenzyme Q10 production. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating a significant decrease in ADCK3 mRNA levels and Coenzyme Q10 concentrations in cells with impaired MTR activity. Refutation would occur if ADCK3 expression and Coenzyme Q10 levels remain unaffected by MTR inhibition.

We hypothesize that PCK1 (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1) contributes to the development of Polyglucosan body myopathy 2 (PGBM2) by disrupting glycogen metabolism. Specifically, PCK1's role in gluconeogenesis leads to altered glucose-6-phosphate levels, which in turn affect glycogen synthase activity. This results in the accumulation of aberrant glycogen inclusions, characteristic of PGBM2. We predict that PCK1 overexpression will increase polyglucosan body formation in muscle cells, whereas PCK1 inhibition will reduce it. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased polyglucosan bodies in PCK1-overexpressing muscle cells, while refutation would be shown by no change in polyglucosan body formation in response to PCK1 modulation.

We hypothesize that UGT8, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Rafiq syndrome by aberrantly glycosylating and thereby inactivating a key protein involved in neuronal function. Specifically, we propose that UGT8-mediated glycosylation of the neuronal protein, syntaxin-1, disrupts synaptic vesicle release, leading to the neurodevelopmental defects characteristic of Rafiq syndrome. We predict that inhibition of UGT8 activity will restore normal syntaxin-1 function and alleviate disease symptoms, whereas overexpression of UGT8 will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing improved neuronal function and reduced disease severity in UGT8-inhibited Rafiq syndrome models, while refutation would be indicated by unchanged or worsened symptoms.

We hypothesize that GPX4, a phospholipid hydroperoxide glutathione peroxidase, plays a crucial role in the development of Juvenile arthritis by regulating oxidative stress and subsequent inflammation in synovial tissues. Specifically, GPX4's antioxidant activity mitigates lipid peroxidation, thereby reducing the formation of pro-inflammatory oxidized lipids. We predict that GPX4 deficiency or inhibition will exacerbate Juvenile arthritis symptoms, characterized by increased synovial inflammation and joint damage. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by elevated disease severity in GPX4-knockout mouse models of Juvenile arthritis, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or improved disease outcomes in these models. This hypothesis is grounded in GPX4's known antioxidant function and the established role of oxidative stress in inflammatory diseases.

We hypothesize that deoxyuridine triphosphatase (DUT) plays a crucial role in the development of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, musculocontractural type 1, by regulating the balance of nucleotide pools. Specifically, DUT's impaired activity leads to an accumulation of deoxyuridine triphosphate, which is incorporated into DNA, causing genetic instability and mutations in genes involved in collagen synthesis, such as KYNU and DSE. This results in defective collagen production, characteristic of the disease. We predict that DUT knockdown in fibroblasts will increase uracil incorporation into DNA and decrease collagen production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, DUT overexpression will rescue collagen production, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in DUT's known role in maintaining nucleotide pool balance and the established genetic defects in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, musculocontractural type 1.

We hypothesize that Protein O-mannose kinase (POMK) plays a crucial role in the development of Histidinemia by phosphorylating and thereby regulating the activity of histidine ammonia lyase (HAL), a key enzyme in histidine catabolism. In Histidinemia, impaired HAL activity leads to histidine accumulation. We predict that POMK-mediated phosphorylation of HAL enhances its enzymatic activity, and that reduced POMK expression or activity will exacerbate histidine accumulation in Histidinemia. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating decreased HAL activity in cells with reduced POMK expression, while refutation would be achieved by showing no effect of POMK modulation on HAL activity or histidine levels. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of protein phosphorylation and its role in regulating enzyme activity.

We hypothesize that MARS1, a methionyl-tRNA synthetase, plays a crucial role in the development of Erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva 4 (EKVP4) by regulating protein synthesis in keratinocytes. Specifically, MARS1's impaired function leads to defective translation of genes involved in skin barrier formation, such as filaggrin and loricrin. This results in disrupted epidermal homeostasis and characteristic skin lesions. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of MARS1 in keratinocytes will decrease filaggrin and loricrin protein levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of MARS1 will rescue protein levels, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in MARS1's known role in aminoacyl-tRNA synthesis and its importance in maintaining protein homeostasis.

We hypothesize that LIPT1, a key enzyme in lipoic acid synthesis, plays a crucial role in mitigating the effects of Urocanase deficiency by regulating the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the liver. In Urocanase deficiency, the accumulation of urocanic acid leads to increased ROS production. LIPT1, by synthesizing lipoic acid, enhances the activity of antioxidant enzymes, thereby reducing ROS levels. We predict that overexpression of LIPT1 in a Urocanase-deficient model will decrease ROS production and alleviate disease symptoms, whereas LIPT1 inhibition will exacerbate the condition. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced oxidative stress markers in LIPT1-overexpressing models, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or increased oxidative stress levels.

We hypothesize that Purine Nucleoside Phosphorylase (PNP) plays a crucial role in the development of Fish-eye disease, a rare genetic disorder characterized by high-density lipoprotein (HDL) deficiency. PNP's enzymatic activity in the liver leads to impaired HDL maturation by disrupting the balance of purine nucleotides, which are essential for apolipoprotein A-I (apoA-I) lipidation. Specifically, we predict that PNP inhibition will increase apoA-I lipidation and HDL levels in Fish-eye disease patients. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased HDL cholesterol levels in patients treated with PNP inhibitors, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in HDL levels despite PNP inhibition. This mechanism is grounded in PNP's known role in purine metabolism and its potential impact on HDL biogenesis.

terminal_shown: Microcephaly, congenital cataract, and psoriasiform dermatitis
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ALOX15, an enzyme involved in lipid peroxidation, contributes to the development of Microcephaly, congenital cataract, and psoriasiform dermatitis through its role in regulating oxidative stress and inflammation in fetal development and skin homeostasis. Specifically, ALOX15's metabolites may disrupt normal lipid metabolism, leading to impaired brain and lens development, and altered skin barrier function. We predict that inhibition of ALOX15 will reduce disease severity, whereas overexpression will exacerbate it. Confirmation would come from observing reduced oxidative stress and improved developmental outcomes in ALOX15-inhibited models, while refutation would result from unchanged or worsened phenotypes. This hypothesis is grounded in ALOX15's known biochemistry and its established role in regulating lipid metabolism and inflammation.

We hypothesize that MTHFD1, a crucial enzyme in one-carbon metabolism, plays a key role in the development of Deafness, sensorineural, mitochondrial. Specifically, we propose that MTHFD1's impairment leads to decreased tetrahydrofolate (THF) production, disrupting mitochondrial DNA replication and maintenance in cochlear cells. This disruption causes mitochondrial dysfunction, ultimately resulting in sensorineural deafness. We predict that MTHFD1 knockdown in cochlear cells will lead to decreased THF levels, increased mitochondrial DNA damage, and impaired auditory function. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by experimental results showing a significant correlation between MTHFD1 expression, THF levels, and auditory function in mitochondrial deafness models. Refutation would be evidenced by normal auditory function and mitochondrial DNA integrity despite MTHFD1 knockdown.

We hypothesize that FDFT1, the enzyme responsible for the first step in cholesterol biosynthesis, plays a role in Gaucher disease pathogenesis by modulating sphingolipid metabolism. Specifically, we propose that FDFT1's product, squalene, inhibits the activity of glucocerebrosidase, the enzyme deficient in Gaucher disease, thereby exacerbating glucocerebroside accumulation. We predict that inhibiting FDFT1 will increase glucocerebrosidase activity and reduce glucocerebroside levels in Gaucher disease cells. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased glucocerebroside accumulation in cells treated with FDFT1 inhibitors, while refutation would be shown by no change in glucocerebroside levels upon FDFT1 inhibition. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemical link between cholesterol and sphingolipid metabolism.

We hypothesize that EHHADH (enoyl-CoA hydratase/3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase) plays a crucial role in the development of 5-oxoprolinase deficiency by regulating the accumulation of 5-oxoproline. Specifically, EHHADH's enzymatic activity influences the metabolism of glutathione, which is linked to 5-oxoproline production. Impaired EHHADH function may lead to an imbalance in glutathione metabolism, resulting in elevated 5-oxoproline levels and subsequent 5-oxoprolinase deficiency. We predict that EHHADH knockdown will increase 5-oxoproline levels, confirming our hypothesis, while EHHADH overexpression will decrease 5-oxoproline levels, refuting it. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of glutathione metabolism and its relationship to 5-oxoproline production.

We hypothesize that CYP3A5, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, contributes to the pathogenesis of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 71 (DEE71) by aberrantly metabolizing a specific neurosteroid, leading to disrupted neuronal excitability. Specifically, we propose that CYP3A5's altered activity affects the conversion of pregnenolone to allopregnanolone, a neurosteroid regulating GABA receptor function. If CYP3A5 is overactive, allopregnanolone levels may decrease, leading to increased neuronal excitability and seizures. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that CYP3A5 inhibitors reduce seizure frequency in DEE71 models, while refutation would result from experiments demonstrating no effect of CYP3A5 modulation on allopregnanolone levels or seizure activity.

We hypothesize that the enzyme Arylsulfatase B (ARSB) plays a crucial role in the development of Anemia, congenital, non-spherocytic hemolytic, 2, by regulating the sulfation status of glycosaminoglycans in erythrocyte membranes. Abnormal ARSB activity leads to altered glycosaminoglycan sulfation, disrupting erythrocyte membrane integrity and causing hemolysis. We predict that ARSB deficiency will result in decreased glycosaminoglycan sulfation, increased erythrocyte fragility, and enhanced hemolysis. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased hemolysis in ARSB-deficient erythrocytes, while refutation would be shown by normal hemolysis rates in ARSB-deficient cells with exogenous glycosaminoglycan sulfation restoration.

We hypothesize that CYP2C9, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, plays a crucial role in the metabolism of oxysterols, which are key regulators of Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) activity. Specifically, CYP2C9 metabolizes 24S-hydroxycholesterol, a potent LCAT activator, to a less active form. In Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase deficiency, impaired LCAT activity leads to accumulation of unesterified cholesterol. We predict that CYP2C9 inhibition will increase 24S-hydroxycholesterol levels, enhancing LCAT activity and alleviating disease symptoms. Confirmation would come from increased LCAT activity and improved cholesterol profiles in patients with LCAT deficiency treated with CYP2C9 inhibitors. Refutation would occur if CYP2C9 inhibition fails to increase 24S-hydroxycholesterol levels or improve LCAT activity in these patients.

We hypothesize that the enzyme beta-glucuronidase (GUSB) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Leber congenital amaurosis 11 (LCA11) by modulating the glycosaminoglycan (GAG) composition in the retina. Specifically, GUSB deficiency leads to accumulation of GAGs, which in turn disrupts the normal functioning of the photoreceptor cells. We predict that overexpression of GUSB in LCA11 patient-derived retinal cells will restore normal GAG composition and improve photoreceptor function, as measured by increased rhodopsin expression. Conversely, inhibition of GUSB activity will exacerbate the disease phenotype, characterized by reduced rhodopsin expression and impaired photoreceptor function. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of GUSB in GAG metabolism and its potential impact on retinal cell function.

We hypothesize that the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R) contributes to the pathogenesis of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 89 (DEE89) by aberrantly regulating neuronal excitability through the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. Specifically, IGF1R hyperactivation leads to increased AKT-mediated inhibition of the tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), resulting in enhanced mTOR activity and subsequent dysregulation of neuronal excitability. We predict that DEE89 patient-derived neurons will exhibit increased IGF1R activity and mTOR signaling, which can be confirmed by measuring elevated p-AKT and p-S6 levels. Conversely, IGF1R inhibition will reduce seizure-like activity in DEE89 neuronal models, refuting the hypothesis if no effect is observed.

We hypothesize that LDHAL6A, a lactate dehydrogenase, contributes to the pathogenesis of N-terminal acetyltransferase deficiency by aberrantly regulating the acetylation status of key metabolic enzymes. Specifically, LDHAL6A's interaction with N-alpha-acetyltransferase 10 (NAA10) disrupts its activity, leading to impaired protein acetylation and altered metabolic flux. We predict that overexpression of LDHAL6A in cells will decrease NAA10 activity, resulting in reduced acetylation of target proteins, whereas LDHAL6A knockdown will restore NAA10 activity and protein acetylation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased acetylation of NAA10 target proteins in LDHAL6A-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by unchanged acetylation patterns.

We hypothesize that AMPD1 (adenosine monophosphate deaminase 1) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long-chain deficiency by regulating the energy metabolism in mitochondria. Specifically, AMPD1's activity affects the AMP/ATP ratio, which in turn influences the NAD+/NADH balance. This balance is essential for the proper functioning of Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, the enzyme deficient in this disease. We predict that overexpression of AMPD1 will exacerbate the disease phenotype by further disrupting the NAD+/NADH balance, leading to decreased fatty acid oxidation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased fatty acid oxidation rates in cells overexpressing AMPD1, while refutation would be seen if no significant change in fatty acid oxidation rates occurs.

We hypothesize that MRI1, a mitochondrial enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of RENI syndrome by regulating the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). Specifically, we propose that MRI1's dysfunction leads to impaired BCAA catabolism, resulting in the accumulation of toxic intermediates that disrupt renal function. We predict that MRI1 deficiency will increase BCAA levels in the urine of RENI syndrome patients. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by elevated urinary BCAA levels in patients with RENI syndrome, while refutation would be shown by normal BCAA levels despite MRI1 dysfunction. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of BCAA metabolism and its link to renal function.

We hypothesize that A4GALT, an enzyme involved in glycosphingolipid biosynthesis, contributes to Male pseudohermaphrodism with gynecomastia through aberrant modulation of androgen receptor signaling. Specifically, A4GALT's product, globotriaosylceramide, alters the membrane microdomain structure, affecting androgen receptor localization and activity. This leads to impaired androgen signaling, resulting in underdeveloped male genitalia and gynecomastia. We predict that A4GALT overexpression in cell models will reduce androgen receptor transactivation, whereas A4GALT inhibition will restore normal androgen signaling. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing decreased androgen receptor activity in A4GALT-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be demonstrated by unchanged androgen receptor activity in response to A4GALT modulation.

We hypothesize that DHCR24, a cholesterol biosynthesis enzyme, contributes to the pathogenesis of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome through modulation of dopamine neurotransmission. Specifically, DHCR24-derived cholesterol affects membrane fluidity and dopamine receptor function, exacerbating the disease's characteristic neurological symptoms. We predict that DHCR24 inhibition will decrease dopamine receptor density in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome models, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if DHCR24 inhibition has no effect on dopamine receptor function, our hypothesis will be refuted. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of cholesterol in modulating membrane-bound receptors and the established link between dopamine dysregulation and Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

We hypothesize that PCYT2, the enzyme responsible for converting CTP to CDP-diacylglycerol, plays a crucial role in regulating phospholipid synthesis in pancreatic beta cells, thereby influencing insulin secretion. Specifically, we propose that altered PCYT2 activity disrupts the phospholipid composition of beta cell membranes, leading to enhanced insulin granule release and hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, as seen in familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia 4. We predict that overexpression of PCYT2 in beta cells will increase phosphatidic acid levels, enhancing insulin secretion, whereas PCYT2 inhibition will reduce insulin release. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by demonstrating a direct correlation between PCYT2 activity and insulin secretion in beta cells, while refutation would be evidenced by the absence of such a correlation.

We hypothesize that PGAM4, a phosphoglycerate mutase, plays a crucial role in the development of Sialuria by regulating the glycolytic pathway and subsequently affecting the synthesis of uridine diphosphate-N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc), a precursor for sialic acid production. In Sialuria, the accumulation of sialic acid is due to a deficiency in the feedback inhibition of UDP-GlcNAc 2-epimerase. We predict that overexpression of PGAM4 will increase glycolytic flux, leading to elevated UDP-GlcNAc levels and exacerbating sialic acid accumulation in Sialuria patients. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased sialic acid levels in cells overexpressing PGAM4, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in sialic acid levels upon PGAM4 overexpression.

terminal_shown: Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal recessive 4
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that PMAIP1, a pro-apoptotic protein, contributes to the pathogenesis of Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal recessive 4, by regulating mitochondrial dynamics and DNA integrity. Specifically, PMAIP1 interacts with mitochondrial fission proteins, leading to excessive mitochondrial fragmentation and increased susceptibility to DNA deletions. We predict that overexpression of PMAIP1 in patient-derived cells will exacerbate mitochondrial DNA deletions, while PMAIP1 knockdown will mitigate this effect. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by an increase in mitochondrial DNA deletions in PMAIP1-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in mitochondrial DNA integrity upon PMAIP1 modulation.

We hypothesize that B3GAT3, a glycosaminoglycan synthase, plays a crucial role in the development of Multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome 2 (MCAHS2) by regulating the synthesis of heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) in the brain and other affected tissues. Specifically, we propose that mutations in B3GAT3 lead to aberrant HSPG structures, disrupting the normal functioning of growth factor signaling pathways, such as the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) pathway. We predict that experimental knockdown of B3GAT3 in neuronal cells will result in decreased FGF signaling and increased cellular apoptosis, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, rescue experiments with wild-type B3GAT3 will restore normal FGF signaling and cellular viability, refuting the hypothesis if unsuccessful.

We hypothesize that activation of the enzyme MCAT (malonyl-CoA:ACP acyltransferase) contributes to Immunodeficiency with hyper-IgM 2 by disrupting fatty acid synthesis in activated B cells. Specifically, MCAT's increased activity leads to altered lipid raft composition, impairing CD40 signaling and subsequent class-switch recombination. We predict that inhibiting MCAT in B cells from Immunodeficiency with hyper-IgM 2 patients will restore normal CD40 signaling and reduce serum IgM levels. Confirmation would come from observing increased class-switched antibodies and reduced IgM in patient B cells treated with MCAT inhibitors. Refutation would occur if MCAT inhibition fails to rescue CD40 signaling defects in these cells. This hypothesis is grounded in the known role of lipid metabolism in immune cell function and the specific biochemical function of MCAT in fatty acid synthesis.

We hypothesize that ALDH9A1, an aldehyde dehydrogenase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Myasthenic syndrome, congenital, 12, by regulating the metabolism of toxic aldehydes in the neuromuscular junction. Specifically, we propose that ALDH9A1 deficiency leads to the accumulation of 4-hydroxynonenal, a toxic aldehyde that modifies and inactivates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, resulting in impaired neuromuscular transmission. We predict that overexpression of ALDH9A1 in patient-derived cells will restore normal receptor function, while inhibition of ALDH9A1 will exacerbate receptor dysfunction. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved neuromuscular transmission in ALDH9A1-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in receptor function.

We hypothesize that NDUFS3, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Retinitis pigmentosa 17. Specifically, we propose that impaired NDUFS3 function disrupts mitochondrial energy metabolism in photoreceptor cells, leading to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and subsequent cellular damage. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of NDUFS3 in retinal cells will result in elevated ROS levels and decreased cell viability, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFS3 will mitigate ROS production and protect cells from damage, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial complex I and its role in maintaining cellular energy homeostasis.

We hypothesize that DHCR24, a 24-dehydrocholesterol reductase, plays a crucial role in the development of Multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome 2 (MCAHS2) by regulating cholesterol biosynthesis and subsequent neurosteroid production. Specifically, DHCR24 deficiency leads to impaired conversion of 24-dehydrocholesterol to cholesterol, disrupting neurosteroid synthesis and neuronal function. We predict that MCAHS2 patients with DHCR24 mutations will exhibit altered neurosteroid profiles, which can be confirmed by measuring decreased levels of cholesterol-derived neurosteroids in patient-derived cells or tissues. Conversely, refutation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by normal neurosteroid levels in MCAHS2 patients with DHCR24 mutations, suggesting an alternative disease mechanism.

We hypothesize that NDUFB3, a subunit of NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (Complex I), plays a crucial role in the development of RENI syndrome, a rare mitochondrial disorder. Specifically, we propose that reduced NDUFB3 expression impairs Complex I function, leading to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and subsequent damage to renal and intestinal tissues. We predict that patients with RENI syndrome will exhibit decreased NDUFB3 protein levels and Complex I activity in affected tissues. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by experimental results showing a significant correlation between NDUFB3 expression and disease severity. Refutation would be evidenced by normal NDUFB3 levels and Complex I activity in RENI syndrome patients, suggesting an alternative disease mechanism.

terminal_shown: Skeletal dysplasia, mild, with joint laxity and advanced bone age
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ACADSB, an enzyme involved in the beta-oxidation of short-chain fatty acids, plays a crucial role in the development of Skeletal dysplasia, mild, with joint laxity and advanced bone age. Specifically, we propose that impaired ACADSB activity disrupts the normal metabolism of short-chain fatty acids, leading to an accumulation of toxic intermediates that interfere with the regulation of chondrocyte differentiation and bone growth. We predict that skeletal tissues from individuals with this disease will exhibit reduced ACADSB expression and activity, resulting in altered fatty acid profiles. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by the observation of decreased ACADSB enzyme activity in patient-derived skeletal cells, while refutation would be indicated by normal or increased ACADSB activity in these cells.

We hypothesize that PTGS1 (prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 1), also known as cyclooxygenase-1, plays a crucial role in the development of acute transient encephalopathy through its regulation of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) production in the brain. Elevated PGE2 levels can lead to increased blood-brain barrier permeability and neuroinflammation, contributing to encephalopathy. We predict that inhibition of PTGS1 will reduce PGE2 production, thereby decreasing the incidence of acute transient encephalopathy. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced encephalopathy severity in animal models treated with PTGS1 inhibitors, while refutation would be shown by no significant difference in encephalopathy severity between treated and untreated models. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of PTGS1 and its role in prostaglandin synthesis.

We hypothesize that TRY-GTA7-1, a specific enzyme involved in ceramide metabolism, plays a crucial role in the development of Farber lipogranulomatosis. We propose that TRY-GTA7-1 regulates the breakdown of ceramides, which accumulate in Farber disease due to acid ceramidase deficiency. Specifically, TRY-GTA7-1 may modulate the formation of pro-inflammatory ceramide species, exacerbating the disease. We predict that overexpression of TRY-GTA7-1 in Farber disease cells will increase ceramide-induced inflammation, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibition of TRY-GTA7-1 will reduce inflammation, refuting our hypothesis. This prediction can be tested through in vitro experiments measuring inflammatory markers in response to TRY-GTA7-1 modulation in Farber disease cells.

We hypothesize that ACACA (acetyl-CoA carboxylase alpha) contributes to the pathogenesis of Fabry disease by regulating the synthesis of fatty acids, which in turn affects the metabolism of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), the lipid that accumulates in Fabry disease. Specifically, ACACA's role in fatty acid synthesis may influence the availability of fatty acids for Gb3 synthesis. We predict that inhibiting ACACA will reduce Gb3 levels in Fabry disease cells. Confirmation would come from decreased Gb3 levels in cells treated with ACACA inhibitors, while refutation would come from unchanged or increased Gb3 levels. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of fatty acid synthesis and its potential impact on sphingolipid metabolism, including Gb3.

We hypothesize that PTK2 (protein tyrosine kinase 2) contributes to the development of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 84 (DEE84) through aberrant regulation of neuronal synaptic plasticity. Specifically, PTK2's kinase activity disrupts the normal balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission, leading to hyperexcitability and seizure susceptibility. We predict that DEE84 patient-derived neurons with PTK2 mutations will exhibit increased synaptic excitability, which can be confirmed by electrophysiological recordings showing enhanced miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) frequencies. Conversely, pharmacological inhibition of PTK2 or rescue of wild-type PTK2 expression will reduce mEPSC frequencies, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed.

We hypothesize that CEPT1, a choline/ethanolamine phosphotransferase, plays a crucial role in the development of Retinitis pigmentosa 53 (RP53) by regulating phospholipid composition in photoreceptor membranes. Specifically, CEPT1's dysfunction leads to altered phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine levels, disrupting membrane structure and function. This disruption impairs phototransduction, ultimately contributing to photoreceptor degeneration in RP53. We predict that CEPT1 knockdown in retinal cells will result in decreased phosphatidylcholine and increased phosphatidylethanolamine, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpressing CEPT1 will rescue photoreceptor function, refuting our hypothesis if no improvement is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in CEPT1's known role in phospholipid biosynthesis and the critical importance of membrane integrity in photoreceptor function.

terminal_shown: Hypercarotenemia and vitamin A deficiency, autosomal dominant
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that MRI1 (methionine-R-sulfoxide reductase 1) plays a crucial role in the development of Hypercarotenemia and vitamin A deficiency, autosomal dominant, by regulating the activity of beta-carotene 15,15'-monooxygenase 1 (BCMO1). Specifically, MRI1's methionine repair function maintains BCMO1's enzymatic activity, which is essential for converting beta-carotene to vitamin A. Impaired MRI1 function leads to BCMO1 inactivation, resulting in decreased vitamin A production and accumulation of beta-carotene. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating decreased BCMO1 activity in cells with impaired MRI1 function, while refutation would involve showing no effect of MRI1 impairment on BCMO1 activity or vitamin A production.

terminal_shown: Combined deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors 1
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that BAK1 (BCL2-antagonist/killer 1) contributes to Combined deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors 1 by regulating the apoptosis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factor-producing cells in the liver. Specifically, BAK1's pro-apoptotic activity may lead to excessive cell death, reducing the production of clotting factors. We predict that overexpression of BAK1 in hepatocytes will decrease the expression of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, while inhibition of BAK1 will increase their expression. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by showing a significant decrease in clotting factor production in BAK1-overexpressing hepatocytes, while refutation would be demonstrated by observing no change in clotting factor production in response to BAK1 modulation. This mechanism is grounded in the known role of BAK1 in regulating apoptosis and the importance of liver cells in producing clotting factors.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder, mitochondrial, with abnormal movements and lactic acidosis, with or without seizures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that UDP-galactose-4'-epimerase (GALE) plays a crucial role in the development of Neurodevelopmental disorder, mitochondrial, with abnormal movements and lactic acidosis, with or without seizures. GALE's impairment leads to galactose accumulation, disrupting mitochondrial function and energy metabolism. This disruption causes an increase in lactic acid production, contributing to lactic acidosis. We predict that GALE deficiency will result in decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased lactate levels in patient-derived cells. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased GALE activity and corresponding increases in lactate levels in patient samples. Refutation would occur if GALE activity is normal in patient samples, and lactate levels do not correlate with GALE deficiency.

We hypothesize that GGPS1, an enzyme involved in the biosynthesis of isoprenoids, plays a crucial role in the development of Yunis-Varon syndrome. Specifically, we propose that reduced GGPS1 activity leads to impaired prenylation of small GTPases, disrupting cellular signaling pathways essential for bone and cartilage development. This results in the characteristic skeletal abnormalities and growth retardation observed in Yunis-Varon syndrome. We predict that experimental reduction of GGPS1 activity in osteoblasts will confirm this hypothesis, leading to decreased prenylation of Rho GTPases and subsequent disruption of bone morphogenetic protein signaling. Conversely, overexpression of GGPS1 will refute this hypothesis, failing to rescue the skeletal defects associated with Yunis-Varon syndrome.

We hypothesize that hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS) plays a crucial role in the development of Muscular dystrophy, limb-girdle, autosomal recessive 21 (LGMDR21) through its involvement in the heme biosynthesis pathway. Specifically, we propose that impaired HMBS activity leads to accumulation of toxic heme precursors, which disrupts mitochondrial function and increases oxidative stress in muscle cells. This, in turn, exacerbates muscle damage and contributes to the progression of LGMDR21. We predict that LGMDR21 patient-derived muscle cells will exhibit decreased HMBS activity and increased levels of heme precursors, which can be confirmed by enzymatic assays and metabolomic analysis. Refutation of this hypothesis would require demonstration of normal HMBS activity and heme precursor levels in LGMDR21 muscle cells.

We hypothesize that Stearoyl-CoA Desaturase (SCD) contributes to the development of Cocoon syndrome by disrupting fatty acid metabolism, leading to impaired skin barrier function. SCD catalyzes the conversion of saturated to monounsaturated fatty acids, which are essential for skin lipid composition. In Cocoon syndrome, we predict that SCD overexpression will result in an imbalance of skin lipids, causing the characteristic skin thickening and cocoon-like lesions. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating increased SCD activity and altered skin lipid profiles in Cocoon syndrome patients. Refutation would occur if SCD inhibition fails to improve skin symptoms or if skin lipid analysis reveals no significant differences between Cocoon syndrome patients and healthy controls.

We hypothesize that alkaline phosphatase, intestinal (ALPI) plays a crucial role in the development of Trichothiodystrophy 8, non-photosensitive, by regulating the bioavailability of inorganic phosphate (Pi) in the hair follicle. Specifically, ALPI's phosphatase activity modulates the Pi levels, which in turn affects the expression of genes involved in hair growth and development. We predict that reduced ALPI activity will lead to increased Pi levels, resulting in aberrant gene expression and hair follicle dysfunction, characteristic of Trichothiodystrophy 8. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the observation of elevated Pi levels and altered gene expression in hair follicles of individuals with Trichothiodystrophy 8, whereas refutation would be shown by normal Pi levels and gene expression despite reduced ALPI activity.

We hypothesize that glutamate-cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC) plays a crucial role in the development of Ghosal hematodiaphyseal dysplasia by regulating the levels of glutathione, a key antioxidant. In this disease, mutations in the TBXAS1 gene lead to impaired osteoclast function and bone abnormalities. We propose that GCLC's dysregulation disrupts glutathione synthesis, increasing oxidative stress and exacerbating osteoclast dysfunction. Specifically, we predict that GCLC overexpression will rescue osteoclast function and improve bone density in Ghosal hematodiaphyseal dysplasia models. Confirmation would come from observing improved bone density and osteoclast function in GCLC-overexpressing models, while refutation would result from unchanged or worsened phenotypes. This hypothesis is grounded in the known role of glutathione in maintaining cellular redox balance and its impact on osteoclast function.

We hypothesize that BAK1 (BCL2-antagonist/killer 1) plays a crucial role in the development of Anterior segment dysgenesis 6 (ASD6) through regulation of mitochondrial apoptosis in the developing eye. Specifically, we propose that BAK1 mediates the mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, leading to abnormal cell death in the anterior segment. We predict that overexpression of BAK1 in the developing eye will exacerbate ASD6 phenotypes, while BAK1 inhibition will rescue them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased ASD6-like defects in BAK1-overexpressing mouse models, while refutation would be shown by lack of rescue in BAK1-inhibited models. This hypothesis is grounded in BAK1's known role in mitochondrial apoptosis and its potential impact on eye development.

We hypothesize that N-acetylglutamate kinase (NAGK) plays a crucial role in the development of Gillessen-Kaesbach-Nishimura syndrome by regulating the arginine biosynthetic pathway. Specifically, we propose that reduced NAGK activity leads to decreased arginine production, which in turn impairs nitric oxide synthesis and subsequent angiogenesis. This results in the characteristic skeletal and vascular abnormalities observed in Gillessen-Kaesbach-Nishimura syndrome. We predict that patients with this syndrome will have lower arginine levels and impaired angiogenic responses, which can be confirmed by measuring arginine levels and assessing angiogenic capacity in patient-derived cells. Refutation of this hypothesis would require demonstration of normal arginine levels and angiogenic responses in affected individuals.

We hypothesize that Diamine Oxidase (DAO) plays a crucial role in the development of Hypotrichosis 14, a rare genetic disorder characterized by hair loss. Specifically, we propose that DAO regulates the metabolism of polyamines, such as putrescine, which are essential for hair follicle growth and maintenance. Impaired DAO activity leads to altered polyamine levels, disrupting the normal functioning of the hair growth cycle. We predict that individuals with Hypotrichosis 14 will exhibit reduced DAO activity and altered polyamine profiles in hair follicle cells. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased DAO enzyme activity and putrescine levels in hair follicle cells of Hypotrichosis 14 patients, while refutation would be shown by normal DAO activity and polyamine levels in these cells.

We hypothesize that COX6A1, a subunit of cytochrome c oxidase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Tyrosinemia 1 by regulating the energy metabolism of hepatocytes. In Tyrosinemia 1, the accumulation of toxic metabolites disrupts mitochondrial function, leading to impaired energy production. We propose that COX6A1 modulates the activity of cytochrome c oxidase, affecting the electron transport chain and ATP synthesis. If COX6A1 expression is decreased in Tyrosinemia 1 patients, it would confirm our hypothesis. Conversely, if COX6A1 overexpression ameliorates the disease phenotype in a cellular model, it would refute our hypothesis. This connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial energy metabolism and its importance in maintaining hepatocyte function.

We hypothesize that the GNAS enzyme, which codes for the stimulatory G-protein alpha subunit, plays a crucial role in regulating eosinophil peroxidase (EPX) expression through a cAMP-dependent signaling pathway. Specifically, GNAS activation leads to increased cAMP levels, which in turn enhance the transcription of the EPX gene. We predict that individuals with Eosinophil peroxidase deficiency will exhibit reduced GNAS activity, resulting in decreased cAMP levels and subsequent downregulation of EPX expression. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating a significant correlation between GNAS activity and EPX expression levels in patient samples. Refutation would occur if GNAS activity is found to be normal or inversely related to EPX expression in individuals with Eosinophil peroxidase deficiency.

We hypothesize that the enzyme 1,4-alpha-glucan branching enzyme 1 (GBE1) plays a crucial role in the development of Spondyloocular syndrome through its involvement in glycogen metabolism. Specifically, mutations in GBE1 lead to impaired glycogen branching, resulting in the accumulation of abnormal glycogen structures that disrupt cellular function in ocular and skeletal tissues. We predict that patients with Spondyloocular syndrome will exhibit altered glycogen branching patterns in affected tissues, which can be confirmed by biochemical analysis of glycogen structure. Refutation of this hypothesis would be provided by the absence of such alterations in glycogen structure or the lack of GBE1 mutations in patients with Spondyloocular syndrome.

We hypothesize that CNPY3-GNMT, a glycine N-methyltransferase, plays a crucial role in the development of Pseudovaginal perineoscrotal hypospadias by regulating the methylation status of key transcription factors involved in genital tubercle formation. Specifically, CNPY3-GNMT methylates and inactivates the transcription factor SOX9, leading to impaired androgen receptor signaling and subsequent abnormal development of the genital tract. We predict that CNPY3-GNMT overexpression in mouse models will result in increased incidence of hypospadias-like phenotypes, whereas CNPY3-GNMT knockdown will rescue normal genital development. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by the observation of SOX9 methylation and decreased androgen receptor activity in CNPY3-GNMT overexpressing mice, while refutation would be indicated by the absence of these effects.

We hypothesize that EHMT2, a histone methyltransferase, contributes to the development of Porokeratosis 1, multiple types, by aberrantly methylating histones at the genes involved in keratinocyte differentiation. Specifically, EHMT2's dysregulation leads to increased methylation of H3K9 at the promoters of differentiation markers, suppressing their expression and resulting in abnormal keratinocyte growth. We predict that EHMT2 inhibition will restore normal keratinocyte differentiation in Porokeratosis 1 patient-derived cells, confirmed by increased expression of differentiation markers. Conversely, EHMT2 overexpression will exacerbate the disease phenotype, characterized by decreased differentiation marker expression and enhanced keratinocyte proliferation. This hypothesis is grounded in EHMT2's known role in epigenetic regulation and the critical importance of keratinocyte differentiation in maintaining skin homeostasis.

We hypothesize that PPA2 (inorganic pyrophosphatase 2) plays a crucial role in the development of Alkaptonuria by regulating the pyrophosphate levels, which in turn affects the activity of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase (HGD), the enzyme deficient in Alkaptonuria. Elevated pyrophosphate levels, resulting from PPA2 inhibition, may lead to increased substrate affinity of HGD, partially compensating for its deficiency. We predict that PPA2 inhibition will reduce urinary homogentisic acid levels in Alkaptonuria patients. Confirmation would come from observing a significant decrease in urinary homogentisic acid levels upon PPA2 inhibition. Refutation would occur if PPA2 inhibition has no effect on urinary homogentisic acid levels or worsens the disease symptoms.

terminal_shown: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with dystonia
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that DHRSX, a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase, contributes to the pathogenesis of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with dystonia by modulating the mitochondrial NAD+/NADH ratio. Specifically, DHRSX's enzymatic activity affects the reduction of oxidized metabolites, thereby influencing the energy metabolism in retinal ganglion cells and dopaminergic neurons. We predict that overexpression of DHRSX will exacerbate the disease phenotype, leading to increased oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating that DHRSX overexpression in cellular models of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with dystonia results in decreased NAD+/NADH ratios and increased markers of oxidative stress. Refutation would be achieved by showing no significant changes in these parameters upon DHRSX overexpression.

We hypothesize that GPAA1, a glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor assembly enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Focal dermal hypoplasia. Specifically, we propose that GPAA1's dysfunction leads to impaired glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor formation, disrupting the function of certain cell surface proteins essential for skin development. This disruption would result in the characteristic skin lesions and abnormalities seen in Focal dermal hypoplasia. We predict that GPAA1 mutations will be found in a subset of Focal dermal hypoplasia patients, and that experimental knockdown of GPAA1 in skin cells will replicate the disease's skin phenotypes. Confirmation would come from identifying GPAA1 mutations in patient samples, while refutation would come from failing to find such mutations or observing no skin phenotype changes upon GPAA1 knockdown.

We hypothesize that Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) plays a crucial role in the development of Pseudovaginal perineoscrotal hypospadias through its impact on androgen biosynthesis. GALT deficiency leads to accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate, which inhibits the enzyme 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, a key regulator of androgen production. Reduced androgen levels impair genital tubercle formation, contributing to hypospadias. We predict that GALT-deficient mice will exhibit decreased androgen production and increased incidence of hypospadias-like genital abnormalities. Confirmation would come from observing these phenotypes in GALT knockout mice, while refutation would result from normal androgen levels and genital development in these mice. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemical roles of GALT and androgen biosynthesis in genital development.

We hypothesize that NARS1, an asparaginyl-tRNA synthetase, plays a crucial role in the development of Trichothiodystrophy 7, non-photosensitive, by impairing protein synthesis in hair follicle cells. Specifically, mutations in NARS1 lead to defective aminoacylation of asparaginyl-tRNA, disrupting the translation of essential proteins involved in hair growth. We predict that cells from Trichothiodystrophy 7 patients will exhibit reduced levels of properly aminoacylated asparaginyl-tRNA, resulting in impaired hair follicle cell proliferation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing decreased asparaginyl-tRNA aminoacylation and subsequent protein synthesis defects in patient-derived cells. Refutation would occur if no significant differences in asparaginyl-tRNA aminoacylation are observed between patient and control cells.

We hypothesize that LARS2, a mitochondrial leucyl-tRNA synthetase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency by regulating the translation of mitochondrial enzymes involved in ketogenesis. Specifically, impaired LARS2 function leads to decreased translation of HMGCL, the enzyme deficient in this disease, resulting in reduced ketone body production. We predict that overexpressing LARS2 in patient-derived cells will increase HMGCL protein levels and restore ketogenesis, whereas LARS2 knockdown will exacerbate the disease phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased HMGCL enzyme activity and ketone body production in LARS2-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by no change in HMGCL activity or ketogenesis despite LARS2 modulation.

We hypothesize that NDUFA10, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Alopecia universalis congenita. We propose that impaired NDUFA10 function leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, resulting in altered energy metabolism and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in hair follicle cells. This, in turn, disrupts the delicate balance of hair growth and maintenance, contributing to the congenital hair loss characteristic of Alopecia universalis congenita. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of NDUFA10 in human hair follicle cells will increase ROS production and decrease hair growth, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFA10 will rescue hair growth, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial complex I and its role in maintaining cellular energy homeostasis.

We hypothesize that NDUFS3, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Epiphyseal dysplasia, multiple, 7. Specifically, we propose that impaired NDUFS3 function disrupts mitochondrial energy metabolism in chondrocytes, leading to altered ATP production and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. This, in turn, affects the expression of genes involved in cartilage and bone development, resulting in the characteristic skeletal abnormalities of Epiphyseal dysplasia, multiple, 7. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of NDUFS3 in chondrocytes will increase ROS levels and decrease ATP production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFS3 will rescue these defects, refuting our hypothesis.

We hypothesize that adenylate kinase 3 (AK3) plays a crucial role in the development of familial erythroleukemia by regulating the energy metabolism of erythroid progenitor cells. Specifically, AK3's phosphotransferase activity maintains the balance of adenine nucleotides, ensuring proper erythropoiesis. Dysregulation of AK3 leads to impaired energy homeostasis, promoting the proliferation and survival of malignant erythroid cells. We predict that AK3 overexpression in erythroid progenitors will enhance their sensitivity to erythropoietin, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, AK3 knockdown will reduce erythroleukemia cell growth, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanism is grounded in AK3's known role in maintaining adenine nucleotide homeostasis and its expression in erythroid cells, suggesting a specific link between AK3 and familial erythroleukemia.

We hypothesize that TRY-GTA7-1, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Focal dermal hypoplasia by regulating the glycosylation of extracellular matrix proteins. Specifically, TRY-GTA7-1 mediates the addition of glycosaminoglycans to collagen fibers, which is essential for maintaining skin integrity. In Focal dermal hypoplasia, mutations in the PORCN gene lead to disrupted TRY-GTA7-1 activity, resulting in aberrant glycosylation and compromised skin development. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of TRY-GTA7-1 in skin fibroblasts will recapitulate the skin defects observed in Focal dermal hypoplasia, whereas overexpression will rescue the phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by the observation of reduced glycosaminoglycan deposition on collagen fibers in TRY-GTA7-1 knockdown cells.

We hypothesize that SRD5A3, a steroid 5-alpha-reductase, contributes to the development of gastric cancer by modulating the metabolism of androgens, which in turn regulate the expression of oncogenic genes. Specifically, SRD5A3 converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, which activates androgen receptors that stimulate cell proliferation and inhibit apoptosis in gastric epithelial cells. We predict that overexpression of SRD5A3 in gastric cancer cells will increase cell growth and tumorigenesis, whereas inhibition of SRD5A3 will suppress these effects. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased SRD5A3 expression in gastric cancer tissues and a significant reduction in tumor growth upon SRD5A3 inhibition. Refutation would be shown by no significant difference in SRD5A3 expression between gastric cancer and normal tissues, or no effect of SRD5A3 inhibition on gastric cancer cell growth.

We hypothesize that SLC27A5, a bile acyl-CoA synthetase, contributes to Hyperaldosteronism, familial, 1, by modulating the biosynthesis of aldosterone-regulating lipids. Specifically, SLC27A5's activity in adrenal glands affects the production of certain fatty acyl-CoA esters, which in turn influence the expression of genes involved in aldosterone production. We predict that overexpression of SLC27A5 in adrenal cells will increase aldosterone production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, SLC27A5 knockdown will decrease aldosterone production, refuting the hypothesis. This proposed mechanism is grounded in the known role of lipid metabolism in regulating steroid hormone production and the specific involvement of SLC27A5 in fatty acid activation. Experimental validation of this hypothesis would provide new insights into the molecular basis of Hyperaldosteronism, familial, 1.

We hypothesize that ZMPSTE24, a metalloprotease involved in prelamin A processing, contributes to the development of Spastic paraplegia 9A, autosomal dominant, by disrupting nuclear lamina integrity. Specifically, we propose that mutations in the ALDH18A1 gene, associated with this disease, lead to altered ZMPSTE24 activity, resulting in aberrant prelamin A processing and subsequent nuclear envelope dysfunction. We predict that experimental inhibition of ZMPSTE24 in patient-derived cells will exacerbate nuclear lamina defects, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, rescue of ZMPSTE24 activity will ameliorate these defects, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known role of ZMPSTE24 in maintaining nuclear envelope homeostasis and the established link between prelamin A processing and neurodegenerative diseases.

We hypothesize that HPGD (hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase 15-(NAD)) plays a crucial role in the development of Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria (HEP) by regulating the levels of prostaglandins, which in turn affect the expression of enzymes involved in heme biosynthesis. Specifically, reduced HPGD activity leads to increased prostaglandin levels, causing a decrease in aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS) expression, thereby exacerbating the accumulation of toxic heme precursors. We predict that HPGD overexpression in HEP patient cells will decrease prostaglandin levels and increase ALAS expression, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, HPGD inhibition will refute our hypothesis by increasing prostaglandin levels and decreasing ALAS expression, worsening HEP symptoms.

We hypothesize that Adenosine Kinase (ADK) plays a crucial role in the development of Myasthenic syndrome, congenital, 14, by regulating adenosine levels in the neuromuscular junction. Elevated ADK activity may lead to decreased adenosine, disrupting its neuromodulatory effects on acetylcholine release. This imbalance impairs neuromuscular transmission, contributing to the disease's characteristic muscle weakness. We predict that ADK inhibition will increase adenosine levels, enhancing neuromuscular transmission and alleviating symptoms in Myasthenic syndrome, congenital, 14 models. Confirmation would come from improved muscle function in ADK-inhibited models, while refutation would result from unchanged or worsened symptoms. This hypothesis is grounded in ADK's known role in adenosine metabolism and the importance of adenosine in neuromuscular transmission.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, ataxia, and seizures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that B3GALNT2, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, ataxia, and seizures by aberrantly glycosylating and modifying the function of neural cell adhesion molecules. Specifically, we propose that reduced B3GALNT2 activity disrupts the proper glycosylation of these molecules, leading to impaired neural cell-cell interactions and synaptic formation. This, in turn, contributes to the neurodevelopmental abnormalities characteristic of the disorder. We predict that experimental knockdown of B3GALNT2 in neural cells will result in decreased cell adhesion and increased synaptic dysfunction, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, rescue of B3GALNT2 activity will restore normal cell adhesion and synaptic function, refuting our hypothesis.

We hypothesize that biliverdin reductase A (BLVRA) plays a crucial role in Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation 8 (NBIA8) by regulating iron homeostasis through the modulation of biliverdin and bilirubin levels. Specifically, BLVRA's enzymatic activity affects the production of bilirubin, which has antioxidant properties and can chelate iron. We predict that decreased BLVRA activity will lead to increased iron accumulation in the brain, exacerbating NBIA8. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that BLVRA knockdown or inhibition increases iron levels and worsens disease symptoms in NBIA8 models. Refutation would occur if BLVRA modulation has no effect on iron accumulation or disease progression.

We hypothesize that GAS6 (growth arrest-specific 6) enzyme plays a crucial role in the development of Hyperlipoproteinemia 1 by regulating the clearance of chylomicrons from the bloodstream. Specifically, GAS6 binds to the Axl receptor on macrophages, enhancing the phagocytosis of chylomicron remnants. Impaired GAS6-Axl signaling leads to decreased clearance, resulting in elevated chylomicron levels characteristic of Hyperlipoproteinemia 1. We predict that GAS6 deficiency will increase chylomicron levels in mice, which can be confirmed by measuring increased triglyceride levels in plasma. Conversely, overexpression of GAS6 will decrease chylomicron levels, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed. This mechanism is grounded in known biochemistry of GAS6-Axl signaling and its role in lipid metabolism.

We hypothesize that the enzyme N-acetylglucosamine-6-sulfatase (GNS) plays a crucial role in the development of L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria by regulating the sulfation status of glycosaminoglycans, which in turn affects the activity of the mitochondrial enzyme L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase. Impaired GNS activity leads to altered glycosaminoglycan sulfation, causing increased L-2-hydroxyglutarate production. We predict that GNS deficiency will result in elevated L-2-hydroxyglutarate levels in patient cells, which can be confirmed by metabolomic analysis. Conversely, overexpressing GNS in patient cells will decrease L-2-hydroxyglutarate levels, refuting the hypothesis if no effect is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of glycosaminoglycan metabolism and its impact on mitochondrial function.

We hypothesize that COX3, a subunit of cytochrome c oxidase, plays a crucial role in the development of Neu-Laxova syndrome 2 by regulating mitochondrial energy metabolism. Specifically, we propose that mutations in the COX3 gene lead to impaired mitochondrial function, resulting in increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and subsequent damage to cellular components. This, in turn, disrupts the normal development of the embryo, leading to the characteristic features of Neu-Laxova syndrome 2. We predict that experimental overexpression of COX3 in Neu-Laxova syndrome 2 patient-derived cells will reduce ROS levels and improve mitochondrial function, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, siRNA-mediated knockdown of COX3 in healthy cells will increase ROS levels and mimic the disease phenotype, refuting our hypothesis if this does not occur.

terminal_shown: Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that GSTZ1, a glutathione S-transferase, plays a crucial role in mitigating oxidative stress in mitochondria, thereby connecting to Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay. Specifically, GSTZ1 facilitates the conjugation of glutathione to toxic metabolites, preventing damage to mitochondrial proteins and DNA. We predict that GSTZ1 deficiency will lead to increased oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction, resulting in the multisystemic symptoms of this disease. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that GSTZ1 overexpression in patient-derived cells reduces oxidative stress and improves mitochondrial function, while refutation would come from experiments demonstrating no effect of GSTZ1 modulation on mitochondrial health in these cells.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 6
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that RRM2B, a ribonucleotide reductase subunit, contributes to Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 6, by regulating the availability of deoxyribonucleotides for mitochondrial DNA replication. Specifically, reduced RRM2B activity may lead to impaired mtDNA replication, resulting in decreased COX6B1 gene expression, a nuclear-encoded subunit of complex IV. We predict that RRM2B knockdown will decrease COX6B1 mRNA levels and increase disease severity. Confirmation would come from observing decreased COX6B1 expression and complex IV activity in cells with reduced RRM2B. Refutation would occur if RRM2B knockdown does not affect COX6B1 expression or complex IV function. This hypothesis is grounded in the known role of RRM2B in nucleotide metabolism and the dependence of mitochondrial DNA replication on deoxyribonucleotides.

We hypothesize that APIP (Apoptotic Protease Activating Factor 1 Interacting Protein) plays a crucial role in the development of Cataract 44 by regulating oxidative stress in the lens epithelial cells. APIP's interaction with apoptotic pathways may lead to an imbalance in redox homeostasis, causing lens protein aggregation and opacity. Specifically, we predict that APIP overexpression will increase reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, APIP knockdown will reduce ROS levels and mitigate cataract formation. Experimental confirmation would involve measuring ROS levels and lens clarity in APIP-modulated lens epithelial cells. Refutation would occur if APIP modulation does not affect ROS production or cataract formation in these cells. This hypothesis is grounded in the known role of oxidative stress in cataractogenesis and APIP's involvement in apoptotic pathways.

We hypothesize that the OGDH (2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase) enzyme plays a crucial role in the development of Oculoskeletodental syndrome through its regulation of alpha-ketoglutarate levels, which in turn affects collagen synthesis. Specifically, impaired OGDH activity leads to decreased alpha-ketoglutarate, reducing collagen hydroxylation and ultimately causing the skeletal, dental, and ocular abnormalities characteristic of the syndrome. We predict that OGDH knockdown in osteoblasts will result in decreased collagen hydroxylation and altered bone matrix composition, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, OGDH overexpression will rescue collagen synthesis defects, refuting the hypothesis if no rescue is observed. This mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of collagen synthesis and the role of alpha-ketoglutarate as a cofactor for collagen hydroxylases.

We hypothesize that ALG1, a mannosyltransferase involved in N-glycosylation, plays a crucial role in the development of Rafiq syndrome. Specifically, we propose that impaired ALG1 activity disrupts the glycosylation of proteins essential for neuronal function, leading to the characteristic neurodevelopmental abnormalities seen in Rafiq syndrome. We predict that patients with Rafiq syndrome will exhibit reduced ALG1 enzyme activity and altered N-glycosylation patterns in neural tissues. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating a significant decrease in ALG1 activity in patient-derived neural cells, while refutation would be achieved by showing no difference in ALG1 activity between patient and control samples. This hypothesis is grounded in the known importance of N-glycosylation in neuronal development and function.

terminal_shown: Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal recessive 3
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ECHDC1, an enzyme involved in mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis, plays a crucial role in maintaining mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) stability. Specifically, we propose that ECHDC1 regulates the production of mitochondrial fatty acids, which are essential for the assembly and function of mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes. In the context of Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal recessive 3, we predict that ECHDC1 deficiency will lead to impaired mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis, resulting in increased mtDNA deletions and disease progression. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased mtDNA deletions in cells with ECHDC1 knockdown, while refutation would be shown by unchanged mtDNA deletion rates in ECHDC1-deficient cells.

We hypothesize that B3GLCT, a glycosyltransferase involved in glycosaminoglycan synthesis, plays a crucial role in the development of sudden cardiac failure in infants. Specifically, we propose that B3GLCT's dysfunction leads to aberrant glycosylation of cardiac proteins, disrupting the structural integrity of the cardiac extracellular matrix. This, in turn, compromises cardiac function and increases the risk of sudden cardiac failure. We predict that infants with B3GLCT mutations will exhibit altered glycosaminoglycan profiles in cardiac tissue, which can be confirmed by mass spectrometry analysis. Refutation of this hypothesis would require the absence of significant glycosaminoglycan alterations in cardiac tissue from affected infants, suggesting an alternative mechanism underlying sudden cardiac failure in this population.

terminal_shown: Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that B4GALNT1, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay. Specifically, we propose that B4GALNT1's abnormal activity disrupts the glycosylation of mitochondrial proteins, leading to impaired mitochondrial function and energy production. This, in turn, affects the high-energy demands of muscle, auditory, and visual tissues, resulting in the characteristic symptoms of the disease. We predict that patients with this disease will exhibit reduced B4GALNT1 activity and altered glycosylation patterns in mitochondrial proteins. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by the identification of B4GALNT1 mutations in patient samples and the observation of rescued mitochondrial function upon B4GALNT1 enzyme replacement. Refutation would be evidenced by the absence of B4GALNT1 mutations and normal glycosylation patterns in affected individuals.

We hypothesize that Hepatocyte Growth Factor (HGF) plays a crucial role in the development of sudden cardiac failure in infants by regulating the metabolism of cardiac myocytes. Specifically, HGF activates the MET receptor, triggering a signaling cascade that enhances glucose uptake and glycolysis in cardiac cells. This leads to an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, causing oxidative stress and ultimately contributing to cardiac cell death. We predict that inhibition of HGF signaling will reduce ROS production and prevent cardiac cell death in infantile cardiac failure models. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through reduced cardiac cell death and improved cardiac function in HGF-inhibited models, while refutation would be seen if HGF inhibition has no effect on cardiac cell survival or function.

We hypothesize that RDH13, a retinol dehydrogenase, plays a crucial role in the development of Fish-eye disease by impairing the conversion of 11-cis retinal to 11-cis retinol, a critical step in the visual cycle. This impairment leads to accumulation of toxic retinaldehyde conjugates in the retina, causing progressive vision loss. We predict that overexpression of RDH13 in retinal cells will rescue the visual cycle and mitigate disease symptoms, whereas knockdown of RDH13 will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved electroretinogram responses in RDH13-overexpressing retinal cells, while refutation would be shown by lack of improvement or worsening of responses. This mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of retinoid metabolism and its importance in maintaining retinal health.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes syndrome
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that the GBA1 enzyme, which breaks down glucocerebrosides, plays a crucial role in maintaining mitochondrial function. Impaired GBA1 activity leads to accumulation of toxic lipid species, disrupting mitochondrial membrane integrity and triggering a cascade of events resulting in Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) syndrome. Specifically, we predict that GBA1 deficiency will increase mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpressing GBA1 in MELAS patient-derived cells will reduce ROS levels, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function, and can be tested through cellular and biochemical assays.

We hypothesize that NDUFB3, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the development of Attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder 7 (ADHD7) through impaired mitochondrial energy metabolism in dopamine-producing neurons. Specifically, reduced NDUFB3 expression or activity leads to decreased complex I activity, resulting in altered dopamine synthesis and release. This, in turn, disrupts normal neuronal signaling and contributes to ADHD7 symptoms. We predict that experimental knockdown of NDUFB3 in dopaminergic neurons will result in hyperactive behavior and attention deficits in animal models, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFB3 will rescue these phenotypes, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed.

We hypothesize that NDUFB9, a subunit of NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Congenital lactase deficiency. Specifically, we propose that impaired NDUFB9 function leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, resulting in decreased ATP production and altered enterocyte energy metabolism. This, in turn, disrupts the proper folding and trafficking of lactase enzyme, leading to its deficiency. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of NDUFB9 in intestinal epithelial cells will result in reduced lactase activity, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of NDUFB9 will rescue lactase activity, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of mitochondrial energy metabolism and its impact on protein folding and trafficking.

We hypothesize that NDUFS2, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, plays a crucial role in the regulation of fatty acid beta-oxidation, which is impaired in 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase deficiency. Specifically, we propose that NDUFS2-mediated electron transport chain activity influences the redox state of the mitochondrial matrix, thereby affecting the activity of 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase. We predict that overexpression of NDUFS2 will increase 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase activity, mitigating the disease phenotype, whereas NDUFS2 knockdown will exacerbate it. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase activity and improved fatty acid oxidation in cells overexpressing NDUFS2, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or worsened disease phenotypes.

We hypothesize that PIGU (Phosphatidylinositol Glycan anchor biosynthesis class U) is mechanistically connected to Atrichia with papular lesions through its role in glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor biosynthesis. Impaired PIGU function may lead to defective GPI anchoring of hair follicle stem cell proteins, disrupting hair growth and development. We predict that PIGU deficiency will result in reduced expression of GPI-anchored proteins in hair follicles, leading to the characteristic hair loss and skin lesions of Atrichia with papular lesions. Confirmation would come from observing decreased GPI-anchored protein expression in patient hair follicle samples, while refutation would result from normal expression levels despite PIGU deficiency. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of GPI anchor biosynthesis and its importance in cell surface protein anchoring.

We hypothesize that WARS2, a tryptophan-tRNA synthetase, plays a crucial role in the development of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, spondylodysplastic type, 2, by impairing collagen synthesis. Specifically, WARS2 mutations lead to defective tryptophan incorporation into collagen proteins, disrupting their triple-helix structure and ultimately causing tissue fragility. We predict that cells from patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, spondylodysplastic type, 2, will exhibit reduced collagen production and increased proteolytic degradation due to misfolded collagen. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing decreased collagen synthesis and increased proteolysis in patient-derived cells with WARS2 mutations. Refutation would occur if collagen production and structure are found to be normal in these cells.

We hypothesize that TOP2A, a DNA topoisomerase, plays a crucial role in the development of Anemia, congenital, non-spherocytic hemolytic, 6, by regulating the expression of genes involved in heme biosynthesis. Specifically, TOP2A's enzymatic activity is required for the proper transcription of the UROS gene, which encodes uroporphyrinogen III synthase, an enzyme essential for heme production. Disruption of TOP2A activity leads to decreased UROS expression, resulting in impaired heme biosynthesis and subsequent anemia. We predict that TOP2A inhibition will decrease UROS mRNA levels in erythroid cells, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, TOP2A overexpression will increase UROS mRNA levels, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of DNA topoisomerases and heme biosynthesis.

We hypothesize that B3GALT2, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Oliver-McFarlane syndrome by aberrantly glycosylating and thereby inactivating a key enzyme involved in cholesterol metabolism. Specifically, we propose that B3GALT2-mediated glycosylation of 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase (DHCR7) impairs its ability to convert 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholesterol, leading to the accumulation of toxic sterol intermediates characteristic of Oliver-McFarlane syndrome.
