We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of B3GALT2 in patient-derived cells will restore DHCR7 activity and reduce toxic sterol levels, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of B3GALT2 will exacerbate the disease phenotype, refuting our hypothesis.

We hypothesize that kynureninase (KYNU) plays a crucial role in the development of Trichothiodystrophy 8, non-photosensitive, by regulating the kynurenine pathway and thereby influencing the levels of toxic tryptophan metabolites. Specifically, impaired KYNU activity leads to the accumulation of 3-hydroxykynurenine, which damages DNA and disrupts transcription. We predict that patients with Trichothiodystrophy 8, non-photosensitive, will exhibit reduced KYNU enzyme activity and elevated 3-hydroxykynurenine levels. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by measuring KYNU activity and 3-hydroxykynurenine levels in patient samples, while refutation would come from finding no significant difference in KYNU activity or 3-hydroxykynurenine levels between patients and healthy controls.

We hypothesize that the enzyme GLA (glutamic acid decarboxylase-like activity, also known as 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase) plays a crucial role in the development of Hypercalciuria absorptive 2 through its involvement in the vitamin D metabolic pathway. Specifically, GLA regulates the conversion of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate to homogentisate, which in turn affects the expression of genes involved in calcium absorption in the intestine. We predict that increased GLA activity will lead to enhanced calcium absorption, resulting in hypercalciuria. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating a significant increase in urinary calcium excretion in response to GLA overexpression, while refutation would be achieved by showing no effect on calcium absorption in GLA-deficient models.

We hypothesize that adenosine deaminase (ADO) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Leber congenital amaurosis 2 (LCA2) by regulating the metabolism of retinal retinol. ADO's enzymatic activity affects the levels of adenosine, which in turn modulates the expression of RPE65, a key enzyme in the visual cycle. Decreased ADO activity leads to increased adenosine levels, resulting in reduced RPE65 expression and impaired 11-cis retinal production, a hallmark of LCA2. We predict that ADO overexpression in LCA2 patient-derived retinal cells will increase RPE65 expression and restore visual cycle function, whereas ADO inhibition will exacerbate the disease phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would require demonstration of improved visual cycle function in ADO-overexpressing cells, while refutation would involve failure to observe any effect on RPE65 expression or visual cycle function.

terminal_shown: Leukoencephalopathy with dystonia and motor neuropathy
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that LANCL1, a lanthionine synthetase, plays a crucial role in the development of Leukoencephalopathy with dystonia and motor neuropathy by regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and function. Specifically, LANCL1's interaction with the mTOR pathway modulates mitochondrial dynamics, leading to impaired energy metabolism in neurons. We predict that LANCL1 overexpression will rescue mitochondrial dysfunction in patient-derived cells, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, LANCL1 knockdown will exacerbate mitochondrial abnormalities, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in LANCL1's known role in regulating cellular metabolism and its potential impact on neurodegenerative diseases. Experimental validation will involve assessing mitochondrial function and morphology in LANCL1-modulated cells from Leukoencephalopathy with dystonia and motor neuropathy patients.

We hypothesize that CDKN2A, a tumor suppressor enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Alzheimer disease mitochondrial dysfunction. Specifically, we propose that CDKN2A regulates the activity of PGC-1α, a key transcriptional coactivator involved in mitochondrial biogenesis and function. Reduced CDKN2A expression leads to increased PGC-1α activity, resulting in mitochondrial overload and subsequent dysfunction. We predict that CDKN2A knockdown in neuronal cells will increase PGC-1α-mediated mitochondrial biogenesis, leading to enhanced mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production and decreased cellular respiration. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased mitochondrial DNA copy number and decreased ATP production in CDKN2A-knockdown cells, while refutation would be shown by unchanged mitochondrial function and biogenesis.

We hypothesize that GSTZ1, a glutathione S-transferase, plays a crucial role in the development of Pseudovaginal perineoscrotal hypospadias by regulating the metabolism of androgens, specifically dihydrotestosterone (DHT). GSTZ1's ability to conjugate glutathione to DHT may modulate its bioavailability and activity during fetal development. We predict that decreased GSTZ1 activity will lead to increased DHT levels, resulting in abnormal genital tubercle formation and hypospadias. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through increased incidence of hypospadias in GSTZ1 knockout models, while refutation would be seen in models with overexpressed GSTZ1 showing no increase in hypospadias incidence. This mechanism is grounded in GSTZ1's known role in steroid hormone metabolism and the critical role of androgens in genital development.

We hypothesize that PNPLA6, a patatin-like phospholipase, contributes to the development of Esophageal cancer by modulating lipid metabolism and promoting cell proliferation. Specifically, PNPLA6 hydrolyzes phospholipids to produce lysophospholipids, which activate PI3K/AKT signaling, a pathway known to be upregulated in Esophageal cancer. We predict that overexpression of PNPLA6 in Esophageal epithelial cells will increase cell proliferation and tumor formation, whereas inhibition of PNPLA6 will suppress these effects. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased PNPLA6 expression in Esophageal cancer tissues and a significant reduction in tumor growth upon PNPLA6 inhibition. Refutation would be shown by no significant difference in cell proliferation or tumor formation between PNPLA6-overexpressing and control cells.

terminal_shown: Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal dominant, 5
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that thyroid peroxidase (TPO) contributes to the pathogenesis of Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal dominant, 5 (PEO) by modulating oxidative stress in mitochondria. TPO's enzymatic activity generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) as a byproduct, which can accumulate in mitochondrial DNA, leading to deletions. We predict that TPO overexpression in patient-derived fibroblasts will increase mitochondrial ROS production and exacerbate mtDNA deletion frequency. Confirmation would come from observing a significant increase in mtDNA deletions in TPO-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be demonstrated by unchanged or decreased mtDNA deletion frequencies. This hypothesis is grounded in TPO's known role in thyroid hormone synthesis and the established link between oxidative stress and mitochondrial DNA damage in PEO.

We hypothesize that Carboxyl Ester Lipase (CEL) contributes to the development of Juvenile arthritis by modulating the production of pro-inflammatory lysophospholipids. Specifically, CEL hydrolyzes phospholipids to generate lysophosphatidylcholine, which is then converted to pro-inflammatory lysophosphatidic acid. This pathway enhances the activation of immune cells, leading to increased inflammation and joint damage in Juvenile arthritis. We predict that inhibition of CEL activity will reduce lysophosphatidic acid production and alleviate disease symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through reduced joint inflammation and immune cell activation in CEL-inhibited models of Juvenile arthritis, while refutation would be indicated by unchanged or exacerbated disease symptoms despite CEL inhibition.

We hypothesize that GMP synthase (GMPS) plays a crucial role in regulating Combined low LDL and fibrinogen through its impact on purine nucleotide synthesis. Specifically, GMPS-generated GMP is used to produce GDP, which in turn activates protein kinases that phosphorylate and inhibit key enzymes involved in LDL and fibrinogen production. We predict that overexpression of GMPS will decrease LDL and fibrinogen levels, whereas GMPS inhibition will increase them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating a significant decrease in LDL and fibrinogen levels in cells or animals overexpressing GMPS, while refutation would be achieved by showing no effect or an opposite effect on LDL and fibrinogen levels upon GMPS modulation. This mechanism is grounded in known biochemistry of purine nucleotide metabolism and its regulatory effects on various cellular processes.

We hypothesize that HRAS, a small GTPase, contributes to the development of Portal hypertension, non-cirrhotic, 1 (PVM) by regulating vascular smooth muscle cell contraction. Specifically, HRAS activates the Rho kinase pathway, leading to increased phosphorylation of myosin light chain and subsequent vasoconstriction. We predict that inhibition of HRAS will reduce portal pressure in PVM patients, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if HRAS inhibition does not affect portal pressure, our hypothesis will be refuted. This mechanism is grounded in known biochemistry, as HRAS is involved in signaling pathways that regulate cell contraction and vascular tone. Experimental confirmation can be achieved through measurement of portal pressure in response to HRAS inhibitors in PVM models.

We hypothesize that HIBADH (3-hydroxyisobutyrate dehydrogenase) plays a crucial role in the development of 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase deficiency by regulating the accumulation of toxic intermediates in the fatty acid beta-oxidation pathway. Specifically, HIBADH's impairment leads to increased levels of 3-hydroxyisobutyrate, which competitively inhibits 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase, exacerbating the deficiency. We predict that overexpressing HIBADH in cells from patients with 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase deficiency will decrease toxic intermediate accumulation and improve fatty acid oxidation. Confirmation would come from measuring increased 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase activity and reduced toxic intermediate levels in treated cells. Refutation would occur if HIBADH overexpression fails to improve fatty acid oxidation or worsens the deficiency.

We hypothesize that HDDC2 (2-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydratase 2) plays a crucial role in the development of Hemochromatosis 5 by regulating the metabolism of fatty acids in the liver, which in turn affects hepcidin expression and iron homeostasis. Specifically, HDDC2's enzymatic activity influences the production of fatty acyl-CoA molecules, which can modulate the activity of transcription factors controlling hepcidin gene expression. We predict that overexpression of HDDC2 will lead to increased hepcidin levels, reducing iron absorption and confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, HDDC2 knockdown will result in decreased hepcidin levels, exacerbating iron accumulation and refuting our hypothesis. This proposed mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of fatty acid metabolism and its intersection with iron homeostasis pathways.

We hypothesize that B4GALT4, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, contributes to the development of Acute hepatic porphyria by modulating the glycosylation and stability of aminolevulinic acid synthase 1 (ALAS1), a key enzyme in the heme biosynthesis pathway. Abnormal glycosylation of ALAS1 by B4GALT4 may lead to its increased activity and subsequent accumulation of toxic heme precursors. We predict that overexpression of B4GALT4 in hepatic cells will increase ALAS1 activity and exacerbate porphyria symptoms, whereas inhibition of B4GALT4 will reduce ALAS1 activity and alleviate symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased ALAS1 activity and porphyrin accumulation in B4GALT4-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by unchanged ALAS1 activity in response to B4GALT4 modulation.

We hypothesize that CHURC1-FNTB, a mitochondrial enzyme, plays a crucial role in regulating the biogenesis of iron-sulfur clusters, which are essential for the function of oxidative phosphorylation complexes. Specifically, CHURC1-FNTB's dysfunction leads to impaired iron-sulfur cluster assembly, resulting in Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 35. We predict that overexpressing CHURC1-FNTB in patient-derived cells will restore iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis and improve oxidative phosphorylation complex activity, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, knocking down CHURC1-FNTB in healthy cells will replicate the disease phenotype, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis and its importance in mitochondrial function.

We hypothesize that GLYCTK (glycerate kinase) plays a crucial role in the development of Ghosal hematodiaphyseal dysplasia by regulating glycerol metabolism in osteoblasts. Specifically, we propose that impaired GLYCTK activity disrupts the conversion of glycerol to glycerate, leading to an accumulation of glycerol and subsequent inhibition of osteoblast differentiation. This, in turn, affects bone mineralization and leads to the characteristic skeletal abnormalities seen in Ghosal hematodiaphyseal dysplasia. We predict that osteoblasts from individuals with Ghosal hematodiaphyseal dysplasia will exhibit reduced GLYCTK activity and altered glycerol metabolism, which can be confirmed by measuring glycerate levels in patient-derived osteoblasts. Refutation of this hypothesis would require demonstration of normal GLYCTK activity and glycerol metabolism in these cells.

We hypothesize that ENTPD8, an ectonucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase, contributes to the development of acute transient encephalopathy by modulating purinergic signaling in the brain. Specifically, ENTPD8 regulates the hydrolysis of ATP to ADP, influencing the activation of P2Y receptors and subsequent neuronal excitability. We predict that overexpression of ENTPD8 will lead to increased ADP production, enhanced P2Y receptor activation, and exacerbated neuronal excitotoxicity, resulting in acute transient encephalopathy. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased ENTPD8 activity and ADP levels in brain tissue of patients with acute transient encephalopathy, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased ENTPD8 activity in affected individuals.

We hypothesize that PTGES3, a specific enzyme involved in the synthesis of prostaglandin E2, plays a crucial role in the development of Occipital horn syndrome. This rare genetic disorder is characterized by defects in copper metabolism and connective tissue. We propose that PTGES3 regulates the expression of genes involved in copper transport, such as ATP7A, through a prostaglandin E2-mediated signaling pathway. Specifically, we predict that increased PTGES3 activity will lead to decreased ATP7A expression, resulting in impaired copper transport and contributing to the development of Occipital horn syndrome. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced ATP7A expression in cells overexpressing PTGES3, while refutation would be shown by unchanged ATP7A expression levels.

We hypothesize that LPCAT2, an enzyme involved in phospholipid biosynthesis, contributes to the development of Deafness, sensorineural, mitochondrial by disrupting mitochondrial membrane integrity. Specifically, LPCAT2's role in generating phosphatidylcholine species essential for mitochondrial function is impaired, leading to altered membrane fluidity and respiratory chain dysfunction. This results in increased reactive oxygen species production, damaging mitochondrial DNA and ultimately leading to sensorineural hearing loss. We predict that LPCAT2 knockdown in cochlear cells will increase mitochondrial oxidative stress and hearing loss, while LPCAT2 overexpression will mitigate these effects. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing decreased hearing thresholds in LPCAT2-deficient mice, while refutation would be indicated by unchanged hearing thresholds despite LPCAT2 manipulation.

We hypothesize that glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase (GRHPR) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Gaucher disease 3C by modulating the glyoxalase pathway, which detoxifies advanced glycosylation end-products (AGEs). In Gaucher disease 3C, the accumulation of glucosylceramide due to beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency leads to increased oxidative stress and AGE formation. GRHPR, by reducing hydroxypyruvate, regulates the glyoxalase pathway's activity. We predict that GRHPR overexpression will reduce AGE accumulation and alleviate disease symptoms, whereas GRHPR inhibition will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced AGE levels and improved clinical outcomes in Gaucher disease 3C models with GRHPR overexpression, while refutation would be shown by unchanged or worsened outcomes.

terminal_shown: Epileptic encephalopathy, infantile or early childhood, 1
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that PSTK (phosphoseryl-tRNA kinase) plays a crucial role in the development of Epileptic encephalopathy, infantile or early childhood, 1, by regulating the phosphorylation of serine-tRNA, which is essential for the synthesis of phosphoserine-containing proteins involved in neuronal function. Impaired PSTK activity leads to aberrant protein synthesis, disrupting neuronal excitability and contributing to the disease. We predict that PSTK knockdown in neuronal cells will result in altered protein synthesis patterns and increased excitability, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of PSTK will rescue these defects, refuting the hypothesis if no effect is observed. This mechanism is grounded in the known biochemistry of tRNA modification and its impact on protein synthesis, and is specifically relevant to the neurological defects observed in Epileptic encephalopathy, infantile or early childhood, 1.

We hypothesize that alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR) plays a crucial role in the development of 3-hydroxyisobutryl-CoA hydrolase deficiency by modulating the accumulation of toxic metabolites. Specifically, AMACR's racemization activity may influence the levels of (R)-3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA, a substrate for the deficient 3-hydroxyisobutryl-CoA hydrolase enzyme. We predict that overexpression of AMACR will exacerbate the disease phenotype by increasing the formation of (R)-3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA, leading to enhanced toxicity. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased disease severity in cells overexpressing AMACR, while refutation would be shown by no significant change in disease phenotype upon AMACR overexpression. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of AMACR and its role in metabolite racemization.

We hypothesize that Dopachrome Tautomerase (DCT) contributes to the development of Esophageal cancer through its role in regulating oxidative stress and inflammation. DCT, also known as Tyrosinase-related protein 2, has been implicated in melanin production and antioxidant defense. In the context of Esophageal cancer, we propose that DCT's antioxidant activity is hijacked to protect cancer cells from oxidative damage, promoting their survival and proliferation. Specifically, we predict that DCT overexpression will correlate with increased tumor growth and poor prognosis in Esophageal cancer patients. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by immunohistochemical analysis showing elevated DCT levels in Esophageal cancer tissues, while refutation would be supported by experiments showing no significant difference in DCT expression between cancerous and non-cancerous Esophageal tissues.

We hypothesize that GDP-mannose 4,6-dehydratase (GMDS) contributes to the development of Glycine N-methyltransferase (GNMT) deficiency by regulating the availability of SAMe (S-adenosylmethionine) through an indirect metabolic pathway. GMDS catalyzes the conversion of GDP-mannose to GDP-4-keto-6-deoxy-mannose, which can influence the methionine cycle and subsequently affect SAMe levels. Low SAMe levels are associated with GNMT deficiency, as GNMT requires SAMe as a methyl donor. We predict that GMDS overexpression will decrease SAMe levels, exacerbating GNMT deficiency, whereas GMDS inhibition will increase SAMe levels, alleviating the deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased GNMT activity in cells overexpressing GMDS, while refutation would be seen if GMDS inhibition fails to rescue GNMT activity in deficient cells.

terminal_shown: Rod-cone dystrophy, sensorineural deafness, and Fanconi-type renal dysfunction
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that the enzyme GNE (glucosamine (N-acetyl)-6-sulfatase) plays a crucial role in maintaining proper glycosylation of proteins in sensory and renal tissues. Specifically, GNE's sulfatase activity is necessary for the biosynthesis of sialic acid, a key component of glycoproteins. Impaired GNE function leads to defective glycosylation, causing protein misfolding and dysfunction in photoreceptors, auditory hair cells, and renal proximal tubules. This results in Rod-cone dystrophy, sensorineural deafness, and Fanconi-type renal dysfunction. We predict that GNE knockdown in these tissues will lead to reduced sialic acid levels and increased protein misfolding, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, GNE overexpression will rescue these phenotypes, refuting our hypothesis if no improvement is observed.

We hypothesize that DHRSX, a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase, plays a crucial role in the development of Laurence-Moon syndrome by modulating the metabolism of retinoic acid, a key regulator of photoreceptor cell differentiation. Specifically, we propose that DHRSX catalyzes the reduction of retinoic acid to its less active form, thereby disrupting the normal differentiation of photoreceptor cells and contributing to the retinal dystrophy characteristic of Laurence-Moon syndrome. We predict that overexpression of DHRSX in retinal cells will lead to decreased retinoic acid levels and impaired photoreceptor cell differentiation, whereas inhibition of DHRSX will have the opposite effect. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experimental evidence showing a direct correlation between DHRSX activity and retinoic acid levels in retinal cells from Laurence-Moon syndrome patients.

We hypothesize that AWAT2, an acyl-CoA wax alcohol acyltransferase, plays a crucial role in the development of Spastic paraplegia 26, autosomal recessive, by regulating the synthesis of very-long-chain fatty acids in the brain. Specifically, AWAT2's dysfunction leads to impaired myelin lipid composition, disrupting axonal integrity and function. We predict that AWAT2 deficiency will result in reduced levels of specific very-long-chain fatty acids in patient-derived cells, which can be confirmed by lipidomics analysis. Conversely, overexpression of AWAT2 in patient cells will rescue the myelin lipid composition defect, refuting our hypothesis if no rescue is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of fatty acid metabolism and its importance in maintaining neural tissue homeostasis.

We hypothesize that sphingosine-1-phosphate phosphatase 2 (SGPP2) contributes to Brugada syndrome 2 by regulating sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) levels, which in turn modulate the activity of the cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5. Elevated S1P levels, resulting from reduced SGPP2 activity, increase Nav1.5 channel inactivation, leading to decreased sodium currents and the characteristic ST-segment elevation in Brugada syndrome 2. We predict that SGPP2 knockdown in cardiomyocytes will increase S1P levels, reduce sodium currents, and recapitulate the Brugada syndrome 2 phenotype. Confirmation would come from observing a significant reduction in sodium currents in SGPP2-knockdown cardiomyocytes, while refutation would result from unchanged sodium currents despite SGPP2 knockdown.

We hypothesize that Methionine synthase (MET) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Fumarase deficiency by regulating the methylation status of key enzymes in the citric acid cycle, including Fumarase. Specifically, MET's activity influences the availability of S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe), which in turn affects the methylation and stability of Fumarase. We predict that decreased MET activity will lead to reduced Fumarase stability and activity, exacerbating the metabolic defects associated with Fumarase deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by experimental results showing that MET overexpression or SAMe supplementation increases Fumarase activity in cells from Fumarase deficiency patients, while refutation would be indicated by no change in Fumarase activity despite MET modulation.

We hypothesize that ATP7A, a copper-transporting ATPase, plays a crucial role in regulating the activity of platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase (PAF-AH) by maintaining optimal copper levels for its function. Copper is a cofactor for PAF-AH, and its deficiency can lead to impaired enzyme activity. We predict that ATP7A deficiency will result in decreased copper delivery to PAF-AH, leading to reduced enzyme activity and contributing to Platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased PAF-AH activity in cells with ATP7A knockdown, while refutation would be seen if PAF-AH activity remains unchanged despite ATP7A deficiency. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of copper-dependent enzymes and highlights a potential link between ATP7A and PAF-AH deficiency.

We hypothesize that HARS2, a histidyl-tRNA synthetase, contributes to the development of Hereditary coproporphyria through impaired heme biosynthesis. Specifically, HARS2's reduced activity leads to decreased translation of genes involved in the heme pathway, including CPOX, which encodes coproporphyrinogen oxidase. This decrease impairs the conversion of coproporphyrinogen to protoporphyrin, resulting in accumulated coproporphyrinogen and its oxidized form, coproporphyrin. We predict that overexpressing HARS2 in Hereditary coproporphyria patient cells will increase CPOX protein levels and reduce coproporphyrin accumulation, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, knocking down HARS2 in healthy cells will decrease CPOX levels and increase coproporphyrin, refuting our hypothesis.

We hypothesize that glucokinase (GCK) plays a crucial role in the development of Hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, familial, 4, by regulating glucose sensing in pancreatic beta-cells. Specifically, we propose that gain-of-function mutations in GCK lead to increased glucose phosphorylation, enhanced ATP production, and subsequent closure of potassium channels, resulting in excessive insulin secretion. We predict that overexpression of mutant GCK in beta-cells will confirm this hypothesis by showing increased insulin release at low glucose concentrations. Conversely, refutation would occur if GCK inhibition in these cells fails to reduce insulin secretion. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of GCK as a key regulator of glucose metabolism in beta-cells.

We hypothesize that Cytochrome c (CYCS) plays a crucial role in the development of Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency. CYCS is essential for electron transfer between complex III and complex IV in the mitochondrial respiratory chain. We propose that decreased CYCS expression or function disrupts this electron transfer, leading to complex IV dysfunction. Specifically, we predict that CYCS overexpression will rescue complex IV activity in cells with Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased complex IV activity and oxygen consumption rates in cells overexpressing CYCS. Refutation would be shown by no change in complex IV activity despite CYCS overexpression, indicating an alternative mechanism underlying the disease.

We hypothesize that CYP2A6, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, contributes to the development of Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency by metabolizing malonyl-CoA, a substrate for the malonyl-CoA decarboxylase enzyme. Specifically, CYP2A6's metabolism of malonyl-CoA reduces its availability for decarboxylation, exacerbating the deficiency. We predict that inhibition of CYP2A6 will increase malonyl-CoA levels and alleviate disease symptoms, whereas overexpression of CYP2A6 will worsen symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased disease severity in cells or animals treated with CYP2A6 inhibitors, while refutation would be shown by no change in disease severity or worsening of symptoms upon CYP2A6 inhibition.

terminal_shown: Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal recessive 3
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CYP2C19, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, contributes to the pathogenesis of Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal recessive 3, by modulating the metabolism of coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10), a crucial electron carrier in the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Impaired CYP2C19 activity may lead to decreased CoQ10 levels, exacerbating mitochondrial dysfunction and DNA deletion formation. We predict that patients with this disease will exhibit reduced CYP2C19 activity and lower CoQ10 levels compared to healthy controls. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating a significant correlation between CYP2C19 activity and CoQ10 levels in patient samples, while refutation would be achieved by showing no such correlation or unchanged CoQ10 levels in CYP2C19-deficient cells.

We hypothesize that GARS1, a key enzyme in aminoacyl-tRNA synthesis, plays a crucial role in the development of Deafness, sensorineural, mitochondrial. Specifically, we propose that mitochondrial GARS1 dysfunction leads to impaired translation of mitochondrial proteins, disrupting the assembly and function of mitochondrial ribosomes. This, in turn, affects the energy metabolism of cochlear hair cells, ultimately resulting in sensorineural hearing loss. We predict that experimental knockdown of GARS1 in cochlear hair cells will lead to decreased mitochondrial protein synthesis and increased hearing loss, whereas overexpression of GARS1 will rescue this phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by demonstrating a direct correlation between GARS1 activity and mitochondrial protein synthesis in cochlear hair cells.

We hypothesize that B4GALT1, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, contributes to the development of seborrheic keratosis by aberrantly glycosylating and activating the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling pathway. This leads to enhanced cell proliferation and survival, characteristic of seborrheic keratosis lesions. Specifically, we predict that B4GALT1-mediated glycosylation of EGFR will increase its binding affinity to its ligands, resulting in elevated downstream signaling. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased EGFR activation and glycosylation in seborrheic keratosis lesions with elevated B4GALT1 expression. Refutation would be shown by unchanged or decreased EGFR activation in lesions with B4GALT1 inhibition or knockdown.

We hypothesize that CYP19A1, an aromatase enzyme, contributes to the pathogenesis of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 29 (DEE29) by disrupting the balance of neuroactive steroids in the brain. Specifically, altered CYP19A1 activity leads to decreased conversion of androgens to estrogens, resulting in an accumulation of neuroexcitatory androgens that exacerbate neuronal hyperexcitability and seizure susceptibility. We predict that CYP19A1 inhibitors will worsen DEE29 symptoms, while CYP19A1 activators will ameliorate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by the observation that CYP19A1 inhibitor treatment increases seizure frequency in DEE29 models, while refutation would be demonstrated by the lack of effect on seizure susceptibility.

We hypothesize that HSD17B3, a 17-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, contributes to the pathogenesis of Retinitis pigmentosa 17 by disrupting the balance of retinoid metabolism in photoreceptor cells. Specifically, HSD17B3's role in converting androstenedione to testosterone may interfere with the retinoid cycle, leading to accumulation of toxic retinoid intermediates. We predict that inhibition of HSD17B3 will reduce retinal degeneration in a mouse model of Retinitis pigmentosa 17, as measured by electroretinography and histological analysis. Confirmation would be observed if HSD17B3 inhibition preserves photoreceptor function and structure, while refutation would occur if no significant difference is seen between treated and untreated models. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of retinoid metabolism and the role of HSD17B3 in steroid hormone biosynthesis.

We hypothesize that the enzyme adenylosuccinate lyase (ADSL) plays a crucial role in the development of Focal dermal hypoplasia (FDH) through its involvement in purine metabolism. Specifically, ADSL's impairment leads to accumulation of toxic intermediates, such as SAICAR, which disrupts cellular energy homeostasis and causes aberrant cell signaling. This disruption affects the function of fibroblasts and adipocytes, leading to the characteristic skin and subcutaneous tissue defects seen in FDH. We predict that ADSL activity will be reduced in FDH patient-derived fibroblasts, and that supplementation with adenylosuccinate will rescue the cellular phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by observing improved cellular morphology and function in response to adenylosuccinate supplementation, while refutation would be indicated by lack of response or worsening of cellular defects.

terminal_shown: Polycystic liver disease 3 with or without kidney cysts
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that Phosphoglucomutase 1 (PGM1) plays a crucial role in the development of Polycystic liver disease 3 with or without kidney cysts through its regulation of glycogen synthesis and glucose metabolism. Specifically, PGM1's impairment leads to altered glucose flux, triggering an increase in AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activity, which in turn promotes cyst growth and proliferation. We predict that PGM1 deficiency will result in increased cyst formation in liver and kidney cells, which can be confirmed by observing enhanced cystogenesis in PGM1-knockdown cellular models. Conversely, overexpression of PGM1 will reduce cyst formation, refuting our hypothesis if no such reduction is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of glycogen metabolism and its impact on cellular energy homeostasis.

We hypothesize that PRODH2, a proline dehydrogenase, plays a role in Congenital lactase deficiency by regulating the redox state of the intestinal epithelium, thereby affecting lactase enzyme activity. PRODH2's proline oxidation activity may modulate the NAD+/NADH ratio, influencing the lactase enzyme's stability and function. We predict that PRODH2 overexpression will decrease lactase activity in intestinal cells, while PRODH2 knockdown will increase lactase activity. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through decreased lactase enzyme activity in PRODH2-overexpressing intestinal cells, while refutation would be seen if lactase activity remains unchanged. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of redox regulation of enzyme activity and its potential impact on Congenital lactase deficiency.

We hypothesize that FGFR3, a receptor tyrosine kinase, contributes to MHC class I deficiency 2 by regulating the expression of genes involved in major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I assembly and transport. Specifically, FGFR3 signaling modulates the activity of the transcription factor NLRC5, which is essential for MHC class I gene expression. We predict that inhibition of FGFR3 will decrease NLRC5 activity, leading to reduced MHC class I surface expression, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if FGFR3 inhibition does not affect NLRC5 activity or MHC class I expression, our hypothesis will be refuted. This proposed mechanism is grounded in the known roles of FGFR3 in cell signaling and NLRC5 in MHC class I regulation, and provides a testable link between FGFR3 and MHC class I deficiency 2.

We hypothesize that the enzyme Dihydrolipoyltransacetylase (DLAT) plays a crucial role in the development of Trichothiodystrophy 8, non-photosensitive, by impairing the function of the mitochondrial trifunctional protein complex. Specifically, DLAT's dysfunction leads to defective fatty acid oxidation, resulting in accumulation of toxic intermediates that damage the TFIIH complex, a critical component in transcription and DNA repair. We predict that DLAT deficiency will lead to decreased fatty acid oxidation rates and increased levels of toxic intermediates in patient-derived cells. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by reduced fatty acid oxidation rates in DLAT-deficient cells, while refutation would be shown by normal fatty acid oxidation rates despite DLAT deficiency.

We hypothesize that B4GALT4, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, primary, autosomal recessive, 1 (PHOAR1) by modulating the glycosylation of fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs). Specifically, B4GALT4's enzymatic activity is necessary for the proper glycosylation and functioning of FGFRs, which are essential for bone growth and development. A deficiency in B4GALT4 activity would lead to aberrant FGFR signaling, resulting in the characteristic bone overgrowth and joint abnormalities seen in PHOAR1. Experimental confirmation of this hypothesis would involve demonstrating reduced FGFR glycosylation and signaling in cells lacking functional B4GALT4, while refutation would involve showing no significant difference in FGFR activity between B4GALT4-deficient and wild-type cells.

We hypothesize that PI4KA, a phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase, plays a crucial role in the development of CLAPO syndrome by regulating phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P) levels, which in turn affect the trafficking of lipids and proteins in the Golgi apparatus. Abnormal PI4KA activity leads to impaired lipid metabolism, contributing to the characteristic lipodystrophy and metabolic abnormalities seen in CLAPO syndrome. We predict that PI4KA inhibition will exacerbate lipid accumulation in patient-derived cells, while PI4KA overexpression will rescue this phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased PI4P levels and improved lipid trafficking in cells overexpressing PI4KA, whereas refutation would be shown by unchanged or worsened lipid metabolism in response to PI4KA modulation.

We hypothesize that ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 7 (ENPP7) contributes to the pathogenesis of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency by modulating the nucleotide triphosphate (NTP) pool, which in turn affects the energy status of the cell. Specifically, ENPP7's NTP hydrolysis activity may lead to decreased ATP levels, exacerbating the energy deficit caused by the deficiency of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase, an enzyme crucial for ketone body production and energy metabolism. We predict that ENPP7 inhibition will increase ATP levels and improve ketone body production in cells from patients with 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency. Confirmation would be demonstrated by increased ATP and ketone body levels in patient cells treated with ENPP7 inhibitors, while refutation would be shown by no change or decreased energy metabolism in response to ENPP7 inhibition.

We hypothesize that ALDH18A1, an enzyme involved in proline biosynthesis, contributes to the development of Argininosuccinic aciduria by regulating the production of delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C), a precursor to proline and a potential inhibitor of argininosuccinate lyase (ASL). In Argininosuccinic aciduria, ASL deficiency leads to accumulation of argininosuccinate. We predict that overexpression of ALDH18A1 will exacerbate Argininosuccinic aciduria by increasing P5C production, thereby inhibiting residual ASL activity and worsening argininosuccinate accumulation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased argininosuccinate levels in cells overexpressing ALDH18A1, while refutation would be shown by no change in argininosuccinate levels upon ALDH18A1 overexpression.

We hypothesize that GCNT2, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Leukodystrophy, hypomyelinating, 18, by regulating the glycosylation of myelin proteins. Specifically, GCNT2's activity is necessary for the proper O-glycosylation of myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), which is essential for myelin stability and maintenance. We predict that reduced GCNT2 activity will lead to hypoglycosylated MAG, resulting in impaired myelin formation and stability, characteristic of Leukodystrophy, hypomyelinating, 18. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing that GCNT2 knockdown or inhibition in oligodendrocytes leads to decreased MAG glycosylation and myelin defects, while refutation would come from experiments demonstrating no effect of GCNT2 manipulation on MAG glycosylation or myelin integrity.

We hypothesize that COX6A1, a subunit of cytochrome c oxidase, plays a crucial role in the regulation of mitochondrial energy metabolism, which is impaired in Urocanase deficiency. In this disease, the accumulation of urocanic acid disrupts mitochondrial function. We propose that COX6A1's modulation of oxidative phosphorylation is sensitive to the redox state, which is altered by urocanic acid. Specifically, we predict that overexpression of COX6A1 will mitigate the energetic deficits in Urocanase-deficient cells, whereas its knockdown will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by improved ATP production in COX6A1-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be shown by no change or worsening of energetic deficits.

We hypothesize that CYP3A5, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, contributes to the pathogenesis of Mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency 1 (MTPD1) by impairing the metabolism of long-chain fatty acids. Specifically, CYP3A5's abnormal metabolism of these fatty acids leads to the accumulation of toxic intermediates, exacerbating the mitochondrial dysfunction characteristic of MTPD1. We predict that CYP3A5 inhibition will reduce the levels of these toxic intermediates, alleviating disease symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased disease severity in MTPD1 patients treated with CYP3A5 inhibitors, whereas refutation would be shown by no significant change in disease severity upon CYP3A5 inhibition. This hypothesis is grounded in the known role of CYP3A5 in fatty acid metabolism and the mitochondrial dysfunction underlying MTPD1.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, impaired language, and gait abnormalities
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that DCTPP1, a nucleotide pyrophosphatase, plays a crucial role in neurodevelopment by regulating nucleotide pools and thereby influencing neuronal proliferation and differentiation. Specifically, we propose that DCTPP1 deficiency leads to an imbalance in nucleotide metabolism, resulting in impaired DNA replication and repair, which in turn contributes to the development of microcephaly, impaired language, and gait abnormalities characteristic of this neurodevelopmental disorder. We predict that DCTPP1 knockdown in neural stem cells will result in decreased neuronal proliferation and increased DNA damage, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, DCTPP1 overexpression will rescue these defects, refuting our hypothesis if no rescue is observed.

We hypothesize that HADHA, a crucial enzyme in mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, plays a role in Uncombable hair syndrome 2 (UHS2) through its impact on scalp skin lipid metabolism. Specifically, HADHA's dysfunction may lead to altered lipid profiles, affecting hair follicle development and structure. We predict that individuals with UHS2 will exhibit decreased HADHA activity in scalp skin, resulting in abnormal lipid accumulation and hair shaft defects. Confirmation of this hypothesis would come from experiments showing decreased HADHA enzyme activity in UHS2 scalp skin samples, while refutation would come from normal HADHA activity levels in affected individuals. This connection is grounded in the known importance of lipid metabolism in skin and hair health, and the specific role of HADHA in fatty acid beta-oxidation.

We hypothesize that the SDHD enzyme, a component of the succinate dehydrogenase complex, plays a crucial role in regulating the activity of N-terminal acetyltransferases (NATs) through the modulation of cellular energy metabolism. Specifically, we propose that SDHD-derived reactive oxygen species (ROS) influence the stability and activity of NATs, leading to impaired protein acetylation in N-terminal acetyltransferase deficiency. We predict that overexpression of SDHD will increase ROS production, resulting in decreased NAT activity and exacerbated disease symptoms, whereas SDHD knockdown will have the opposite effect. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant decrease in NAT activity in cells overexpressing SDHD, while refutation would be shown by no change in NAT activity despite altered SDHD expression.

We hypothesize that CYP2W1, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, contributes to the development of ischemic stroke by metabolizing arachidonic acid to epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), which in turn modulate vascular tone and platelet aggregation. Specifically, we propose that CYP2W1-derived EETs increase the expression of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), leading to enhanced nitric oxide production and subsequent vasodilation. We predict that inhibition of CYP2W1 will reduce EET production, decrease eNOS expression, and increase the incidence of ischemic stroke in animal models. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by decreased infarct volume and improved neurological function in CYP2W1-overexpressing animals subjected to middle cerebral artery occlusion, while refutation would be shown by no difference in stroke outcome between CYP2W1-inhibited and control animals.

We hypothesize that CYP11B2, an aldosterone synthase, contributes to the development of Fanconi renotubular syndrome 1 by modulating the renal expression of SLC2A2, a glucose transporter. Specifically, we propose that excessive aldosterone production, catalyzed by CYP11B2, leads to increased SLC2A2 expression, resulting in enhanced glucose reabsorption and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction in renal proximal tubular cells. This, in turn, impairs the cells' ability to maintain proper solute transport, leading to the characteristic renal tubular defects of Fanconi renotubular syndrome 1. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by the observation that CYP11B2 inhibition reduces SLC2A2 expression and alleviates renal tubular dysfunction in affected individuals, whereas refutation would be indicated by the absence of such effects.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, impaired language, and gait abnormalities
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that Farnesyl Diphosphate Synthase (FDPS) plays a crucial role in the development of Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, impaired language, and gait abnormalities. FDPS is involved in the mevalonate pathway, which produces isoprenoids essential for protein prenylation and cholesterol synthesis. We propose that impaired FDPS activity disrupts the prenylation of small GTPases, such as Ras and Rho, which are critical for neuronal development and migration. This disruption leads to abnormal brain development, resulting in microcephaly and subsequent neurodevelopmental impairments. Experimental confirmation would involve demonstrating reduced FDPS activity and altered protein prenylation patterns in patient-derived cells, while refutation would require showing no significant differences in FDPS activity or protein prenylation between patient and control cells.

We hypothesize that PLPP1 (phospholipid phosphatase 1) contributes to the development of Anemia, sideroblastic, 1 by regulating mitochondrial membrane phospholipid composition, which is crucial for normal mitochondrial function and heme synthesis. Specifically, PLPP1's dephosphorylation activity may modulate the levels of phosphatidic acid, affecting the transport of iron into mitochondria. We predict that PLPP1 overexpression will lead to decreased mitochondrial iron uptake, resulting in impaired heme synthesis and increased ring sideroblasts, characteristic of Anemia, sideroblastic, 1. Confirmation would come from experiments showing that PLPP1 overexpression in erythroblast cells reduces iron uptake and heme production, while refutation would be provided by data demonstrating no effect of PLPP1 overexpression on mitochondrial iron transport or heme synthesis.

We hypothesize that Isoprenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase (ICMT) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Glycine N-methyltransferase (GNMT) deficiency by regulating the methylation status of key proteins involved in glycine metabolism. Specifically, ICMT's methylation activity on isoprenylcysteine residues may modulate the function of proteins that interact with GNMT, leading to impaired glycine regulation. We predict that ICMT inhibition will exacerbate the metabolic abnormalities associated with GNMT deficiency, resulting in increased levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe) and decreased glycine N-methylation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased SAMe levels and decreased GNMT activity in cells treated with ICMT inhibitors, while refutation would be shown by no significant changes in these metabolites.

We hypothesize that MOGAT1, a monoacylglycerol O-acyltransferase, contributes to the development of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2D, by disrupting lipid metabolism in peripheral nerves. Specifically, MOGAT1's dysregulation leads to altered triglyceride synthesis, causing lipotoxicity and axonal damage. We predict that MOGAT1 inhibition will reduce triglyceride accumulation and alleviate axonal degeneration in CMT2D models. Confirmation would come from decreased triglyceride levels and improved nerve function in MOGAT1-inhibited CMT2D mouse models. Refutation would occur if MOGAT1 inhibition fails to reduce triglyceride accumulation or improve nerve function, indicating an alternative disease mechanism. This hypothesis is grounded in MOGAT1's known role in lipid metabolism and the established link between lipid dysregulation and neurodegenerative diseases.

We hypothesize that B3GNT3, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, contributes to the development of Esophageal cancer by aberrantly glycosylating and thereby stabilizing the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) on the surface of esophageal epithelial cells. This leads to enhanced EGFR signaling, promoting cell proliferation and tumor growth. We predict that overexpression of B3GNT3 in esophageal epithelial cells will increase EGFR-mediated signaling and cell growth, whereas knockdown of B3GNT3 will decrease EGFR stability and reduce tumor growth. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased B3GNT3 expression in Esophageal cancer tissues and inhibition of tumor growth in response to B3GNT3 knockdown. Refutation would be shown by lack of correlation between B3GNT3 expression and EGFR stability or tumor growth in Esophageal cancer models.

We hypothesize that PI4KA, a phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase, plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Mucopolysaccharidosis 3A (MPS3A) by regulating the trafficking of the defective enzyme, SGSH, in lysosomes. Specifically, PI4KA-generated phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P) modulates the recruitment of SGSH to lysosomal membranes, affecting its ability to break down heparan sulfate. We predict that overexpression of PI4KA will increase SGSH activity and reduce heparan sulfate accumulation in MPS3A cells, while PI4KA inhibition will exacerbate the disease phenotype. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by increased SGSH activity and reduced heparan sulfate levels in PI4KA-overexpressing MPS3A cells, whereas refutation would be shown by unchanged or worsened disease markers in response to PI4KA modulation.

We hypothesize that IMPA1, an enzyme involved in inositol phosphate metabolism, contributes to the pathogenesis of Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency by modulating homocysteine levels. Specifically, IMPA1's regulation of inositol trisphosphate affects calcium signaling, which in turn influences the expression of cystathionine beta-synthase. We predict that IMPA1 inhibition will decrease homocysteine levels in cells from patients with Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, if IMPA1 inhibition has no effect on homocysteine levels, our hypothesis will be refuted. This proposed mechanism is grounded in the known biochemical links between inositol phosphate metabolism, calcium signaling, and enzyme regulation.

We hypothesize that RETSAT, an acyl-CoA thioesterase, plays a crucial role in the development of Encephalopathy, porphyria-related, by regulating the accumulation of toxic heme intermediates. Specifically, RETSAT's dysregulation leads to an imbalance in the acyl-CoA pool, disrupting the normal functioning of the heme biosynthetic pathway. This disruption causes an accumulation of neurotoxic porphyrin precursors, such as delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG), which are known to contribute to the pathogenesis of porphyria-related encephalopathy. We predict that RETSAT overexpression will reduce ALA and PBG levels, confirming our hypothesis, while its knockdown will increase these toxic intermediates, refuting it.

We hypothesize that AKR1C8, an aldo-keto reductase, contributes to Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 2 by modulating the metabolism of prostaglandin J2, a regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. Specifically, AKR1C8's reduced activity leads to decreased conversion of prostaglandin J2 to its inactive form, resulting in increased prostaglandin J2 levels, which in turn inhibit the expression of mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), essential for mitochondrial DNA replication. We predict that overexpressing AKR1C8 in cells from Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 2 patients will increase TFAM expression and mitochondrial DNA content, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, inhibiting AKR1C8 will exacerbate mitochondrial DNA depletion, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanism is grounded in known biochemistry of aldo-keto reductases and prostaglandin J2's role in mitochondrial biogenesis.

We hypothesize that dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH, enzyme ID: 107987478) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of Retinitis pigmentosa 73 (RP73). Specifically, we propose that DHODH's involvement in pyrimidine biosynthesis leads to an imbalance in nucleotide pools, affecting the expression of the PRPF31 gene, which is mutated in RP73. This imbalance disrupts the assembly of the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP complex, essential for pre-mRNA splicing. We predict that DHODH inhibition will reduce RP73-associated splicing defects, confirmed by improved splicing patterns in patient-derived cells. Conversely, DHODH overexpression will exacerbate splicing defects, refuting our hypothesis. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of pyrimidine metabolism and its impact on RNA processing.

terminal_shown: Hyperornithinemia with gyrate atrophy of choroid and retina
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CYP2W1, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, plays a crucial role in the metabolism of ornithine in the retina, thereby influencing the development of Hyperornithinemia with gyrate atrophy of choroid and retina. Specifically, we propose that CYP2W1 catalyzes the conversion of ornithine to a downstream metabolite, which in turn regulates the expression of the OAT gene, mutated in this disease. We predict that overexpression of CYP2W1 in retinal cells will decrease ornithine levels and alleviate disease symptoms, whereas its inhibition will exacerbate them. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be provided by experimental evidence showing reduced ornithine levels and improved retinal function in CYP2W1-overexpressing cells, while refutation would be indicated by unchanged or worsened disease outcomes.

We hypothesize that ATP6V1FP2, a V-ATPase assembly factor, plays a crucial role in maintaining proper acid-base balance in the renal tubules by regulating V-ATPase activity. In Renal tubular dysgenesis, mutations in ATP6V1FP2 lead to impaired V-ATPase assembly, resulting in defective proton secretion and subsequent tubular dysfunction. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of ATP6V1FP2 in renal tubular cells will decrease V-ATPase activity, leading to increased intracellular pH and reduced ammoniagenesis. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by a significant decrease in V-ATPase activity and ammonium production in ATP6V1FP2-knockdown cells. Refutation would be shown by unchanged V-ATPase activity and ammonium production, indicating an alternative mechanism underlying Renal tubular dysgenesis.

We hypothesize that PLA2G4B, a phospholipase A2 enzyme, contributes to Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 2 by disrupting mitochondrial membrane phospholipid homeostasis. Specifically, PLA2G4B's excessive activity leads to an imbalance in cardiolipin and other phospholipids, impairing mitochondrial DNA replication and maintenance. This prediction can be confirmed by observing decreased mitochondrial DNA copy numbers in cells overexpressing PLA2G4B, and refuted by showing no effect on mitochondrial DNA levels in PLA2G4B-knockout cells. This hypothesis is grounded in the known role of phospholipids in mitochondrial function and the established link between mitochondrial membrane dysfunction and DNA depletion syndromes.

We hypothesize that NAT2 (N-acetyltransferase 2) plays a role in the pathogenesis of Fumarase deficiency by modulating the acetylation status of key proteins involved in the citric acid cycle, including Fumarase. Specifically, we propose that NAT2-mediated acetylation of Fumarase alters its enzymatic activity, leading to impaired fumarate metabolism. We predict that increased NAT2 activity will exacerbate Fumarase deficiency by reducing Fumarase activity, resulting in elevated fumarate levels. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by experimental results showing that NAT2 inhibition reduces fumarate accumulation in Fumarase-deficient cells. Refutation would be evidenced by unchanged fumarate levels following NAT2 inhibition.

We hypothesize that A4GALT, an enzyme involved in glycosphingolipid biosynthesis, contributes to the development of Cataract 38 through aberrant glycosylation of lens proteins. Specifically, A4GALT's activity leads to altered expression of glycosylated crystallins, disrupting lens fiber cell architecture and transparency. We predict that increased A4GALT expression in lens epithelial cells will correlate with Cataract 38 onset, whereas A4GALT inhibition will reduce cataract formation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be demonstrated by elevated A4GALT activity and crystallin glycosylation in Cataract 38 patient lens tissues, while refutation would be shown by unchanged A4GALT expression and crystallin glycosylation patterns in Cataract 38 patients compared to controls.

We hypothesize that HRAS, a small GTPase, plays a crucial role in the development of Tyrosinemia 3 by regulating the expression of the tyrosine aminotransferase (TAT) enzyme. Specifically, activated HRAS stimulates the MAPK/ERK pathway, leading to increased TAT expression and subsequent tyrosine degradation. We predict that HRAS inhibition will decrease TAT activity and alleviate Tyrosinemia 3 symptoms. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be observed through reduced TAT enzyme activity and decreased tyrosine levels in cells treated with HRAS inhibitors. Refutation would occur if HRAS inhibition has no effect on TAT activity or tyrosine levels, indicating an alternative mechanistic pathway. This hypothesis is grounded in known biochemistry, as HRAS is involved in various cellular signaling pathways, including those regulating enzyme expression.

We hypothesize that the enzyme Aminolevulinate Dehydratase (ALAD) plays a crucial role in the development of Hemochromatosis 5 by regulating iron metabolism through the heme biosynthesis pathway. Specifically, ALAD's activity affects the production of heme, which in turn influences the expression of hepcidin, a key regulator of iron homeostasis. We predict that decreased ALAD activity will lead to increased iron accumulation in the liver, characteristic of Hemochromatosis 5. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating a significant correlation between ALAD activity and hepcidin expression in liver tissues of Hemochromatosis 5 patients. Refutation would occur if ALAD activity is found to be unchanged in these patients, or if hepcidin expression is not affected by ALAD activity.

terminal_shown: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young 8 with exocrine dysfunction
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that B3GALT2, a glycosyltransferase enzyme, plays a crucial role in the development of Maturity-onset diabetes of the young 8 (MODY8) with exocrine dysfunction. Specifically, we propose that B3GALT2-mediated glycosylation of pancreatic transcription factors regulates their activity, impacting insulin and digestive enzyme production. We predict that reduced B3GALT2 activity will lead to impaired glycosylation, resulting in decreased insulin and digestive enzyme secretion, characteristic of MODY8 with exocrine dysfunction. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by demonstrating decreased B3GALT2 activity and altered glycosylation patterns in MODY8 patient samples. Refutation would occur if B3GALT2 knockdown or inhibition in pancreatic cells does not affect insulin or digestive enzyme production.

We hypothesize that FKRP (fukutin-related protein) plays a crucial role in the development of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 50 (DEE50) through its involvement in the O-glycosylation of neuronal proteins. Specifically, FKRP's phosphotransferase activity is essential for the proper glycosylation of ion channels and receptors, which is critical for maintaining neuronal homeostasis. Disruption of FKRP function leads to aberrant glycosylation, causing altered neuronal excitability and ultimately contributing to the development of DEE50. We predict that FKRP knockdown in neuronal cells will result in decreased glycosylation of target proteins and increased neuronal excitability, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, rescue of FKRP function will restore normal glycosylation patterns and neuronal activity, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed.

We hypothesize that CDS1 (CDP-diacylglycerol--inositol 3-phosphatidyltransferase), an enzyme involved in phosphatidylinositol biosynthesis, plays a crucial role in the development of Alopecia universalis congenita. We propose that CDS1 regulates the phosphatidylinositol signaling pathway, essential for hair follicle development and maintenance. Specifically, we predict that reduced CDS1 activity will lead to impaired phosphatidylinositol signaling, resulting in hair follicle abnormalities characteristic of Alopecia universalis congenita. Confirmation of this hypothesis would be obtained by showing that CDS1 knockout or inhibition in a mouse model leads to congenital alopecia, while refutation would be demonstrated by normal hair follicle development in CDS1-deficient mice. This hypothesis is grounded in the known role of phosphatidylinositol signaling in cellular development and differentiation.

We hypothesize that ASAH1 (acid ceramidase) plays a crucial role in the development of Congenital disorder of glycosylation 1Q (CDG-1Q) through its impact on sphingolipid metabolism and subsequent effects on protein glycosylation. Specifically, ASAH1's dysregulation leads to altered ceramide levels, disrupting the function of glycosyltransferases involved in glycoprotein synthesis. We predict that ASAH1 overexpression will rescue glycosylation defects in CDG-1Q patient cells, confirming this hypothesis. Conversely, ASAH1 inhibition will exacerbate glycosylation defects, refuting it. This hypothesis is grounded in the known biochemistry of sphingolipid metabolism and its intersection with glycoprotein synthesis, providing a testable mechanistic connection between ASAH1 and CDG-1Q.

We hypothesize that monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) contributes to the development of Anemia, congenital, non-spherocytic hemolytic, 3 by regulating the degradation of polyamines, which are essential for erythrocyte maturation. Specifically, MAOA's metabolic byproducts may alter the activity of key enzymes involved in heme synthesis, leading to impaired hemoglobin production. We predict that inhibition of MAOA will increase polyamine levels, enhancing erythrocyte maturation and reducing hemolysis in patients with this anemia. Confirmation would come from observing increased erythrocyte counts and reduced reticulocyte counts in response to MAOA inhibition. Refutation would occur if MAOA inhibition fails to improve erythrocyte parameters or if polyamine levels are unaffected by MAOA activity.

We hypothesize that ACADM (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase medium chain) is mechanistically connected to Visceral neuropathy, familial, 1, autosomal recessive, through impaired fatty acid oxidation in enteric neurons. Specifically, ACADM deficiency leads to accumulation of toxic medium-chain acyl-CoA intermediates, causing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in enteric neurons. This results in neuronal damage and degeneration, contributing to the development of visceral neuropathy. We predict that enteric neurons from patients with ACADM deficiency will exhibit increased oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, which can be confirmed by measuring elevated levels of 4-HNE and decreased mitochondrial membrane potential. Refutation would come from finding no difference in oxidative stress or mitochondrial function between patient and control enteric neurons.

We hypothesize that ATP6V1H, a regulatory subunit of the V-ATPase complex, plays a crucial role in maintaining proper pH homeostasis in vascular smooth muscle cells, thereby preventing arterial calcification. Specifically, ATP6V1H regulates V-ATPase activity, which is necessary for acidifying the golgi apparatus and preventing excessive mineralization. In Arterial calcification of infancy, generalized, 2, mutations in ATP6V1H lead to impaired V-ATPase function, resulting in increased golgi pH and subsequent calcification. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of ATP6V1H in vascular smooth muscle cells will increase calcification markers, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, overexpression of ATP6V1H will reduce calcification, refuting our hypothesis if no effect is observed.

We hypothesize that GNPNAT1, a glucosamine-phosphate N-acetyltransferase, contributes to the development of Essential hypertension through its role in regulating the hexosamine biosynthesis pathway (HBP). Specifically, GNPNAT1's activity leads to increased production of O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modified proteins, which in turn enhance the expression of the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) in the kidney. This results in increased sodium reabsorption, contributing to blood pressure elevation. We predict that GNPNAT1 inhibition will decrease SGLT2 expression and lower blood pressure in hypertensive models. Confirmation would come from observing decreased blood pressure in GNPNAT1 knockout mice or upon treatment with a GNPNAT1 inhibitor, while refutation would result from unchanged blood pressure in response to GNPNAT1 modulation.

We hypothesize that 3-ketodihydrosphingosine reductase (KDSR) plays a crucial role in the development of Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 35 (COXPD35) by regulating the biosynthesis of sphingolipids, which are essential for mitochondrial membrane integrity. Impaired KDSR activity leads to altered sphingolipid composition, disrupting mitochondrial function and contributing to COXPD35. We predict that KDSR knockdown in cellular models will result in decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased oxidative stress, confirming our hypothesis. Conversely, KDSR overexpression will rescue mitochondrial function, refuting our hypothesis if no improvement is observed. This mechanistic connection is grounded in the known biochemistry of sphingolipid metabolism and its impact on mitochondrial function.
